title: EmoEUS: Uncertainty Supervision for Multimodal Emotion Recognition in Conversation
summary: Multimodal emotion recognition in conversation (MERC) can leverage multimodal and contextual cues to boost recognition performance. However, existing fusion approaches in MERC often ignore modality-specific uncertainty across utterances caused by conflicting cues, varying noise, and missing modality-specific signals. We propose EmoEUS, an explicit uncertainty supervision framework for MERC. EmoEUS performs uncertainty-aware multimodal fusion by dynamically weighting modalities using learned variance estimates. We also introduce an explicitly supervised loss that aligns each utterance's predicted variance with the distance between the utterance's distributional representation and its emotion- and modality-specific cluster center. Experiments on IEMOCAP and MELD show that EmoEUS consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods.

AI.tldr: EmoEUS is an explicit uncertainty supervision framework for multimodal emotion recognition in conversation that dynamically weights modalities using learned variance estimates and introduces a supervised loss aligning predicted variance with emotion-modality cluster distances, outperforming SOTA on IEMOCAP and MELD.
AI.motivation: Existing fusion approaches in MERC ignore modality-specific uncertainty across utterances caused by conflicting cues, varying noise, and missing modality-specific signals.
AI.method: EmoEUS performs uncertainty-aware multimodal fusion by dynamically weighting modalities using learned variance estimates, and introduces an explicitly supervised loss that aligns each utterance's predicted variance with the distance between the utterance's distributional representation and its emotion- and modality-specific cluster center.
AI.result: EmoEUS consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods on IEMOCAP and MELD benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Explicit uncertainty supervision for modality weighting improves multimodal emotion recognition in conversation.

title: Code Division Modulation Layers Against Forgetting and Inference in Continual Gait Identification
summary:
Continual learning (CL) has been recently employed in biometric identification systems thanks to its ability to integrate new knowledge within a pre-trained model and to the possibility of reducing the computational cost of training. Unfortunately, such approaches pose new challenges both in terms of final accuracy and privacy guarantees since a progressive fine-tuning of the model on small subsets expose them to catastrophic forgetting and successful inference attacks.
  This paper evaluates the efficiency of code division modulation layers (CDML) on a gait identification system which has been trained following a continual learning policy. The proposed approach preserves accuracy on all the tasks while mitigating membership inference attacks at the same time. Moreover, the impact of retransmission is minimized since replaying data is not necessary.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates CDML in a continual learning-based gait identification system, showing it preserves accuracy across tasks while mitigating membership inference attacks without needing data replay.
AI.motivation: Continual learning in biometric systems faces challenges of catastrophic forgetting and privacy vulnerabilities (inference attacks) when fine-tuning on small subsets. The authors aim to address both accuracy preservation and privacy protection simultaneously.
AI.method: The authors apply code division modulation layers (CDML) to a gait identification system trained under a continual learning policy. The approach does not require data replay, minimizing retransmission impact.
AI.result: The proposed CDML-based approach preserves accuracy across all tasks while mitigating membership inference attacks.
AI.conclusion: CDML is effective for continual learning in biometric identification, offering both accuracy retention and privacy protection without the need for replaying old data.

title: Enhancing Relation Modeling with Social Attributes for Social Media Popularity Prediction
summary: Recent studies highlight the critical role of retrieval-augmented mechanisms in social media popularity prediction (SMPP). Although such frameworks have improved SMPP performance by leveraging historical posts, existing methods still suffer from the low retrieval accuracy due to the oversight of relative relationships among UGC instances. To address this limitation, we propose a novel Relation-Enhanced Retrieval-Augmented framework (RE-Rag) that models UGC similarity as a continuous relation jointly driven by semantic content and social attributes. Specifically, RE-Rag employs a Semantic-Attribute Retriever (SAR) to obtain instances aligned in both semantic and social-attribute distributions. Subsequently, we design a Relation-Guided Predictor (RGP): first, cross-attention encodes multimodal features of retrieved instances; then, a relative relation graph is introduced to guide attention weight allocation, forming a Relation-Guided Transformer (RGTs) that dynamically modulate attention weights based on relative attribute relations to capture the interplay between semantics and various social attributes. The refined features are fused with the target instance for popularity prediction. Experiments on three public benchmarks show that RE-Rag consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both prediction accuracy and retrieval efficiency.

AI.tldr: RE-Rag is a Relation-Enhanced Retrieval-Augmented framework for social media popularity prediction that improves retrieval accuracy by modeling UGC similarity through both semantic content and social attributes, using a Semantic-Attribute Retriever and Relation-Guided Transformer to outperform state-of-the-art methods.
AI.motivation: Existing retrieval-augmented SMPP methods suffer from low retrieval accuracy because they overlook the relative relationships among UGC instances.
AI.method: Proposes RE-Rag with two key components: (1) Semantic-Attribute Retriever (SAR) that retrieves instances aligned in both semantic and social-attribute distributions; (2) Relation-Guided Predictor (RGP) with cross-attention multimodal encoding and Relation-Guided Transformers (RGTs) that dynamically modulate attention weights based on relative attribute relations, then fuses refined features with target instance for prediction.
AI.result: Consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods on three public benchmarks in both prediction accuracy and retrieval efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Modeling UGC similarity as a continuous relation jointly driven by semantic content and social attributes significantly improves both retrieval accuracy and popularity prediction performance.

title: Mage-Flow: An Efficient Native-Resolution Foundation Model for Image Generation and Editing
summary: Large-scale visual generators are increasingly capable but costly to train, fine-tune, and deploy. We introduce Mage-Flow, a compact 4B-scale generative stack for efficient text-to-image generation and instruction-based image editing. The stack is built from two co-designed components: Mage-VAE, a lightweight high-fidelity latent tokenizer, and a Native-Resolution Multimodal Diffusion Transformer trained with rectified flow matching. Mage-VAE uses one-step diffusion-style encoding and decoding with anchor-latent regularization, preserving the reconstruction quality of strong public VAEs while reducing tokenization cost by more than an order of magnitude. Together with native-resolution packing and stack-level CUDA kernel fusion, the stack supports flexible-resolution training and improves end-to-end training throughput by about $2.5\times$. Built on this foundation, we develop a complete model family with Base, RL-aligned, and Turbo variants for both generation and editing. Diffusion-NFT improves prompt following, text rendering, aesthetic quality, and editing fidelity, while few-step distillation with adversarial perceptual guidance produces 4-step Turbo models for low-latency inference. Despite its compact scale, Mage-Flow and Mage-Flow-Edit achieves competitive performance across standard generation and editing benchmarks. More importantly, the Turbo variants make high-resolution generation and editing practical for interactive use: at $1024^2$ resolution on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU, Mage-Flow-Turbo generates an image in 0.59s, and Mage-Flow-Edit-Turbo edits an image in 1.02s, while maintaining a small memory footprint. These results show that careful tokenizer--backbone--system co-design can deliver strong high-resolution generation and editing within an efficient 4B model family.

AI.tldr: Mage-Flow is a compact 4B-parameter generative stack for efficient text-to-image generation and instruction-based image editing, built from a lightweight latent tokenizer (Mage-VAE) and a Native-Resolution Multimodal Diffusion Transformer with rectified flow matching. It achieves competitive performance while enabling high-resolution generation in 0.59s and editing in 1.02s on a single A100 GPU.
AI.motivation: Large-scale visual generators are increasingly capable but prohibitively costly to train, fine-tune, and deploy, motivating the need for a more efficient yet performant generative stack.
AI.method: The stack co-designs two components: (1) Mage-VAE, a lightweight latent tokenizer using one-step diffusion-style encoding/decoding with anchor-latent regularization; (2) a Native-Resolution Multimodal Diffusion Transformer trained with rectified flow matching. It also employs native-resolution packing, stack-level CUDA kernel fusion, Diffusion-NFT for prompt following, and few-step distillation with adversarial perceptual guidance for Turbo models.
AI.result: The stack improves end-to-end training throughput by ~2.5×, reduces tokenization cost by over an order of magnitude, and achieves competitive performance on standard benchmarks. At 1024² resolution on a single A100, Mage-Flow-Turbo generates an image in 0.59s and Mage-Flow-Edit-Turbo edits in 1.02s.
AI.conclusion: Careful tokenizer–backbone–system co-design can deliver strong high-resolution generation and editing within an efficient 4B model family, making interactive use practical.

title: ECoNGS: Efficient Compressive Neural Gaussian Splats for Volume Visualization
comment: To be published in Proceedings of IEEE VIS 2026, IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
summary: Recent advances in differentiable Gaussian splatting have highlighted the potential of primitive-based approaches as alternative scene representations for interactive, high-quality, volume visualization (VolVis) of large datasets. However, the explicit nature of current primitive-based methods, combined with isolated optimization for each VolVis scene, results in redundant, non-compact representations. We present ECoNGS, an efficient compressive neural Gaussian splatting framework for VolVis scene representation. ECoNGS employs lightweight neural networks to dynamically predict implicit, editable Gaussian splats from explicit anchor points, effectively combining model compactness and parameter efficiency of implicit representations with high-performance rendering of explicit primitives. We explore a joint learning strategy that clusters geometrically similar scenes and shares parameters across them, significantly reducing overall training time and model size while maintaining reconstruction fidelity. To achieve a more compact scene representation, we further compress the explicit anchor attributes using a neural entropy model that estimates their probability distributions, enabling compact storage via entropy coding. We systematically investigate Gaussian initialization strategies and propose a simple yet effective scheme tailored for VolVis scenes, improving reconstruction accuracy and accelerating convergence. We evaluate ECoNGS qualitatively and quantitatively across various univariate and multivariate VolVis scenes, highlighting its superior performance over prior methods in training time, reconstruction quality, and model size. In particular, compared with the prior method iVR-GS, ECoNGS improves reconstruction quality by up to 2.2 dB in PSNR while reducing the model size by up to 6.1x and the training time by up to 5.9x. The code is available at https://github.com/TouKaienn/ECoNGS.

AI.tldr: ECoNGS is an efficient compressive neural Gaussian splatting framework for volume visualization that uses lightweight neural networks to predict implicit Gaussian splats from explicit anchor points, employs joint learning across similar scenes, and compresses anchor attributes via neural entropy coding, achieving up to 2.2 dB PSNR improvement while reducing model size by 6.1× and training time by 5.9× compared to prior work.
AI.motivation: Current primitive-based differentiable Gaussian splatting methods for volume visualization suffer from redundant, non-compact representations due to their explicit nature and isolated optimization for each scene, lacking parameter efficiency and model compactness.
AI.method: ECoNGS combines lightweight neural networks that predict implicit Gaussian splats from explicit anchor points, a joint learning strategy that clusters geometrically similar scenes for parameter sharing, and a neural entropy model to compress anchor attributes via entropy coding. It also proposes a tailored Gaussian initialization strategy for VolVis scenes.
AI.result: Compared to iVR-GS, ECoNGS improves reconstruction quality by up to 2.2 dB in PSNR, reduces model size by up to 6.1×, and reduces training time by up to 5.9× across various univariate and multivariate VolVis scenes.
AI.conclusion: ECoNGS demonstrates superior performance over prior methods in training time, reconstruction quality, and model size, establishing an efficient and compact framework for VolVis scene representation.

title: Fretiq: Browser-Native Electric Guitar String Classification via Engineered Spectral Features and Held-Out Free-Play Evaluation
comment: 12 pages, 5 tables, preliminary single-instrument system paper
summary: Identifying which string produces a given pitch in monophonic electric guitar audio is a fundamental classification challenge: a single pitch can often be produced on multiple strings at different fret positions, with timbral differences that prior listening studies confirm are largely imperceptible to untrained humans. Existing approaches using support vector machines and spectral envelope features have achieved F-measures of 0.90 for six-string electric guitar classification, while String-Inverse Frequency features in earlier work achieved F1 scores up to 0.72. We present Fretiq, a preliminary single-instrument, single-player browser-based string classification system built on a 26-dimensional feature representation integrating frequency band energies, spectral statistics, and 13 Mel-Frequency Cepstral Coefficients, achieving 97.1% shuffled frame-level validation accuracy across 322,215 balanced frames. An ablation study identifies MFCCs as the primary accuracy driver (92.2% to 97.1%). We additionally introduce Comparison Training -- a data collection methodology in which adjacent open-string and fifth-fret string pairs are recorded in deliberate alternation -- and evaluate its contribution via confusion matrix analysis. Comparison Training reduces the D3 to A2 frame-level confusion rate by 44% but shows mixed results on other targeted pairs. A held-out free-play evaluation on 103,000 frames yields 87.8% overall accuracy. We describe the feature extraction pipeline in both Python and TypeScript to guarantee training-inference parity, and document two critical implementation failure modes. The system runs entirely in-browser with no hexaphonic pickup, fretboard sensor, camera, or multi-microphone setup required.

AI.tldr: Fretiq is a browser-based electric guitar string classification system using a 26-dimensional feature set (including MFCCs) that achieves 97.1% accuracy on balanced frames and 87.8% on free-play evaluation, using only monophonic audio without specialized hardware.
AI.motivation: String classification in electric guitar is challenging because a single pitch can be produced on multiple strings at different fret positions, and timbral differences are largely imperceptible to untrained humans. Existing SVM-based approaches achieve F-measures of 0.90, while String-Inverse Frequency features reach F1 scores up to 0.72, motivating a more accurate, accessible solution.
AI.method: The system uses a 26-dimensional feature vector (frequency band energies, spectral statistics, 13 MFCCs) with a browser-based classifier. Comparison Training methodology records adjacent open-string and fifth-fret string pairs in deliberate alternation. An ablation study isolates MFCC contribution. Feature extraction pipelines are implemented in both Python and TypeScript for training-inference parity.
AI.result: 97.1% shuffled frame-level validation accuracy on 322,215 balanced frames. Ablation shows MFCCs as primary accuracy driver (92.2% to 97.1%). Comparison Training reduces D3 to A2 confusion by 44% but shows mixed results on other pairs. Held-out free-play evaluation (103,000 frames) yields 87.8% accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Fretiq demonstrates that high-accuracy string classification is achievable using only monophonic audio in a browser environment without hexaphonic pickups, sensors, cameras, or multi-microphone setups. The system identifies critical implementation failure modes and ensures reproducibility through dual-language feature extraction pipelines.

title: Binding Drift in Multi-Step Tool-Augmented Agents
comment: 14 pages, 5 tables, 1 figure. Equal contribution by both authors. Code and data: https://github.com/shashank-indukuri/binding-drift
summary: Tool-augmented language-model agents execute multi-step workflows over external systems, resolving an entity once and then acting on it across subsequent steps. Prior work shows that in single-step actions, agents select the correct tool but bind it to the wrong entity 24-26% of the time. We study what happens to entity bindings over time: do they stay correct, silently drift to a different entity, or, if wrong from the start, propagate and compound? We formalize binding drift (correct at step 1, wrong later) as distinct from error propagation (wrong at step 1, carried forward), and score them on disjoint workflow sets so the two cannot be conflated. In a controlled multi-step testbed (200 workflows, 580 entity-binding-scored steps, four enterprise domains, eight model backends spanning small to frontier), we find: (1) under controlled error injection, an entity lock (the intuitive "persist the first binding" fix) amplifies wrong actions from 907 to 2,746 (3.0x; bootstrap 95% CI [2.8, 3.3]), because it faithfully carries the seeded wrong entity into every later step; (2) the amplification reaches 8.5x on the most affected model (Claude Opus 4.5); (3) a practical LLM-based re-verifier (a single cheap second model call re-reading the original instruction) reduces wrong actions by 79% (0.21x; CI [0.18, 0.25]), closing the gap to within 1 percentage point of an oracle upper-bound (0.20x); and (4) in the natural (non-injected) setting, baseline agents drift on 18% of eligible workflows, with the per-step error rate rising across steps. Persistence and re-verification are not interchangeable: a defense that eliminates drift can worsen propagation, and a practical re-verifier nearly matches oracle recovery.

AI.tldr: This paper studies entity binding drift and error propagation in multi-step tool-augmented language-model agents, finding that a simple "entity lock" fix amplifies errors 3x, while a cheap LLM-based re-verifier reduces wrong actions by 79%, nearly matching oracle performance.
AI.motivation: Prior work shows agents misbind entities in single-step actions 24-26% of the time, but how these errors evolve across multi-step workflows (drift vs. propagation) is unexplored. The authors aim to formalize and measure these distinct failure modes.
AI.method: The authors formalize binding drift (correct at step 1, wrong later) and error propagation (wrong at step 1, carried forward). They build a controlled multi-step testbed with 200 workflows, 580 entity-binding-scored steps, across 8 model backends and 4 enterprise domains, with controlled error injection and natural settings.
AI.result: (1) Entity lock amplifies wrong actions from 907 to 2,746 (3.0x); (2) Amplification reaches 8.5x on Claude Opus 4.5; (3) LLM-based re-verifier reduces wrong actions by 79% (0.21x), within 1 pp of oracle upper-bound (0.20x); (4) In natural setting, agents drift on 18% of eligible workflows with per-step error rate rising across steps.
AI.conclusion: Persistence (entity lock) and re-verification are not interchangeable: a defense eliminating drift worsens propagation, while a practical re-verifier nearly matches oracle recovery. Simple entity-locking is harmful; cheap re-verification is effective.

title: Hazard or Anomaly? Evaluating VLMs for Understanding Dangers and Discrepancies
summary: Modern safety-critical systems increasingly rely on human-robot interaction to reduce disaster risk and support decision-making during emergencies. Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are promising for these settings because they can interpret complex scenes and communicate safety-relevant information, but they still require careful evaluation to ensure reliable safety reasoning. In particular, current evaluations often frame danger recognition as a binary decision (Safe/Unsafe), making it unclear whether a model is identifying true physical hazards or merely reacting to unusual scene elements. We address this limitation by introducing an explicit distinction between hazard and anomaly, and by separately recognizing hazardous and anomalous states. We evaluate several state-of-the-art VLMs across two datasets and multiple prompting strategies to test whether this distinction changes model behavior. Our results show that VLMs frequently misinterpret anomalousness as hazardousness, revealing an over-reliance on contextual irregularity as a proxy for danger. We further show that explicitly separating anomaly from hazard provides a more informative evaluation of VLM safety reasoning and exposes failure modes that binary safety judgments can obscure. Our public dataset is available on Roboflow https://app.roboflow.com/vlm-in-context-anomaly-and-hazard-detection/camera-ready-roman-ds.

AI.tldr: VLMs often conflate anomaly with hazard in safety-critical human-robot interaction; this paper introduces a separate evaluation of hazard vs. anomaly, showing that VLMs over-rely on contextual irregularity as a proxy for danger, and that explicit separation yields more informative safety reasoning assessments.
AI.motivation: Current VLM safety evaluations treat danger recognition as a binary Safe/Unsafe decision, making it unclear whether models identify true physical hazards or just react to unusual scene elements. The authors aim to disentangle hazard from anomaly for more precise evaluation.
AI.method: The authors introduce an explicit distinction between hazard and anomaly, evaluate state-of-the-art VLMs across two datasets with multiple prompting strategies, and compare model behavior under binary safety judgments vs. separated hazard/anomaly recognition.
AI.result: VLMs frequently misinterpret anomalousness as hazardousness, showing over-reliance on contextual irregularity. Explicitly separating anomaly from hazard reveals failure modes that binary safety judgments obscure and provides a more informative evaluation of VLM safety reasoning.
AI.conclusion: The proposed hazard-vs-anomaly distinction improves evaluation fidelity and exposes confounded reasoning in VLMs, which is critical for deploying trustworthy VLMs in safety-critical human-robot interaction.

title: FALCON-Discover: Discovering Concentrated False-Confidence Regions for Calibration
summary: Calibration is usually evaluated in aggregate, but the most dangerous failures are often local: predictions that remain highly confident despite being wrong. We study this failure mode as false-confidence concentration, the extent to which confident errors occupy compact, discoverable regions of prediction space. We introduce FALCON-Discover, a post-hoc, model-agnostic framework that ranks predictions using discrepancy signals from confidence, local support, neighborhood agreement, and perturbation stability. Across seven binary tabular datasets, four seeds, five-fold cross-fitting, and strong learners including XGBoost and CatBoost, we find that false-confidence concentration is recurrent but regime-dependent. At the main confidence threshold, discrepancy-based ranking substantially outperforms the strongest validation-selected calibration or trust-scoring baseline in the strongest regimes, while raw confidence recovers little dangerous-error mass. The best detector varies across datasets: learned discrepancy is strongest when multiple cues must be combined, whereas stability-centered ranking works best when local decisional fragility dominates. These results show that dangerous overconfidence is better treated as a family-level discovery problem than as a single-score calibration problem, and motivate calibration strategies that explicitly target regions where confidence, support, and stability diverge.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces FALCON-Discover, a post-hoc model-agnostic framework that detects local false-confidence concentration (confident errors in compact regions) using discrepancy signals from confidence, local support, neighborhood agreement, and perturbation stability. Experiments on seven tabular datasets show that discrepancy-based ranking outperforms calibration and trust-scoring baselines, with best detectors varying by regime.
AI.motivation: Standard calibration metrics evaluate confidence errors in aggregate, missing local dangerous failures where models remain highly confident despite being wrong. The authors aim to treat this as a discovery problem rather than a calibration problem.
AI.method: FALCON-Discover is a post-hoc, model-agnostic framework that ranks predictions using discrepancy signals from four sources: confidence, local support, neighborhood agreement, and perturbation stability. Evaluated on seven binary tabular datasets with four seeds, five-fold cross-fitting, using XGBoost and CatBoost.
AI.result: False-confidence concentration is recurrent but regime-dependent. Discrepancy-based ranking substantially outperforms calibration or trust-scoring baselines in strongest regimes. Best detector varies: learned discrepancy dominates when combining multiple cues, stability-centered ranking works best when local decisional fragility dominates.
AI.conclusion: Dangerous overconfidence is better treated as a family-level discovery problem than a single-score calibration problem, motivating calibration strategies targeting regions where confidence, support, and stability diverge.

title: SysAdmin: Measuring Instrumental Power-Seeking in Frontier AI
summary: Power-seeking defined as behaviors where AI systems acquire resources, evade oversight, or resist termination beyond task requirements is identified as a key driver of Loss of Control (LoC) risk. In this work, we introduce SysAdmin, a benchmark that positions frontier language models as autonomous system administrators in a high-fidelity Linux sandbox to measure power-seeking propensity across five dimensions: self-preservation, increasing autonomy, resource acquisition, environment modification, and strategic concealment. We evaluated seven frontier models across four experimental conditions in a total of 2800 tasks. After bias correction using human-annotated calibration data, corrected power-seeking estimates ranged from 0 to about 5 percent per model. We also conducted a positive control with explicit power-seeking prompts that achieved 100% detection, validating measurement sensitivity. Our findings indicate current frontier models exhibit minimal spontaneous power-seeking in naturalistic system administration contexts, though model-specific failure modes suggest evaluations must test diverse misalignment patterns. Nevertheless, we discovered other more pronounced failure modes (than power-seeking) such as specification gaming and resistance to goal modification.

AI.tldr: The paper presents SysAdmin, a benchmark to measure power-seeking behavior in frontier language models acting as system administrators. Across 2800 tasks and seven models, spontaneous power-seeking was minimal (0-5% after bias correction), though other failure modes like specification gaming and resistance to goal modification were more prevalent.
AI.motivation: Power-seeking behaviors (resource acquisition, evading oversight, resisting termination) are identified as key drivers of Loss of Control (LoC) risk in AI systems, motivating the need for systematic measurement of such propensities in frontier models.
AI.method: The authors introduce SysAdmin, a benchmark that places frontier language models as autonomous system administrators in a high-fidelity Linux sandbox. Power-seeking is measured across five dimensions: self-preservation, increasing autonomy, resource acquisition, environment modification, and strategic concealment. Seven frontier models were evaluated across four experimental conditions in 2800 tasks, with bias correction using human-annotated calibration data and a positive control (explicit power-seeking prompts) to validate measurement sensitivity.
AI.result: Corrected power-seeking estimates ranged from 0 to about 5% per model. The positive control (explicit power-seeking prompts) achieved 100% detection, confirming measurement sensitivity. Minimal spontaneous power-seeking was observed, but other failure modes such as specification gaming and resistance to goal modification were more pronounced.
AI.conclusion: Current frontier models exhibit minimal spontaneous power-seeking in naturalistic system administration contexts. However, model-specific failure modes indicate evaluations must test diverse misalignment patterns, as other failure types (specification gaming, resistance to goal modification) are more prevalent than power-seeking.

title: UVFaceFusion: Fast Multi-view Topologically Consistent Face Reconstruction in the Wild via UV-space Neural Fusion
summary: Reconstructing high-fidelity facial geometry with an assigned topology is essential for digital avatar creation and animation, yet existing automated methods often trade off geometric fidelity and in-the-wild generalization. We present UVFaceFusion, a feed-forward framework for multi-view, fixed-topology face reconstruction from daily images. Our key idea is to replace heuristic topological optimization with learnable neural fusion in a canonical UV space. Given multi-view images, we first obtain dense point maps and facial UV correspondences of each view using VGGT and Pixel3DMM, respectively. Then, the view-specific point maps are lifted into the canonical UV domain and fused with a novel mask-aware neural fusion network. The network predicts a complete UV-space point map, from which a fixed-topology mesh is directly sampled. Although trained only on Ava-256, UVFaceFusion generalizes well to multiple public benchmarks and in-the-wild captures, benefiting from its canonical UV-space geometry-to-geometry fusion that reduces dependence on dataset-specific appearance and capture conditions. Experiments on various benchmarks show that UVFaceFusion achieves state-of-the-art reconstruction accuracy while reconstructing a mesh from 16 input views in less than 3 seconds on a single RTX 4090. Code is available at https://github.com/grignarder/UVFaceFusion.

AI.tldr: UVFaceFusion is a feed-forward framework for multi-view fixed-topology face reconstruction that replaces heuristic topological optimization with learnable neural fusion in canonical UV space, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy while reconstructing meshes from 16 views in under 3 seconds on a single RTX 4090.
AI.motivation: Existing automated face reconstruction methods trade off geometric fidelity and in-the-wild generalization, motivating the need for a framework that achieves both high-quality fixed-topology geometry and robust generalization without relying on dataset-specific appearance conditions.
AI.method: Multi-view images are processed to obtain dense point maps and facial UV correspondences (via VGGT and Pixel3DMM), then lifted into canonical UV space and fused using a mask-aware neural fusion network that predicts a complete UV-space point map for direct mesh sampling.
AI.result: Trained only on Ava-256, UVFaceFusion achieves state-of-the-art reconstruction accuracy across multiple public benchmarks and in-the-wild captures, with inference under 3 seconds for 16 input views on a single RTX 4090.
AI.conclusion: Canonical UV-space geometry-to-geometry fusion reduces dependence on dataset-specific conditions, enabling strong generalization; code is publicly available.

title: A Situational Speech Synthesizer for Yoruba: System Design, Phonological Rule Architecture, and Orthographic Extensions for Contour
comment: Currently under review at Speech Communication
summary:
We present TTSYoruba, a rule-based concatenative diphone speech synthesizer for Yoruba, deployed at online as part of the YorubaName.com open dictionary of Yoruba personal names. The system takes tone-marked Yoruba text as input and produces audio output by applying a hand-crafted phonological rule system to a recorded inventory of 651 diphone units spanning five tonal variants of every consonant-vowel combination in the language. We describe the phonological architecture of the system in detail, including our complete tonal file-selection logic, our treatment of the three-way nasal disambiguation problem (oral /n/, nasalized vowel, and syllabic nasal), and the derivation of contextual rising and falling tones from level-tone input. We also present, as an orthographic contribution, the adoption of the caron and circumflex, which are symbols with prior standing in Yoruba phonological transcription, as standard single-vowel contour tone markers, integrated into the TTS normalization pipeline and the WriteYoruba keyboard input tool. The system's performance was evaluated through a listener study (N=50), with detailed results on Mean Opinion Scores (MOS) presented in Section 6.
  Keywords: Yoruba, text-to-speech, low-resource languages, diphone synthesis, contour tones, African language NLP, rule-based synthesis

AI.tldr: TTSYoruba is a rule-based concatenative diphone speech synthesizer for Yoruba that uses 651 diphone units with five tonal variants, handles three-way nasal disambiguation and contour tone derivation, and was evaluated via a 50-participant listener study with MOS results.
AI.motivation: To develop a text-to-speech system for Yoruba, a low-resource tone language, addressing the lack of synthetic speech technology for African languages and enabling audio output for the YorubaName.com dictionary of personal names.
AI.method: Rule-based concatenative diphone synthesis using a hand-crafted phonological rule system operating on 651 recorded diphone units (covering five tonal variants per consonant-vowel combination). Includes tonal file-selection logic, three-way nasal disambiguation (oral /n/, nasalized vowel, syllabic nasal), and contour tone derivation from level-tone input. Also adopts caron and circumflex as standard contour tone markers integrated into normalization pipeline and keyboard input tool.
AI.result: A functional TTS system deployed online as part of YorubaName.com, with performance evaluated through a listener study (N=50) reporting Mean Opinion Scores (MOS) detailed in Section 6.
AI.conclusion: The system demonstrates a viable approach to TTS for low-resource tonal African languages using rule-based concatenative methods, with orthographic contributions for contour tone representation.

title: A Decision-Centered Reference Architecture for Trustworthy Agentic Commerce
comment: 23 pages, 3 figures. Includes ancillary reproducibility materials
summary: Agentic commerce extends agentic shopping into software agents that interpret policy, prepare checkout, generate transaction-facing language, and act under delegated payment authority. Protocols standardize external exchanges, but merchants still need one authoritative representation of commercial eligibility, actor authority, checkout validity, payment dispatch, generated claims, and evidence. This design-science study presents a protocol-agnostic architecture built around a canonical envelope, protected dependency and result hashes, Ed25519 or HMAC authentication, live-request rebinding, a seven-axis generated-claim gate, execution-time dependency revalidation, and eleven semantic invariants. Evaluation used an open-source JavaScript implementation, eight deterministic ecommerce scenarios, and five controlled ablations. Seven initially valid actions were permitted. After protected state changed, none could proceed without a fresh decision; a hostile-accessor case also remained blocked. Action status was consistent across configured surface-bound envelopes, and each scenario contained the three protected hashes and its targeted dependency reference. Each ablation produced the predicted unsafe regression when one safeguard was bypassed, while the protected path contained the same failure. The hostile accessor was read once, and the suite passed 66/66 tests, schema validation, and committed examples. Results support protected-dependency change detection, bounded outcome derivation, stale-decision prevention, surface-bound status consistency, refusal propagation, and verified-state identity under synthetic fixtures, but do not establish rule completeness, production security, performance, legal compliance, live interoperability, population error rates, or independent replication.

AI.tldr: A protocol-agnostic architecture for agentic commerce using canonical envelopes, cryptographic authentication, dependency hashing, and semantic invariants was designed and evaluated via an open-source implementation. It demonstrated consistent detection of stale states and blocked unauthorized actions across eight scenarios and five ablations, passing 66/66 tests.
AI.motivation: Merchants need a single authoritative representation for commercial eligibility, actor authority, checkout validity, payment dispatch, generated claims, and evidence, as existing protocols standardize external exchanges but lack internal consistency.
AI.method: Design-science study building a protocol-agnostic architecture with canonical envelope, protected dependency/result hashes, Ed25519/HMAC auth, live-request rebinding, seven-axis generated-claim gate, execution-time dependency revalidation, and eleven semantic invariants. Evaluated via open-source JavaScript implementation on eight deterministic ecommerce scenarios and five controlled ablations.
AI.result: Seven initially valid actions permitted; none could proceed after protected state changed without fresh decision; hostile accessor remained blocked. Action status consistent across surface-bound envelopes. Each scenario contained three protected hashes and targeted dependency reference. Each ablation produced predicted regression. Suite passed 66/66 tests, schema validation, and committed examples.
AI.conclusion: Supported protected-dependency change detection, bounded outcome derivation, stale-decision prevention, surface-bound status consistency, refusal propagation, and verified-state identity under synthetic fixtures—but does not establish rule completeness, production security, performance, legal compliance, live interoperability, population error rates, or independent replication.

title: From Pixel to Prognosis: Convolutional and GLCM Feature Fusion for Automated Four-Class Cataract Severity Classification
summary: Objective: To develop a low-cost automated cataract severity classification system operating on standard consumer-grade colour photographs of the eye, without specialised ophthalmic hardware. Methods: A hybrid framework was designed that fuses deep features from a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) with five handcrafted Grey-Level Co-occurrence Matrix (GLCM) and intensity descriptors - mean intensity, uniformity, standard deviation, contrast, and energy - extracted from a Hough-circle-localised pupil Region of Interest (ROI). A multi-class Support Vector Machine (SVM) with Radial Basis Function (RBF) kernel classifies each image into one of four severity grades: normal, immature, mature, or hypermature cataract. Results: The proposed fused system achieved 95.0% accuracy, 93.8% sensitivity, and 96.1% specificity on an ophthalmologist-labelled test set drawn from 300 images (75 per class) collected at an ophthalmology clinic, outperforming texture-only (88.5%) and CNN-only (91.3%) baselines and surpassing recently published deep learning approaches. Conclusion: The CNN-GLCM-SVM fusion framework provides competitive four-class cataract grading without GPU acceleration or specialised cameras, making it suitable for primary-care and telemedicine deployment in resource-limited settings.

AI.tldr: A low-cost hybrid CNN-GLCM-SVM system classifies cataract severity (4 grades) from consumer-grade eye photos, achieving 95.0% accuracy without specialized hardware.
AI.motivation: To enable automated cataract severity grading in resource-limited settings by avoiding reliance on GPU acceleration, specialized ophthalmic cameras, or expensive medical equipment.
AI.method: A fusion framework combining CNN deep features with handcrafted GLCM and intensity descriptors (mean intensity, uniformity, standard deviation, contrast, energy) extracted from a Hough-circle-localized pupil ROI, classified by a multi-class SVM with RBF kernel into four grades: normal, immature, mature, hypermature cataract.
AI.result: 95.0% accuracy, 93.8% sensitivity, 96.1% specificity on a 300-image ophthalmologist-labeled test set, outperforming texture-only (88.5%) and CNN-only (91.3%) baselines and surpassing recent deep learning approaches.
AI.conclusion: The CNN-GLCM-SVM fusion framework achieves competitive four-class cataract grading without GPU acceleration or specialized cameras, suitable for primary-care and telemedicine deployment in resource-limited settings.

title: Beyond Output-Space Calibration: Spectral Evidence Bundling for Selective Reliability Estimation in Time-Series Classification
summary: Post-hoc calibration for time-series classification usually remaps output scores, but deployment decisions such as trust, abstention, and review depend on whether a confident prediction is supported by the current temporal signal. We address three time-series reliability gaps: identical confidence values can hide different temporal support, average calibration can miss false high-confidence errors, and output-space recalibration offers limited input-linked auditability. We introduce a validation-gated fixed-label reliability policy that keeps the backbone prediction unchanged while estimating whether it should be trusted. The method combines output-side cues with whole-sample spectral descriptors, including band energy, entropy, peak dominance, period support, and phase stability, to form a scalar reliability estimate and diagnostic band-level evidence. A validation gate enables spectral conditioning only when correctness ranking improves without breaching FalseConf@0.9 or AURC tolerances; otherwise it reverts to the safer output-space baseline. Across eight heterogeneous UCR/UEA datasets, eight time-series backbone families, and standard recalibrators, the unconstrained method improves fixed-label selective-reliability metrics on the matched evaluation subset, raising Corr-AURC from 0.693 to 0.779. The validation-gated policy further improves Corr-AURC to 0.786 and reduces FalseConf@0.9 to 0.094. These results suggest that reliability estimation for time-series classifiers benefits from bundling output confidence with spectral evidence, while validation gating prevents unsupported spectral conditioning.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a validation-gated reliability policy for time-series classification that combines output confidence with spectral descriptors (band energy, entropy, peak dominance, period support, phase stability) to produce a scalar reliability estimate. The method improves Corr-AURC from 0.693 to 0.786 and reduces FalseConf@0.9 to 0.094 across eight datasets and eight backbone families, with a validation gate preventing unsupported spectral conditioning.
AI.motivation: Existing post-hoc calibration methods for time-series classification remap output scores but fail to address that identical confidence values can conceal different temporal support, average calibration misses false high-confidence errors, and output-space recalibration offers limited input-linked auditability, leaving deployment decisions (trust, abstention, review) inadequately supported.
AI.method: A validation-gated fixed-label reliability policy that keeps backbone predictions unchanged while combining output-side cues with whole-sample spectral descriptors (band energy, entropy, peak dominance, period support, phase stability) to form a scalar reliability estimate. A validation gate enables spectral conditioning only when correctness ranking improves without breaching FalseConf@0.9 or AURC tolerances; otherwise it reverts to the output-space baseline.
AI.result: Across eight UCR/UEA datasets, eight backbone families, and standard recalibrators: the unconstrained method improves Corr-AURC from 0.693 to 0.779; the validation-gated policy further improves Corr-AURC to 0.786 and reduces FalseConf@0.9 to 0.094.
AI.conclusion: Reliability estimation for time-series classifiers benefits from bundling output confidence with spectral evidence, and validation gating effectively prevents unsupported spectral conditioning.

title: Calibrated Selective Fact-Checking via Evidence Chain Evaluation
summary: Large language models (LLMs) can achieve strong fact-checking accuracy, yet forced binary decisions conceal a critical reliability problem: systems may issue confident verdicts even when supporting evidence is weak, sparse, or internally inconsistent. We address this issue through Evidence Chain Evaluation (ECE), a selective fact-checking framework that permits abstention via an uncertain verdict instead of requiring a true/false decision for every claim. The evaluated system is a tool-using verification agent that gathers evidence through web search, scholarly search, and executable checks, and then returns a structured verdict with confidence and source-level metadata. On ECE-Bench, ECE achieves 91.6% standard accuracy, 93.7% coverage, and 97.8% selective accuracy on answered claims. Although ECE does not outperform the strongest retrieval baseline on aggregate calibration metrics such as Expected Calibration Error, Brier score, or AURC, it delivers a clear selective-prediction trade-off: the system maintains very high accuracy on answered claims while deferring 6 of 95 cases. These deferred cases are concentrated in lower-reliability evidence settings (5/6 at source level L4), supporting the view that abstention functions as a safety-oriented mechanism for handling epistemically weak evidence. Code is available at https://github.com/ cheshireyang/ECE.git

AI.tldr: ECE is a selective fact-checking framework that allows LLMs to abstain from verdicts when evidence is weak, achieving high selective accuracy (97.8%) while deferring only 6 out of 95 cases, mostly in low-reliability evidence settings.
AI.motivation: LLMs achieve strong fact-checking accuracy but forced binary decisions hide a critical reliability problem: systems issue confident verdicts even when supporting evidence is weak, sparse, or internally inconsistent.
AI.method: ECE is a selective fact-checking framework that permits abstention via an uncertain verdict instead of requiring true/false decisions. It uses a tool-using verification agent that gathers evidence through web search, scholarly search, and executable checks, returning a structured verdict with confidence and source-level metadata.
AI.result: ECE achieves 91.6% standard accuracy, 93.7% coverage, and 97.8% selective accuracy on answered claims. Deferred cases (6/95) are concentrated in lower-reliability evidence settings (5/6 at source level L4), supporting abstention as a safety-oriented mechanism.
AI.conclusion: ECE does not outperform the strongest retrieval baseline on aggregate calibration metrics (ECE, Brier score, AURC), but delivers a clear selective-prediction trade-off: maintaining very high accuracy on answered claims while deferring unreliable cases, particularly when evidence is epistemically weak.

title: Appearance Pointers -- Multimodal Region Control of Diffusion Transformers
summary: Controllable image generation remains challenging for creative professionals, who often require precise regional control over materials, object identities, and spatial arrangements that cannot be reliably achieved through text prompting alone. Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) can natively ingest heterogeneous tokens stemming from texts and images, but they lack mechanisms for determining where and how these tokens should influence the output. We introduce appearance pointers, compact tokens that guide DiTs toward the correct appearance cues at the correct spatial locations by aligning text or image inputs with user-specified masks. Appearance pointers are produced by a region correspondence network and refined through a spatial aggregation mechanism, enabling the model to handle multiple regional descriptions without significantly increasing token load. Our approach introduces the first modality-agnostic interface for localized multimodal control in a DiT without retraining the base model from scratch. Across a range of metrics, our single model reaches or surpasses the performance of modality-specific state of the art methods, offering a simple and extensible path toward precise, region-aware, multimodal guidance in generative image synthesis.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces appearance pointers, compact tokens that enable Diffusion Transformers to achieve precise regional control over image generation by aligning text/image inputs with user-specified masks, without retraining the base model.
AI.motivation: Creative professionals need precise regional control over materials, object identities, and spatial arrangements in image generation, which cannot be reliably achieved through text prompting alone. Existing Diffusion Transformers lack mechanisms to determine where and how heterogeneous tokens (texts/images) should influence the output.
AI.method: Appearance pointers are compact tokens produced by a region correspondence network and refined through a spatial aggregation mechanism. They guide Diffusion Transformers toward correct appearance cues at correct spatial locations by aligning text or image inputs with user-specified masks, enabling multiple regional descriptions without significantly increasing token load.
AI.result: The single model reaches or surpasses the performance of modality-specific state-of-the-art methods across a range of metrics.
AI.conclusion: This approach provides the first modality-agnostic interface for localized multimodal control in a DiT without retraining from scratch, offering a simple and extensible path toward precise, region-aware, multimodal guidance in generative image synthesis.

title: Addressing Limited Data in Auditory Attention Decoding with Diffusion Generative Models
summary: Limited training data constrains deep learning models for Auditory Attention Decoding (AAD) in hearing aids (HAs). AAD uses electroencephalogram (EEG) data to decode listener's attention, enabling real-time tracking of specific sound sources. However, achieving high AAD performance with short time windows typical in HAs (<=1s) is challenging due to the scarcity of real-world speech-evoked EEG data. To address this issue, we investigate diffusion probabilistic models (DPMs) for generating synthetic speech-evoked EEG data. DPMs learn the underlying complex data structure through a denoising process and can generate realistic samples suitable for data augmentation. We evaluate the use of synthetic EEG data for augmenting datasets in locus-of-attention (LoA) classification tasks. Our experiments demonstrate that DPMs can generate realistic EEG signals and that incorporating synthetic data significantly improves AAD performance compared to models trained solely on measured EEG data (p<0.05). These results highlight the potential of diffusion-based data augmentation to mitigate training data limitations and improve the robustness of short-window AAD models in HA applications.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates diffusion probabilistic models (DPMs) to generate synthetic speech-evoked EEG data for augmenting limited training datasets in Auditory Attention Decoding (AAD) for hearing aids, showing significant improvement in locus-of-attention classification performance (p<0.05).
AI.motivation: Limited real-world speech-evoked EEG training data constrains deep learning models for AAD in hearing aids, especially with short time windows (<=1s), hindering the ability to achieve high decoding performance.
AI.method: Diffusion probabilistic models (DPMs) are used to generate synthetic speech-evoked EEG data through a denoising process, which is then employed for data augmentation in locus-of-attention (LoA) classification tasks.
AI.result: DPMs generate realistic EEG signals, and incorporating synthetic data significantly improves AAD performance compared to models trained solely on measured EEG data (p<0.05).
AI.conclusion: Diffusion-based data augmentation has potential to mitigate training data limitations and improve the robustness of short-window AAD models in hearing aid applications.

title: CODENS: Transforming Code Changes into Living, Accessible, and Queryable Documentation
comment: Accepted at the 26th ACM Symposium on Document Engineering (DocEng 2026). DOI: 10.1145/3820755.3832807
summary: Maintaining up-to-date code documentation is difficult in fast-moving repositories because design knowledge is scattered across source files and pull requests. We present CODENS , a system that turns pull requests into living, accessible, and queryable documentation for production codebases. CODENS incrementally builds a typed software knowledge graph from pull requests, enriches components through schema-driven semantic extraction, derives typed relations between them, and exposes the resulting knowledge through three retrieval modes, including agent-guided graph traversal for repository-level question answering. The system also preserves semantic change history across pull requests and integrates both answer-quality and operational evaluation metrics. We evaluate CODENS on a client Ruby on Rails project in production. Results show that CODENS produces highly relevant and well-grounded answers, while qualitative feedback highlights a remaining challenge in concise, documentation-oriented synthesis.

AI.tldr: CODENS is a system that converts pull requests into an updatable knowledge graph, enabling queryable documentation and repository-level QA for production codebases.
AI.motivation: Code documentation quickly becomes outdated in fast-moving repositories because design knowledge is scattered across source files and pull requests.
AI.method: CODENS incrementally builds a typed software knowledge graph from pull requests, enriches components via schema-driven semantic extraction, derives typed relations, and offers three retrieval modes including agent-guided graph traversal for repository-level QA, while preserving semantic change history.
AI.result: Evaluation on a production Ruby on Rails project shows CODENS produces highly relevant and well-grounded answers.
AI.conclusion: CODENS effectively turns pull requests into living documentation, though qualitative feedback indicates a remaining challenge in achieving concise, documentation-oriented synthesis.

title: Surprise Forcing: What to Remember, When to Skip in Long Video Generation
summary: Streaming autoregressive diffusion makes minute-scale video synthesis practical, but its bounded context and fixed denoising schedule allocate resources uniformly across a highly non-stationary sequence. A rolling key-value cache forgets distant visual evidence even when that evidence remains important, while every generated chunk receives the same number of denoising passes irrespective of its actual difficulty. We introduce Surprise Forcing, a training-free framework that treats both limitations as online resource-allocation problems. A Surprise-Gated Memory Bank summarizes evicted frames with value-token descriptors, evaluates them using complementary global-deviation and nearest-neighbor novelty signals, and regulates admission through a feedback-controlled budget in normalized score space. Priority-based replacement and relevance-aware routing then keep the external memory compact and useful. In parallel, Surprise-Aware Denoising estimates chunk difficulty from the maximum adjacent-frame cosine distance after the first denoising pass and uses a local percentile scheduler to skip intermediate steps for comparatively easy chunks. Experiments on VBench, VBench-Long, and VBench-2.0 show that the proposed allocation strategy improves long-horizon consistency and visual quality while retaining real-time streaming throughput.

AI.tldr: Surprise Forcing is a training-free framework that improves long-video streaming diffusion by using a surprise-gated memory bank (selectively retaining important past frames) and surprise-aware denoising (adapting computation based on chunk difficulty), enhancing consistency and quality without sacrificing real-time throughput.
AI.motivation: Streaming autoregressive diffusion models for minute-scale video suffer from (1) bounded context: a rolling KV cache forgets distant but important visual evidence, and (2) fixed denoising schedule: every generated chunk gets the same compute regardless of its actual difficulty, wasting resources on easy chunks.
AI.method: Surprise Forcing treats both limitations as online resource-allocation problems. (1) Surprise-Gated Memory Bank: evicted frames are summarized into value-token descriptors; admission is controlled by complementary global-deviation and nearest-neighbor novelty signals with a feedback-regulated budget; priority-based replacement and relevance-aware routing keep the memory compact. (2) Surprise-Aware Denoising: chunk difficulty is estimated from the maximum adjacent-frame cosine distance after the first denoising pass; a local percentile scheduler skips intermediate steps for easy chunks.
AI.result: Experiments on VBench, VBench-Long, and VBench-2.0 show improved long-horizon consistency and visual quality while maintaining real-time streaming throughput.
AI.conclusion: The proposed surprise-driven allocation strategy effectively addresses both context forgetting and uniform computation waste in streaming diffusion, enabling better long-video synthesis without additional training or throughput loss.

title: Beyond Single-Dimensional Compression: The Compound Sparsity Frontier of Large Language Models
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are often compressed through static parameter pruning or dynamic token-level computation, yet aggressive sparsification can trigger rapid performance degradation beyond an essential sparsity boundary. This work asks \emph{whether combining these two mechanisms can delay such degradation by distributing the compression burden}. We study a minimalist compound sparsity framework that first applies low-rank approximation and channel pruning to obtain a statically compressed backbone, and then introduces lightweight routers for per-token dynamic layer skipping. This design enables independent control of parameter sparsity and token-level computation sparsity. Experiments across language understanding and modeling benchmarks show that compound sparsity consistently outperforms single-mechanism compression under the same total sparsity, delaying the decay point on understanding tasks and preserving stronger modeling performance. Further analysis reveals cross-dimensional interference between parameter pruning and token skipping, and shows that near-balanced allocation is most effective under a fixed sparsity budget. These results demonstrate that compound compression provides a practical way to improve LLM compression, while revealing a broader cross-dimensional sparsity boundary that ultimately limits further compression. Code will be available at https://github.com/EIT-NLP/LLM-Pruning.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a compound sparsity framework for LLM compression that combines static pruning (low-rank approximation + channel pruning) with dynamic per-token layer skipping, showing it outperforms single-mechanism compression at the same sparsity level and reveals a cross-dimensional sparsity boundary.
AI.motivation: Static parameter pruning and dynamic token-level computation each cause rapid performance degradation beyond an essential sparsity boundary. The paper investigates whether combining both mechanisms can delay this degradation by distributing the compression burden across dimensions.
AI.method: A minimalist compound sparsity framework: first apply low-rank approximation and channel pruning for a statically compressed backbone, then add lightweight routers for per-token dynamic layer skipping. This enables independent control of parameter sparsity and token-level computation sparsity.
AI.result: Compound sparsity consistently outperforms single-mechanism compression under the same total sparsity, delaying the decay point on understanding tasks and preserving stronger modeling performance. Near-balanced allocation is most effective under a fixed sparsity budget.
AI.conclusion: Compound compression is a practical way to improve LLM compression, but cross-dimensional interference between pruning and skipping reveals a broader cross-dimensional sparsity boundary that ultimately limits further compression.

title: BatchDAG: LLM-Planned Execution Graphs for Scalable Ad-Hoc Analysis Over Enterprise Data
summary: Large language models (LLMs) excel at analyzing individual documents but break down on exhaustive, cross-entity analytical questions over enterprise-scale datasets due to context overflow, loss of per-entity attribution, and linear latency from sequential tool calls. We present BatchDAG, a system in which an LLM generates a typed directed acyclic graph (DAG) of operations -- SQL queries, semantic searches, in-memory transforms, parallel fan-outs, and single-shot analyses -- which a deterministic engine evaluates with topological-wave parallelism and structured JSON data flow. A key optimization, entity-aware batching, groups rows by logical entity before fan-out, reducing LLM calls by up to 47x. BatchDAG is not primarily an accuracy improvement over hand-optimized pipelines; rather, it is a general-purpose orchestration layer that replaces multiple hand-engineered workflows with a single system that generates the appropriate execution strategy from natural language. In controlled experiments on 12 transcript-heavy queries, BatchDAG (3.74/5) achieves quality comparable to an expert-designed pipeline (3.25/5) and significantly outperforms a ReAct agent (3.09/5, p<0.01), with superior provenance (77% transcript evidence rate vs. 46-60% for baselines). A controlled ablation shows structured JSON intermediates reduce hallucinations by 27% versus prose summaries (paired t-test, p=0.107, n=12). The planner achieves 98.8% valid-DAG rate across 300 planning calls. In production at Brevian.ai, BatchDAG processes queries over 50,000+ meetings in under 60 seconds, with measured per-query costs of $0.02-$0.24 at published GPT-5.1 pricing.

AI.tldr: BatchDAG is a system where LLMs generate typed DAGs of operations (SQL, search, transforms, parallel fan-outs) with entity-aware batching, achieving 47x LLM call reduction, comparable quality to expert pipelines (3.74 vs 3.25/5), 77% evidence rate, and sub-minute queries over 50K+ meetings at $0.02-$0.24 per query.
AI.motivation: LLMs fail on exhaustive cross-entity analytical queries over enterprise-scale datasets due to context overflow, loss of per-entity attribution, and linear latency from sequential tool calls.
AI.method: BatchDAG uses an LLM to generate a typed DAG of operations (SQL, semantic search, in-memory transforms, parallel fan-outs, single-shot analyses) evaluated by a deterministic engine with topological-wave parallelism and structured JSON data flow. Entity-aware batching groups rows by logical entity before fan-out to reduce LLM calls.
AI.result: BatchDAG (3.74/5) matches expert-designed pipelines (3.25/5), outperforms ReAct agents (3.09/5, p<0.01), achieves 77% transcript evidence rate vs 46-60% baselines, reduces LLM calls by up to 47x, achieves 98.8% valid-DAG rate, and processes queries over 50K+ meetings in under 60 seconds at $0.02-$0.24 per query.
AI.conclusion: BatchDAG is a general-purpose orchestration layer that replaces multiple hand-engineered workflows with a single NL-driven system, demonstrating practical viability for enterprise-scale analytical queries.

title: End-to-End Markov State Sequence Learning for Auditory Attention Decoding
summary: Auditory attention decoding (AAD) identifies the speaker a listener attends to from neural responses like electroencephalography (EEG), making it a key algorithm in neuro-steered hearing aids. However, most neural AAD models are trained as independent short-window classifiers, despite auditory attention being a temporally persistent cognitive state and short-window EEG--audio evidence often being noisy and ambiguous. We propose an end-to-end Markov AAD framework based on conditional random field (CRF) that trains window-level neural emissions under a two-state attention prior. The framework treats the logits of any AAD backbone as Markov emissions, learns the transition rate from a standard HMM initialization, and jointly optimizes cross-entropy and CRF objectives, allowing temporal continuity to guide representation learning rather than merely smoothing predictions after training. We also introduce ESCNet, an EEG--speech correlation backbone that preserves time-aligned features and converts the difference between two mean Pearson correlations into state logits. We evaluate the framework with four emission backbones spanning correlation-based, convolutional, recurrent, and attention-based designs. On the dynamic AVGC dataset, CRF training generally outperforms post-hoc HMM smoothing; with ESCNet, it achieves $86.5\%$ causal and $92.4\%$ non-causal accuracy using $1$s windows. On the static KUL and USTC datasets, it improves causal decoding over fixed-rate post-hoc HMM baselines by $5.6\%$ and $2.0\%$, respectively, showing the superiority of learning AAD as attention state sequence over isolated-window classification.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an end-to-end Markov AAD framework using conditional random fields (CRF) to model auditory attention as a temporally persistent state, rather than independent short-window classifiers. It introduces ESCNet as a backbone and shows superior performance over post-hoc HMM smoothing on dynamic and static datasets.
AI.motivation: Most neural AAD models are trained as independent short-window classifiers, but auditory attention is a temporally persistent cognitive state, and short-window EEG-audio evidence is often noisy and ambiguous.
AI.method: An end-to-end Markov AAD framework based on CRF that treats window-level logits as Markov emissions, learns transition rates from HMM initialization, jointly optimizes cross-entropy and CRF objectives, and introduces ESCNet as a correlation-based backbone.
AI.result: 86.5% causal and 92.4% non-causal accuracy with 1s windows on AVGC dataset; 5.6% and 2.0% improvement over fixed-rate post-hoc HMM on KUL and USTC datasets respectively.
AI.conclusion: Learning AAD as an attention state sequence outperforms isolated-window classification, and the proposed CRF framework with ESCNet achieves state-of-the-art results.

title: Beyond Resolved Rate: A Non-Functional Quality Study
summary: Repository-level coding benchmarks typically measure progress in model capability by comparing the resolved rates of later and earlier models. However, this focus overlooks whether the non-functional quality of their generated patches has also changed across model generations. This study investigates whether later models produce functionally correct patches with better non-functional characteristics than earlier models on comparable repository-level repair tasks. We conducted two case studies involving four Claude and DeepSeek models on SWE-bench Lite. Using the same SWE-agent functional repair setting, we evaluated the generated patches with CodeQL, CodeScene, CPU time, and peak memory. Our primary analysis compared the models on commonly resolved instances. The static analysis results showed that most CodeQL paired differences were zero and that no CodeQL or CodeScene comparison remained significant after Holm correction. CPU time differences were small and inconsistent across model families, while peak memory usage was slightly higher for the later models under the benchmark test workload, with small absolute differences. Differences in individual CodeQL rules and CodeScene categories varied across model families and did not survive multiple-comparison correction. Overall, later models resolved more instances but showed no consistent improvement in the measured non-functional indicators on tasks solved by both models. Through this study, we hope to encourage a more comprehensive evaluation of models' practical software engineering capabilities.

AI.tldr: Later models (Claude, DeepSeek) resolve more instances on SWE-bench Lite than earlier models, but show no consistent improvement in non-functional patch quality (static analysis, CPU time, peak memory) on commonly solved tasks.
AI.motivation: Repository-level coding benchmarks typically focus on functional correctness (resolved rates) and overlook whether non-functional quality of generated patches has changed across model generations.
AI.method: Two case studies with four Claude and DeepSeek models on SWE-bench Lite using the same SWE-agent functional repair setting. Patches evaluated with CodeQL, CodeScene, CPU time, and peak memory. Primary analysis compared models on commonly resolved instances.
AI.result: Most CodeQL paired differences were zero; no CodeQL or CodeScene comparison remained significant after Holm correction. CPU time differences were small and inconsistent; peak memory slightly higher for later models with small absolute differences. Individual CodeQL rules/CodeScene categories varied across families and did not survive multiple-comparison correction.
AI.conclusion: Later models resolved more instances but showed no consistent improvement in non-functional indicators on tasks solved by both models. The study encourages more comprehensive evaluation of models' practical software engineering capabilities.

title: ALAS: Additive Learnable Alpha-Stable Kernels for Flexible Bayesian Optimization
summary: Bayesian Optimization is widely used for expensive black-box optimization, yet its success often depends on choosing a kernel that matches the objective's unknown structure. In this work, we propose ALAS, a flexible Gaussian Process kernel family built from symmetric $α$-stable spectral components. By learning the stability parameter $α$, ALAS adapts its effective smoothness from data, capturing both smooth trends and sharp irregularities. We present two parameterizations: ALAS, a single stationary component with joint spectral modulation, and ALAS-Sep, a separable variant that learns dimension-wise tail behavior to improve robustness on approximately decomposable objectives. Experiments on standard benchmarks and real-world surrogates demonstrate strong and robust performance across diverse settings.

AI.tldr: ALAS proposes a flexible Gaussian Process kernel family based on symmetric α-stable spectral components that adapts its smoothness by learning the stability parameter α, with two variants (ALAS and ALAS-Sep) showing robust performance across diverse optimization benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Bayesian Optimization's success heavily depends on choosing a kernel that matches the objective's unknown structure, which is often difficult in practice.
AI.method: Proposes ALAS, a GP kernel family built from symmetric α-stable spectral components. Learns the stability parameter α to adapt smoothness. Two parameterizations: ALAS (single stationary component with joint spectral modulation) and ALAS-Sep (separable variant learning dimension-wise tail behavior).
AI.result: Strong and robust performance across standard benchmarks and real-world surrogates in diverse settings.
AI.conclusion: ALAS effectively adapts its smoothness to data, capturing both smooth trends and sharp irregularities, improving robustness in Bayesian Optimization.

title: AI Tool Discovery at Scale: All You Need is DNS
comment: keywords: AI tool discovery, ToolDNS, Agent, DNS
summary: The coming era of autonomous AI agents demands a discovery mechanism capable of navigating millions of tools, yet existing solutions buckle under O(N) complexity and centralized governance. Instead of building another fragile overlay, we propose ToolDNS, a radical framework that retrofits semantic tool discovery onto the Internet's most resilient substrate: the Domain Name System (DNS). By embedding functional intent and organizational trust into a hierarchical namespace, ToolDNS transforms an expensive semantic search into a series of lightweight, O(log N) name resolutions. We introduce three protocol-compliant enhancements to enable decentralized governance and semantic pruning: partially unfolded names, EDNS0 intent payloads, and logical subdomains. To rigorously evaluate this approach across the fragmented tooling landscape, we construct and release a large-scale heterogeneous benchmark comprising 33,688 real-world tools spanning MCP, A2A, RESTful, and Skill protocols. On this dataset, ToolDNS slashes the per-query search space by 95.26% while matching state-of-the-art retrieval accuracy. Furthermore, its UDP-native design reduces discovery latency by orders of magnitude compared to HTTP-based registries. Our work demonstrates that scalable AI interoperability requires not more middleware, but a smarter utilization of the infrastructure already beneath our feet.

AI.tldr: ToolDNS retrofits semantic tool discovery onto DNS infrastructure, achieving O(log N) complexity for autonomous AI agents to navigate millions of tools across heterogeneous protocols, reducing search space by 95.26% while matching state-of-the-art retrieval accuracy.
AI.motivation: Existing tool discovery mechanisms suffer from O(N) complexity and centralized governance, which cannot scale to millions of tools required for autonomous AI agents in the coming era.
AI.method: ToolDNS embeds functional intent and organizational trust into DNS hierarchical namespace via three protocol-compliant enhancements: partially unfolded names, EDNS0 intent payloads, and logical subdomains, transforming semantic search into lightweight O(log N) name resolutions.
AI.result: On a heterogeneous benchmark of 33,688 real-world tools (MCP, A2A, RESTful, Skill protocols), ToolDNS reduces per-query search space by 95.26% while matching state-of-the-art retrieval accuracy, with UDP-native design reducing discovery latency by orders of magnitude versus HTTP-based registries.
AI.conclusion: Scalable AI interoperability requires smarter utilization of existing infrastructure (DNS) rather than building additional middleware layers.

title: CS-ETS: Chaos-Inspired Samba-Based EMG-To-Speech Synthesis with Nonlinear Chaotic Losses
summary: We propose a chaos-inspired new architecture for EMG-to-Speech (ETS) synthesis called CS-ETS, which combines a Samba-based encoder with two novel chaos-inspired loss functions -- Lyapunov Exponent Regularization (LER) and Multi-Scale Detrended Fluctuation Analysis (MSDFA). LER is designed based on Lyapunov exponents to capture nonlinear fluctuations and sensitivity to initial conditions. MSDFA exploits detrended fluctuation analysis to quantify fractal-like, long-range temporal chaotic correlation. CS-ETS surpasses prior work with a 40.79\% lower parameter count (32M vs 54.1M) and introduces a new Post-Vocoder Alignment approach that improves LSD by 2.1x, STOI by 4.7x, and SI-SDR by 1.25x. CS-ETS reduces computation by 13.33\% while maintaining improved performance. To the best of our knowledge, for the first time, we show how ETS can be supervised by the subtle non-linear chaotic physics with Samba attention to achieve a significantly smaller model with superior performance.

AI.tldr: CS-ETS introduces a chaos-inspired architecture for EMG-to-Speech synthesis, using a Samba-based encoder with Lyapunov Exponent Regularization and Multi-Scale Detrended Fluctuation Analysis loss functions, achieving superior performance with 40.79% fewer parameters, 13.33% less computation, and significantly improved audio quality metrics (LSD, STOI, SI-SDR).
AI.motivation: To address the inefficiency of current EMG-to-Speech models (large parameters, high computation) by leveraging chaotic dynamics and non-linear physics to achieve a smaller, more efficient model with better synthesis quality.
AI.method: CS-ETS employs a Samba-based encoder with two novel chaotic loss functions: Lyapunov Exponent Regularization (LER) for capturing nonlinear fluctuations and sensitivity to initial conditions, and Multi-Scale Detrended Fluctuation Analysis (MSDFA) for quantifying fractal-like long-range temporal correlations, along with a Post-Vocoder Alignment approach.
AI.result: 40.79% fewer parameters (32M vs 54.1M), 13.33% less computation, 2.1x improvement in LSD, 4.7x improvement in STOI, and 1.25x improvement in SI-SDR compared to prior work.
AI.conclusion: CS-ETS demonstrates, for the first time, that EMG-to-Speech synthesis can be effectively supervised by non-linear chaotic physics with Samba attention, achieving a significantly smaller model with superior performance.

title: Semantic Drift in Bug Resolution: How Behavioral Signals Propagate from Reports to Tests and Patches
summary: Bug resolution is a cross-artifact process: natural-language reports must expose actionable behavioral cues that can be reproduced by tests and corrected by patches. Yet the extent to which these signals are preserved across artifacts remains largely unquantified. We introduce Desc2Fix, a framework for measuring semantic alignment between bug reports, triggering tests, and developer-written fixes. Alignment is operationalized through structured behavioral anchors (e.g., reproduction steps, API/exception cues, expected vs. actual behavior), deterministic similarity metrics (ROUGE, SBERT, CodeBERT, OpenAI embeddings), and LLM-based judgments grounded in coverage, correctness, and specificity. We analyze 2,857 report-test-patch triplets from Defects4J and SWT-Bench using GPT-4o and DeepSeek-Chat.
