The traceability graph maintains consistency across various artifacts and serves as a structured context for efficient memory management, supporting reliable repository-level code generation. We evaluate TraceDev on two widely used datasets (including 125 use cases) compared with two state-of-the-art approaches. On the ETOUR dataset, TraceDev achieves a success rate of 53.63\%, outperforming baseline approaches by up to 186.63\%. A similar trend is observed on the SMOS dataset, where TraceDev attains a success rate of 56.82\%, exceeding baseline approaches by up to 340.80\%. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of TraceDev in repository-level code generation from requirements.

AI.tldr: TraceDev is a multi-agent framework that transforms natural language requirements into repository-level code using five specialized agents and a traceability graph linking requirements, design, and code artifacts. It significantly outperforms baselines on two datasets, improving success rates by up to 186–340%.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based code generation approaches rely on simplified instructions (e.g., single-sentence descriptions) and lack explicit requirement traceability mechanisms, making it difficult to precisely align and validate generated code against original complex requirements.
AI.method: TraceDev is a multi-agent framework with five role-specific agents (Requirement Refiner, Designer, Developer, Tester, and Validator). The Validator Agent constructs a heterogeneous traceability graph that links requirements, design models, and code artifacts, maintaining consistency across artifacts and serving as structured context for memory management and reliable code generation.
AI.result: On the ETOUR dataset (use cases), TraceDev achieves 53.63% success rate, outperforming baselines by up to 186.63%. On the SMOS dataset, TraceDev achieves 56.82% success rate, exceeding baselines by up to 340.80%.
AI.conclusion: TraceDev effectively addresses the limitations of existing approaches by enabling repository-level code generation from complex, multi-functional natural language requirements through explicit traceability and multi-agent collaboration.

title: Attention Without Grounding: Causal Evaluation of Visual Explanations in Medical VLMs
summary: Attention and saliency heatmaps are widely used to explain medical Vision-Language Model (VLM) outputs on chest X-rays, yet whether they truly highlight the image evidence driving predictions has not been causally tested. We audit faithfulness via overlap with radiologist bounding boxes on PadChest (n=637), attribution mass within radiologist masks on CheXlocalize (n=643), and 16x16 patch-occlusion maps that record which regions, when hidden, change the answer. We study three MedGemma-4B variants, cross-family probes on LLaVA-RAD and Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, and the specialist CheXagent-2-3b, with two CXR-trained classifiers (DenseNet121, ResNet50) as positive controls. A heatmap is faithful only if the model uses the image and attention concentrates on regions whose occlusion alters the prediction. No evaluated VLM meets both criteria. MedGemma and Qwen3-VL use the image, but attention anti-correlates with patch-occlusion importance (rho < 0 with 95% bootstrap CIs below zero). LLaVA-RAD's attention correlates positively, but the model is almost text-only (99.1% text-only agreement, near-zero causal mass), so correlation ties two near-zero signals. Attention also misses annotated anatomy: overlap with true regions never beats shifted or random controls, and no method places more than 22% of its mass inside radiologist masks. The two CXR classifiers pass all metrics, indicating the failure is specific to VLM heatmaps, not the evaluation. These heatmaps are visually reassuring but not faithful; clinical explanations require controlled localization metrics and causal perturbation, not visual inspection alone.

AI.tldr: Attention/saliency heatmaps in medical VLMs (MedGemma, LLaVA-RAD, Qwen3-VL, CheXagent) appear interpretable but are unfaithful: they fail causal occlusion tests, anti-correlate with true predictive regions, and miss radiologist-annotated anatomy. Only CXR-specific classifiers (DenseNet121, ResNet50) pass all faithfulness metrics, confirming the failure is specific to VLM heatmaps.
AI.motivation: To causally test whether attention and saliency heatmaps in medical VLMs faithfully highlight the image evidence driving predictions, rather than relying on visual plausibility alone.
AI.method: Audited heatmap faithfulness via (1) overlap with radiologist bounding boxes on PadChest (n=637), (2) attribution mass within radiologist masks on CheXlocalize (n=643), and (3) 16x16 patch-occlusion mapping. Evaluated three MedGemma-4B variants, LLaVA-RAD, Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, and CheXagent-2-3b, with DenseNet121 and ResNet50 as positive controls.
AI.result: No evaluated VLM met both faithfulness criteria. MedGemma and Qwen3-VL use images but attention anti-correlates with patch-occlusion importance (rho < 0, 95% CI below zero). LLaVA-RAD's attention correlates positively but the model is nearly text-only (99.1% text-only agreement). Overlap with annotated anatomy never beats shifted/random controls; no method places >22% of mass inside radiologist masks. Both CXR classifiers passed all metrics.
AI.conclusion: VLM heatmaps are visually reassuring but not causally faithful; clinical explanations require controlled localization metrics and causal perturbation, not visual inspection alone.

title: Towards Principled Continual Anomaly Detection: A Systematic Framework and Benchmark Scenarios
summary: Continual anomaly detection (CAD) studies how models can adapt to evolving data distributions while retaining performance on previously observed regimes. CAD benchmarks, however, depend critically on how tasks are defined, filtered, ordered, and validated. In tabular domains, task boundaries are rarely given, and arbitrary splits can create unlearnable, redundant, or overly transferable tasks that obscure genuine continual-learning behavior. To this end, we introduce a systematic framework for reproducible benchmark scenario design from existing tabular anomaly-detection datasets. The framework discovers candidate tasks, filters unsuitable tasks, and derives principled orderings that expose diverse dynamics. The framework allows us to deliver five benchmark-ready scenarios from three large-scale cybersecurity anomaly detection datasets, yielding both single-dataset and multi-dataset CAD settings.

AI.tldr: A systematic framework for designing reproducible continual anomaly detection benchmarks from tabular datasets, yielding five benchmark-ready scenarios from three cybersecurity datasets.
AI.motivation: Tabular CAD benchmarks suffer from arbitrary task definitions, splits, and orderings that obscure genuine continual learning behavior, necessitating a principled framework for reproducible scenario design.
AI.method: The framework systematically discovers candidate tasks, filters unsuitable ones, and derives principled orderings from existing tabular anomaly detection datasets to create reproducible benchmark scenarios.
AI.result: Five benchmark-ready scenarios from three large-scale cybersecurity anomaly detection datasets, producing both single-dataset and multi-dataset CAD settings.
AI.conclusion: A structured approach to benchmark design enables more meaningful and reproducible evaluation of continual anomaly detection methods in tabular domains.

title: Cross-Dialect Generalization Without Retraining: Benchmarks and Evaluation of Schema-Derived Constrained Decoding for MLIR
comment: 27 pages (9 main + bibliography + appendix), 9 figures, 9 tables. Code, benchmarks, and reproducibility Docker image at https://github.com/plawanrath/slm-to-mlir-constrained-emitter
summary: Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR) underlies modern ML compiler infrastructure (TensorFlow, JAX/StableHLO, PyTorch Inductor, IREE), yet appears only in trace amounts in code-LM pretraining corpora. MLIR is also extensible by design: new dialects ship per application domain, so a fine-tuned model per dialect does not scale. We ask whether inference-time priors derived mechanically from each dialect's Operation Definition Specification (ODS) can substitute for gradient-based adaptation. First, we release four natural-language-to-MLIR benchmarks across three dialects - MLIR-Spec-150, Linalg-Spec-30, StableHLO-Spec-30, and StableHLO-Held-Out-200 - totaling 410 in-scope NL-to-MLIR pairs, plus a 25-program out-of-grammar stress set and a hand-authored n=30 functional reference set, shipped under Apache-2.0 with Gebru datasheets and Croissant 1.0 metadata. Second, we build a three-layer schema-derived constraint stack: a CFG over op signatures(C1), type-domain splits from an ODS-extracted type lattice (C2), and an SSA-scope validator driving five-retry rejection sampling (C3). Porting from arith+func+memref+linalg to StableHLO required no new constraint-layer code. On dialects whose verifier semantics are dominated by structural constraints, schema-derived priors let SmolLM2-1.7B match or exceed 15B-34B code LMs at 8-25x the per-generation speed: on linalg, SmolLM2 reaches 80.0% verify-valid (three-seed mean, n=125), beating CodeLlama-34B, Granite-Code-34B, and StarCoder2-15B by 21-44 percentage points with non-overlapping CIs. On arith+func and on the templated parametric StableHLO-Held-Out-200, where verifier semantics turn on attribute values rather than structure, the same baselines match or beat the SLM; we scope these as non-win cells. We release benchmarks, decoder, all per-prompt generations, and a reproducibility Docker image.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces four NL-to-MLIR benchmarks across three dialects (410 in-scope pairs), proposes a schema-derived constraint stack (C1-C3) that lets small models (SmolLM2-1.7B) match or exceed large code LMs (15B-34B) on structurally-verifiable MLIR dialects at 8-25x speed, while identifying failure cases where attribute-value semantics dominate.
AI.motivation: MLIR code seldom appears in LM pretraining corpora, and fine-tuning a separate model per dialect is unscalable due to MLIR's extensible dialect design. The authors ask whether inference-time priors derived mechanically from each dialect's ODS can substitute for gradient-based adaptation.
AI.method: The authors release 4 NL-to-MLIR benchmarks (410 pairs + stress set + reference set). They build a three-layer constraint stack: (C1) CFG over op signatures, (C2) type-domain splits from ODS-extracted type lattice, (C3) SSA-scope validator with 5-retry rejection sampling. The constraint stack is portable (arith+func+memref+linalg to StableHLO required no new code).
AI.result: On linalg, SmolLM2-1.7B achieves 80.0% verify-valid, beating CodeLlama-34B, Granite-Code-34B, and StarCoder2-15B by 21-44 percentage points with non-overlapping CIs, at 8-25x generation speed. On arith+func and StableHLO-Held-Out-200 (attribute-value semantics), large models match or beat the SLM.
AI.conclusion: Schema-derived priors can effectively substitute for scale in structurally-constrained MLIR dialects, but not in cases where verifier semantics depend on attribute values rather than structure. The benchmarks, decoder, generations, and reproducibility Docker image are released under Apache-2.0.

title: Skillware: A Software Ontology and Engineering Lifecycle for Persistent Behavioral Artifacts
summary: Agent Skills have become persistent behavioral artifacts across independent AI agent systems. They combine natural-language task specifications with metadata and optional references, scripts, assets, hooks, package manifests, tests, and companion interfaces. Existing studies explain how Skills are specified, executed, maintained, and evolved, but lack an ontology that defines these artifacts as independent software objects. This paper introduces Skillware as the software abstraction that extends software engineering to persistent Behavioral Artifacts in agent systems. A Skill Artifact specifies reusable task behavior; a Skillware Unit manages that artifact as software through an independent identity and lifecycle. A compatible Agent Host activates the unit for runtime interpretation. Three necessary conditions operationalize category membership: behavioral primacy, independent software identity, and an Agent Host execution relationship. Lifecycle Continuity records whether the same unit identity persists through update, maintenance, rollback, and removal as a separate software-grade property. Evidence combines the Agent Skills specification, a frozen corpus of 138,133 content-deduplicated SKILL.md records associated with 20,556 repository identifiers, independent empirical studies, 15 category-boundary cases, and 13 fixed-revision engineering implementations. The evidence establishes a recurring artifact envelope, separable software identities, compatible execution paths, and lifecycle engineering pressure. Skillware provides the software ontology and engineering lifecycle through which agent capabilities can become identifiable, composable, maintainable, and evolvable software artifacts.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Skillware as a software abstraction and ontology that defines agent skills as persistent, independently-identifiable software artifacts with their own lifecycle, identity, and execution relationships, supported by empirical evidence from over 138,000 skill records and multiple engineering implementations.
AI.motivation: Existing studies describe how Agent Skills are specified, executed, maintained, and evolved, but lack a formal ontology that defines these behavioral artifacts as independent software objects with proper software engineering properties.
AI.method: The paper proposes Skillware as a software abstraction comprising: (1) Skill Artifact (specifying reusable task behavior), (2) Skillware Unit (managing the artifact with independent identity and lifecycle), and (3) Agent Host (activating the unit at runtime). Three necessary conditions are defined: behavioral primacy, independent software identity, and Agent Host execution relationship. Lifecycle Continuity tracks identity persistence through updates. Evidence includes the Agent Skills specification, 138,133 SKILL.md records from 20,556 repositories, empirical studies, 15 boundary cases, and 13 implementation case studies.
AI.result: The evidence demonstrates a recurring artifact envelope, separable software identities, compatible execution paths, and lifecycle engineering pressure, confirming the existence of Skillware as a distinct software category.
AI.conclusion: Skillware provides the necessary software ontology and engineering lifecycle to make agent capabilities identifiable, composable, maintainable, and evolvable as proper software artifacts, extending software engineering to persistent behavioral artifacts in agent systems.

title: Norm or Direction? Decoding Vision Mambas for High-Resolution Vision
summary: Vision Mamba models replace quadratic self-attention with linear complexity selective state space models (SSMs), emerging as efficient visual backbones. However, MambaOut demonstrates that a Gated CNN block can match or exceed VMamba on image classification, questioning the necessity of SSMs for vision. This raises a fundamental question: do VMamba and MambaOut encode visual information differently at the representation level? To investigate, we apply cross model centered kernel alignment (CKA) analysis and find that VMamba's final stage blocks form representations distinctly different from both MambaOut and its own preceding blocks. We therefore focus on the final block features, decomposing each spatial token into magnitude and direction. MambaOut concentrates class-discriminative information in high-norm foreground tokens that align with Grad-CAM attribution. VMamba, by contrast, produces high-norm tokens predominantly in background regions, misaligned with Grad-CAM, yet preserves discriminative signals primarily in token directions. These observations reveal that the two models rely on different encoding strategies. We connect this difference to high-resolution classification and semantic segmentation. VMamba distributes logit support broadly across object regions, whereas MambaOut relies on sparse dominant tokens, a strategy that becomes less stable as token counts grow. Under full fine-tuning for segmentation, VMamba consistently outperforms MambaOut. These results suggest that VMamba's advantage in dense prediction stems not merely from the SSM mechanism or sequence length, but from how semantic evidence is organized across token magnitude, direction. Ultimately, we conclude that token magnitude and directional structure serve as critical axes for improving visual backbones, particularly under dense supervision.

AI.tldr: VMamba and MambaOut encode visual information differently: VMamba distributes discriminative signals across token directions (with high-norm tokens in background regions), while MambaOut concentrates them in high-norm foreground tokens aligned with Grad-CAM. This structural difference explains VMamba's advantage in dense prediction tasks like segmentation, where broad logit support across object regions proves more robust than relying on sparse dominant tokens.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether VMamba (SSM-based) and MambaOut (Gated CNN) encode visual information differently at the representation level, given that MambaOut matches VMamba on image classification despite lacking selective state space models.
AI.method: Applied cross-model centered kernel alignment (CKA) analysis to compare representations; decomposed spatial tokens into magnitude and direction; used Grad-CAM attribution; compared models on high-resolution classification and semantic segmentation under full fine-tuning.
AI.result: VMamba's final stage blocks produce representations distinct from MambaOut. VMamba generates high-norm tokens in background regions (misaligned with Grad-CAM) but preserves discriminative signals in token directions. MambaOut concentrates class information in high-norm foreground tokens. VMamba distributes logit support broadly across object regions; MambaOut relies on sparse dominant tokens, which is less stable at high resolution. VMamba outperforms MambaOut in dense prediction (segmentation).
AI.conclusion: VMamba's advantage in dense prediction stems not from the SSM mechanism or sequence length per se, but from how semantic evidence is organized across token magnitude and direction. Token magnitude and directional structure are critical axes for improving visual backbones, especially under dense supervision.

title: SechKAN: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks with Hyperbolic Secant Functions
summary: In recent years, Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) have attracted increasing attention due to their effectiveness in machine learning and scientific computing tasks, offering a new paradigm for neural network design. In this paper, we present SechKAN, a KAN architecture based on hyperbolic secant (sech) functions. The hyperbolic secant basis is used for its smooth bell-shaped form, localized responses, and stable gradients. We employ 1D linear transformations to reduce the number of parameters, allowing SechKAN to remain comparable to multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) in model size. Experimental results indicate the effectiveness of SechKAN in function fitting, PDE problems, and image classification tasks on benchmark datasets, including MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100. SechKAN achieves superior performance compared to MLPs and other KAN variants while maintaining a similar number of parameters. However, its running time, while better than that of other KAN variants, is slightly longer than that of MLPs.

AI.tldr: SechKAN is a KAN architecture using hyperbolic secant functions as basis, offering smooth bell-shaped responses and stable gradients, achieving superior performance over MLPs and other KAN variants on function fitting, PDEs, and image classification, with comparable parameter counts but slightly longer runtime than MLPs.
AI.motivation: To design a KAN architecture that leverages hyperbolic secant functions for their smooth bell-shaped form, localized responses, and stable gradients, while maintaining parameter efficiency comparable to MLPs.
AI.method: SechKAN replaces traditional basis functions with hyperbolic secant (sech) functions and employs 1D linear transformations to reduce parameter count, resulting in an architecture that balances expressivity with model size.
AI.result: SechKAN achieves superior performance compared to MLPs and other KAN variants on function fitting, PDE problems, and image classification (MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100) with similar parameter counts, though its runtime slightly exceeds that of MLPs.
AI.conclusion: SechKAN effectively demonstrates that hyperbolic secant-based KANs can outperform both MLPs and existing KAN variants in accuracy while maintaining parameter efficiency, albeit with a modest computational overhead trade-off.

title: Semantic Cooperative Games for Contribution Attribution in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Contribution attribution has become a central problem in LLM-based multi-agent systems, where final outputs are produced through multiple agents, message exchanges, and ordered workflow dependencies. Existing attribution methods often rely on counterfactual valuation, such as removing agents or comparing score changes across altered agent subsets. In language-mediated workflows, these methods require repeated model calls, introduce high variance, and do not explicitly capture the intermediate semantic states through which agents produce, preserve, and transform task-relevant information. We propose Semantic Cooperative Games (SCG), a framework that represents a realized language flow as a semantic generation hypergraph and induces an agent-level semantic value function on this structure. We define the Semantic Shapley Value (SSV) to allocate contribution over semantic support logic, and introduce SLIC, a single-trajectory algorithm that constructs the semantic hypergraph, recovers minimal semantic supports, applies Boolean absorption, and computes SSV without rerunning agent subsets. We prove that SSV reduces to the classical Shapley value under standard set-based, fully observable, and no-order-dependence conditions. On a medical benchmark satisfying these conditions, SLIC reduces computation cost by 93.3% while remaining highly consistent with a Monte Carlo Shapley baseline. In more general multi-role workflows, SSV aligns with perturbation-induced score-drop profiles and exposes cases where semantic contribution and failure impact diverge. Overall, SLIC provides a fast, counterfactual-free, and interpretable attribution method for complex LLM-based multi-agent systems.

AI.tldr: SCG/SLIC proposes a counterfactual-free, semantically-grounded Shapley value (SSV) for agent contribution attribution in LLM multi-agent systems, using a semantic hypergraph and single-trajectory algorithm that reduces computation cost by 93.3% while maintaining consistency with Monte Carlo baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing attribution methods in LLM-based multi-agent systems rely on counterfactual valuation (e.g., removing agents), which requires repeated model calls, introduces high variance, and fails to capture intermediate semantic states where agents produce, preserve, or transform task-relevant information.
AI.method: (1) Represent a realized language flow as a semantic generation hypergraph; (2) induce an agent-level semantic value function; (3) define Semantic Shapley Value (SSV) to allocate contribution over semantic support logic; (4) introduce SLIC, a single-trajectory algorithm that constructs the hypergraph, recovers minimal semantic supports, applies Boolean absorption, and computes SSV without rerunning agent subsets.
AI.result: On a medical benchmark, SLIC reduces computation cost by 93.3% while remaining highly consistent with Monte Carlo Shapley baseline. In general multi-role workflows, SSV aligns with perturbation-induced score-drop profiles and reveals cases where semantic contribution and failure impact diverge.
AI.conclusion: SLIC provides a fast, counterfactual-free, and interpretable attribution method for complex LLM-based multi-agent systems, with theoretical proof that SSV reduces to classical Shapley value under standard conditions.

title: From Collaboration to Regulation: Characterizing Governance Practice in Three Deep Learning Open Source Communities
summary: Collaboration in Open Source Software (OSS) projects creates substantial coordination and quality-control challenges across diverse contributor bases. Projects address these challenges through documented governance rules, yet maintainers have limited systematic guidance on what rules to codify, when to introduce or revise them, and how to organize them across documents. We conducted a mixed-methods empirical study of three mature deep learning frameworks: PyTorch, TensorFlow, and Paddle. Using the Institutional Analysis and Development framework, we analyzed 109 documents and identified 17 rule themes across seven rule types. Operational rules, such as workflows, appeared across all three projects, whereas structural rules, such as role hierarchies, varied more substantially. Tracing more than 1,700 commits, we found that operational rule themes generally appeared earlier and were revised more frequently, while many structural rule themes emerged later and changed less often. Rule-bearing content also became increasingly specialized across task- and role-specific files. We further identified four governance functions reflected in substantive rule changes: Norm Alignment, Workflow Refinement, Coordination Structuring, and Community and Governance Development. Synthesizing these findings, we derive 33 actionable governance practices for mature, large-scale OSS projects with substantial coordination demands and organizational involvement.

AI.tldr: A mixed-methods study of three deep learning OSS frameworks (PyTorch, TensorFlow, Paddle) using the IAD framework to analyze 109 governance documents, 17 rule themes, and 1,700+ commits, resulting in 33 actionable governance practices for mature large-scale OSS projects.
AI.motivation: OSS projects face coordination and quality-control challenges due to diverse contributor bases. Maintainers lack systematic guidance on what governance rules to codify, when to introduce/revise them, and how to organize them across documents.
AI.method: Mixed-methods empirical study using the Institutional Analysis and Development (IAD) framework. Analyzed 109 governance documents from PyTorch, TensorFlow, and Paddle, tracing over 1,700 commits to study rule evolution.
AI.result: Identified 17 rule themes across seven rule types. Operational rules appeared earlier and were revised more frequently; structural rules emerged later and changed less often. Rule content became increasingly specialized across task- and role-specific files. Four governance functions were identified: Norm Alignment, Workflow Refinement, Coordination Structuring, and Community and Governance Development.
AI.conclusion: Synthesized findings into 33 actionable governance practices for mature, large-scale OSS projects with substantial coordination demands and organizational involvement.

title: Seeing Before Generating: Object Perception Enhances Single-View 3D Reconstruction
summary: The relationship between object perception and reconstruction is well established in human vision, yet remains underexplored in computer vision. In this paper, we demonstrate that learnt object perception can significantly enhance 3D reconstruction. Focusing on the challenging task of single-view 3D object reconstruction, we propose a method that leverages perceptual signals extracted from pretrained perception models capturing semantic and geometric information to drive the reconstruction of an object from its single image. Our approach is model-agnostic and can be integrated into various reconstruction methods in a plug-and-play manner. Experiments with two state-of-the-art single-view 3D reconstruction pipelines in a benchmark dataset show consistent and substantial improvements achieved by our method, validating the effectiveness of incorporating perception into generation. We provide in-depth analysis of various aspects of our method and its application. Our project page is at https://ynhuhuynh.github.io/perception-3d/.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates that incorporating perceptual signals from pretrained perception models (capturing semantic and geometric info) can significantly improve single-view 3D object reconstruction, with a plug-and-play approach that works across different reconstruction methods.
AI.motivation: The relationship between object perception and reconstruction is well-established in human vision but underexplored in computer vision; the authors aim to bridge this gap by leveraging perceptual knowledge to enhance 3D reconstruction.
AI.method: A model-agnostic, plug-and-play method that extracts perceptual signals (semantic and geometric) from pretrained perception models and uses them to drive single-view 3D object reconstruction.
AI.result: Experiments with two state-of-the-art single-view 3D reconstruction pipelines on a benchmark dataset show consistent and substantial improvements, validating the effectiveness of incorporating perception into generation.
AI.conclusion: Learnt object perception can significantly enhance 3D reconstruction; the proposed perceptual integration strategy is effective, model-agnostic, and broadly applicable.

title: Dual-domain fused LSTM modeling for efficient time-dependent reliability analysis
summary: Time-dependent reliability analysis is crucial for ensuring the long-term safety and performance of engineering systems under uncertainties. However, traditional surrogate model methods often struggle to incorporate time-independent random variables and capture their complex interactions with time-dependent stochastic processes. To overcome this limitation, this paper proposes a dual-domain fused long short-term memory (DDF-LSTM) model for efficient and accurate time-dependent reliability analysis. A novel network architecture is developed to jointly process information from both time-dependent and time-independent domains. Specifically, the time-independent variables are embedded into the initial hidden states, and a fully connected layer is introduced to map both LSTM outputs and time-independent variables into the final output space. Furthermore, an improved loss function is designed to emphasize the model's sensitivity to minimum responses, thereby improving the precision of failure probability estimation. The proposed method effectively captures the dependencies among random variables, stochastic processes, and the temporal behavior of limit state functions. Once trained, the DDF-LSTM model enables efficient Monte Carlo simulation to estimate time-dependent failure probabilities with minimal computational cost. Four case studies validate the proposed method's enhanced computational efficiency and predictive accuracy.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Dual-Domain Fused LSTM (DDF-LSTM) model that jointly processes time-independent random variables and time-dependent stochastic processes for efficient and accurate time-dependent reliability analysis, with an improved loss function emphasizing minimum responses.
AI.motivation: Traditional surrogate model methods struggle to incorporate time-independent random variables and capture their complex interactions with time-dependent stochastic processes in time-dependent reliability analysis.
AI.method: A DDF-LSTM network architecture embeds time-independent variables into initial hidden states and uses a fully connected layer to map both LSTM outputs and time-independent variables into the final output space, with an improved loss function emphasizing sensitivity to minimum responses.
AI.result: Four case studies validate that the proposed method achieves enhanced computational efficiency and predictive accuracy compared to traditional approaches.
AI.conclusion: The DDF-LSTM model effectively captures dependencies among random variables, stochastic processes, and temporal behavior of limit state functions, enabling efficient Monte Carlo simulation for time-dependent failure probability estimation with minimal computational cost.

title: PEARL: Solver-in-the-Loop Interactive Optimization Modeling from Natural Language
summary: Optimization modeling is the process of translating real-world decision problems, often described in natural language, into formal mathematical formulations and executable solver code. While recent advances in large language models have shown promise in automating this process, most existing approaches remain one-shot: a model produces a formulation once, without executing it, conditioning on solver feedback, or iteratively revising errors. This stands in sharp contrast to real-world optimization modeling, which is inherently interactive and proceeds through repeated solve-debug-revise cycles. We introduce PEARL, a system for interactive optimization modeling that uses Python execution and mathematical programming solvers inside this loop. Rather than relying on a fixed repair workflow, PEARL learns when to test partial models, how to revise from solver diagnostics, and when to stop. It operates in a multi-turn tool-integrated setting where intermediate execution results, feasibility signals, and solution checks are used to improve both formulations and solver code before finalization. Across diverse optimization benchmarks, PEARL substantially improves verified solve rates over strong one-shot and tool-augmented baselines; notably, our PEARL-Qwen3-\textbf{4B} model outperforms the much larger DeepSeek-V3.2-\textbf{685B} in both macro- and micro-averaged accuracy on optimization modeling tasks.

AI.tldr: PEARL is an interactive optimization modeling system that iteratively tests, debugs, and revises mathematical formulations using solver feedback, achieving better solve rates than one-shot approaches and outperforming a 685B-parameter model with just 4B parameters.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based optimization modeling approaches are one-shot (generate a formulation without execution or iterative revision), which contrasts with real-world optimization modeling that is inherently interactive and requires repeated solve-debug-revise cycles.
AI.method: PEARL uses a multi-turn tool-integrated system that incorporates Python execution and solver feedback in a loop, learning when to test partial models, how to revise from solver diagnostics, and when to stop, instead of relying on a fixed repair workflow.
AI.result: PEARL substantially improves verified solve rates over strong one-shot and tool-augmented baselines across diverse optimization benchmarks. PEARL-Qwen3-4B outperforms DeepSeek-V3.2-685B in both macro- and micro-averaged accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Interactive optimization modeling with iterative solver feedback significantly outperforms one-shot approaches, and smaller models can surpass much larger ones when equipped with this interactive capability.

title: SciCodePile: A 128GB Corpus and Executable Benchmark for Challenging Scientific Code Generation
summary: Large language models (LLMs) excel at general-purpose code generation, yet how well they handle scientific code remains an open question. Existing datasets and benchmarks are limited in scale, domain coverage, or executable verification, leaving the true gap between current LLMs and reliable scientific code generators inadequately assessed. To address these limitations, we present SciCodePile, the largest scientific code corpus to date, constructed from 37,737 public repositories and collectively comprising 128GB of code that spans multiple computational science disciplines. From this corpus, we further curate an executable benchmark of 200 tasks, each equipped with a sandboxed execution environment and an automated test harness for functional verification. We evaluate 15 LLMs from both open-source and closed-source families on three tasks: prefix-to-suffix completion, fill-in-the-middle infilling, and executable code generation. Results show that scientific code generation remains highly challenging: The best CodeBLEU reaches only 38.13 and 38.37 on the two completion tasks, while the strongest model achieves just 12.30\% Pass@1 on the executable benchmark, underscoring how far current models remain from reliable scientific code generation. To demonstrate the training utility of SciCodePile, we further show that continued pretraining on our corpus improves CodeBLEU by $\times$2.84 on scientific code completion, and instruction tuning on our data improves Pass@1 by $\times$4.79 on the executable benchmark. All code and data are available at https://huggingface.co/SciCodePile.

AI.tldr: The paper presents SciCodePile, a 128GB scientific code corpus from 37,737 repositories, and a 200-task executable benchmark. Evaluation of 15 LLMs shows scientific code generation remains highly challenging (best CodeBLEU 38.37, Pass@1 12.30%), but continued pretraining on SciCodePile yields significant improvements (CodeBLEU ×2.84, Pass@1 ×4.79).
AI.motivation: Existing datasets and benchmarks for scientific code generation are limited in scale, domain coverage, or executable verification, making it difficult to assess the true gap between current LLMs and reliable scientific code generators.
AI.method: Constructed SciCodePile from 37,737 public repositories (128GB across multiple scientific disciplines), curated 200 executable benchmark tasks with sandboxed execution environments and automated test harnesses, and evaluated 15 LLMs on prefix-to-suffix completion, fill-in-the-middle infilling, and executable code generation.
AI.result: Best CodeBLEU reaches 38.13 and 38.37 on completion tasks; strongest model achieves 12.30% Pass@1 on executable benchmark. Continued pretraining improves CodeBLEU by ×2.84 on completion; instruction tuning improves Pass@1 by ×4.79 on executable benchmark.
AI.conclusion: Scientific code generation remains highly challenging for current LLMs, but training on SciCodePile significantly boosts performance, demonstrating its utility for advancing scientific code generation.

title: Deep Learning Estimation of Sex, Age, Height, and Weight from CT-derived Digitally Reconstructed Radiographs
summary: Purpose: To develop and validate a deep learning ensemble for estimating adult sex, age, height, and weight from coronal digitally reconstructed radiographs (DRRs) generated from diagnostic CT. Materials and Methods: This retrospective study included 128,621 CT examinations from 80,004 adults at nine institutions in Japan. Three multitask models-ConvNeXt-Base, ViT-Base/16, and MaxViT-Base-were fine-tuned using coronal DRRs and combined by weighted averaging. Data were split by institution into training (114,147 examinations; seven institutions), tuning (4,305; one institution), and test (10,169; one institution) sets; generalizability was assessed on two non-Japanese datasets. Accuracy and mean absolute error (MAE) were used to evaluate sex classification and age, height, and weight regression, respectively. Body surface area (BSA)-corrected heart and liver volume trends were compared using true versus estimated height and weight. Results: In the test set (median age, 69.9 years; 4,899 of 10,169 [48.2%] male), overall sex-classification accuracy was 0.997 (95% CI, 0.996-0.998), and MAEs were 3.57 years (3.51-3.63), 2.59 cm (2.54-2.64), and 3.40 kg (3.34-3.47) for age, height, and weight, respectively. In examinations covering the chest through pelvis, accuracy was 1.000, and MAEs were 3.15 years, 2.28 cm, and 3.18 kg, respectively. BSA calculated from estimated values reproduced age-related heart and liver volume trends obtained using true values. On non-Japanese datasets, height error increased but was reduced by continued fine-tuning. Conclusion: The ensemble estimated adult sex, age, height, and weight from CT-derived DRRs, with generally lower errors in examinations with broader anatomical coverage.

AI.tldr: A deep learning ensemble (ConvNeXt-Base, ViT-Base/16, MaxViT-Base) fine-tuned on coronal DRRs from 128,621 CT exams across nine Japanese institutions achieved high accuracy in estimating adult sex (0.997), age (MAE 3.57 years), height (2.59 cm), and weight (3.40 kg), with better performance on chest-to-pelvis scans and generalizable to non-Japanese data after fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: To develop a non-invasive method for estimating demographic and physical attributes (sex, age, height, weight) from CT-derived radiographs, which could be useful for missing metadata, forensic applications, or body-size-adjusted organ volume analysis.
AI.method: Three multitask deep learning models (ConvNeXt-Base, ViT-Base/16, MaxViT-Base) were fine-tuned on coronal DRRs from 128,621 CT exams (80,004 adults, nine Japanese institutions) and combined via weighted averaging. Data split by institution: training (114,147 exams, 7 institutions), tuning (4,305, 1), test (10,169, 1). Generalizability tested on two non-Japanese datasets.
AI.result: Test set (median age 69.9, 48.2% male): sex accuracy 0.997, age MAE 3.57 yr, height MAE 2.59 cm, weight MAE 3.40 kg. Chest-to-pelvis exams: sex accuracy 1.000, age MAE 3.15 yr, height MAE 2.28 cm, weight MAE 3.18 kg. BSA from estimated values reproduced true age-related heart/liver volume trends. Non-Japanese datasets showed higher height error, reduced by continued fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: The ensemble accurately estimates adult sex, age, height, and weight from CT-derived DRRs, with lower errors for broader anatomical coverage. Demonstrates potential for clinical and forensic applications, with generalizability improved via fine-tuning on target populations.

title: Reliability Scales Inversely: Bigger Models Compound Mistakes Faster via a Hidden Auto-Regressive Risk Regime
summary: As language models scale, answers start truer but degrade faster: scaling buys capability but erodes reliability. The knowledge-gap account - more data, retrieval, or scale - misses an auto-regressive risk residual that scale sharpens: the model commits to a low-probability token, conditions on it as established, and snowballs. We track this through per-position disagreement $δ= \log p_M - \log p_O$ against a stronger same-family oracle, whose second moment splits exactly into bias$^2$ $\mathrm{KL}(p_M \,\|\, p_O)^2$ and risk $\mathrm{Var}[δ]$. We present four findings: (i) under scaling, the knowledge gap falls $\approx$$6\times$ while knowledge degradation grows $11$-$39\times$; (ii) at a fabrication, felt uncertainty $H(p_M)$ relaxes quickly while oracle-referenced risk persists up to $17\times$ longer, leaving a confident-but-precarious risk regime that bridges consecutive fabrications ($+69\%$ at $14$B); (iii) this regime is causal - an on-policy, fixed-$\mathrm{KL}$ variance contraction cuts web-verified hallucination by $35$-$74\%$ across three model families; and, (iv) it structurally evades self-monitoring, with $p_M$-only detectors (e.g. semantic entropy) firing $\approx$$30\%$ less ($p<10^{-16}$) on the risky branch holding nearly $4\times$ more fabrications. Bigger models snowball mistakes faster, through a failure mode that is dominant, self-perpetuating, causal and invisible to the model itself.

AI.tldr: Larger language models produce more factually accurate answers on average but suffer from faster degradation and error snowballing due to an auto-regressive risk residual that scaling sharpens. The paper identifies a confident-but-precarious risk regime that bridges consecutive fabrications, is causal, and evades self-monitoring, leading to 11-39× faster degradation and 35-74% hallucination reduction via targeted intervention.
AI.motivation: Existing accounts attribute model unreliability to knowledge gaps solvable by more data, retrieval, or scale, but miss a fundamental auto-regressive risk residual that worsens with scaling: once the model commits to a low-probability token, it conditions on that error and error snowballs.
AI.method: Per-position disagreement δ = log p_M - log p_O between a model and a stronger same-family oracle, decomposed into bias² (KL divergence squared) and risk (variance of δ). Analyzed across scales to track knowledge gap vs. knowledge degradation, with interventions including on-policy, fixed-KL variance contraction.
AI.result: (i) Knowledge gap falls ~6× while degradation grows 11-39× under scaling; (ii) Felt uncertainty (entropy) relaxes quickly but oracle-referenced risk persists up to 17× longer, creating a confident-but-precarious regime (+69% at 14B); (iii) Variance contraction cuts hallucination by 35-74%; (iv) Self-monitoring fails ~30% more on the risky branch containing ~4× more fabrications.
AI.conclusion: Bigger models snowball mistakes faster through a failure mode that is dominant, self-perpetuating, causal, and invisible to the model itself, challenging the knowledge-gap account and suggesting that scaling alone cannot fix reliability without addressing this auto-regressive risk residual.

title: S2T-RLHF: Hierarchical Credit Assignment for Stable Preference-Based RLHF
summary: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) with preference-based reward models often exhibits unstable training dynamics. A key contributing factor is that standard RLHF relies on a single sequence-level scalar reward, which is propagated to token-level policy updates and leaves credit assignment within a response inherently ambiguous. Recent work has attempted to address this issue by refining rewards into denser token-level supervision, often relying on the implicit assumption that finer-grained credit assignment improves optimization. We argue that this assumption is incomplete: when preference signals are noisy and only defined at the response level, overly fine-grained reward refinement can amplify reward uncertainty and destabilize learning. To address this problem, we propose a granularity-aware principle for hierarchical credit assignment, emphasizing stability-oriented reward design rather than maximal allocation precision. Under this principle, sentences serve as a natural intermediate granularity, balancing semantic coherence with robustness to token-level noise. Guided by this view, we introduce S2T-RLHF. This sentence-to-token reward decomposition framework first allocates sequence-level preference rewards across sentences and then applies bounded token-level refinement within each sentence, without reward-model retraining or token-level supervision. Experiments across multiple datasets and optimization settings show that S2T-RLHF improves training stability and robustness while maintaining competitive preference alignment.

AI.tldr: S2T-RLHF proposes a granularity-aware, sentence-to-token reward decomposition framework for RLHF that improves training stability by avoiding overly fine-grained credit assignment, using sentences as an intermediate granularity to balance semantic coherence and noise robustness.
AI.motivation: Standard RLHF uses a single sequence-level scalar reward, making credit assignment within a response ambiguous and leading to unstable training dynamics. Recent work tries to address this by refining rewards to denser token-level supervision, but this can amplify reward uncertainty when preference signals are noisy and only defined at the response level.
AI.method: S2T-RLHF is a sentence-to-token reward decomposition framework that first allocates sequence-level preference rewards across sentences, then applies bounded token-level refinement within each sentence, without requiring reward-model retraining or token-level supervision.
AI.result: Experiments across multiple datasets and optimization settings show that S2T-RLHF improves training stability and robustness while maintaining competitive preference alignment.
AI.conclusion: A granularity-aware principle for hierarchical credit assignment is beneficial, and sentences serve as a natural intermediate granularity that balances semantic coherence with robustness to token-level noise.

title: EmbeddedKittens: An Evaluation of Code Embeddings for Scratch
comment: Submitted to ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology (TOSEM)
summary: The trend of embedding source code for machine learning applications also enables new opportunities in learning analytics in programming education, but which code embedding approach is most suitable for learning analytics remains an open question. A common approach to embedding source code lies in treating the code as a token sequence similar to natural language when training large language models~(LLMs). However, in case of visual block-based programming languages like Scratch, this approach cannot be applied directly. While text-based representations of block-based code can be created to apply LLMs to this problem, other dedicated embedding models could potentially exhibit improved performance by capturing additional structural information. In this paper, we therefore instantiate four LLMs and five different popular embedding approaches for Scratch programs, create a token-prediction and two different classification tasks with corresponding datasets, and empirically evaluate the models on them. Our experiments demonstrate that a transfer of code embeddings to the educational environment of Scratch is feasible. The embedding models trained on large open Scratch datasets capture relevant structural and semantic information about the code to enable learning analytics like predicting functional correctness of student programs, in the typically small classroom setting without requiring further task-specific model fine-tuning.

AI.tldr: This paper empirically evaluates four LLMs and five embedding approaches for Scratch block-based programming code, demonstrating that code embeddings trained on large open Scratch datasets can predict functional correctness and enable learning analytics in small classroom settings without task-specific fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: The suitability of different code embedding approaches for learning analytics in block-based programming education (specifically Scratch) remains an open question, as natural language-based LLM approaches cannot be directly applied to visual block-based languages.
AI.method: The authors instantiate four LLMs and five different embedding approaches for Scratch programs, create a token-prediction task and two classification tasks with corresponding datasets, and empirically evaluate the models on these tasks.
AI.result: Code embedding transfer to the educational environment of Scratch is feasible. Embedding models trained on large open Scratch datasets capture relevant structural and semantic information, enabling learning analytics like predicting functional correctness of student programs without task-specific fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: Code embeddings effectively support learning analytics in Scratch-based programming education, even in small classroom settings, without requiring additional fine-tuning.

title: Fluid-SDF: Ultra-Lightweight and Editable Implicit Shape Representation via Differentiable Primitives
summary: Implicit Neural Representations (INRs) have become the standard for continuous 2D shape modeling, but they suffer from black-box uneditability, vulnerability to noise, and high parameter counts that severely hinder deployment on edge devices. We introduce Fluid-SDF, a highly compressed, differentiable Constructive Solid Geometry (CSG) framework that models shapes using explicit geometric primitives blended via a smooth minimum function. By replacing traditional multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) with a parameterized primitive engine, Fluid-SDF reconstructs complex, non-convex topologies using strictly under 100 parameters, achieving comparable or superior intersection-over-union (mIoU) to standard neural baselines. Furthermore, we demonstrate that Fluid-SDF acts as a powerful geometric prior, inherently resisting high-frequency dataset noise where capacity-matched neural networks catastrophically overfit. Finally, unlike standard INRs, Fluid-SDF's explicit parameter space allows for direct, zero-shot user editing of local and global shape features without retraining. By bypassing expensive on-device gradient updates entirely, Fluid-SDF is uniquely suited for mobile AI, augmented reality, and resource-constrained embedded environments

AI.tldr: Fluid-SDF is a highly compressed CSG framework using explicit geometric primitives with smooth blending, achieving under 100 parameters for complex shape reconstruction, with noise robustness and zero-shot editability, suitable for edge devices.
AI.motivation: Existing INRs for 2D shape modeling suffer from black-box uneditability, vulnerability to noise, and high parameter counts that hinder deployment on resource-constrained edge devices.
AI.method: Fluid-SDF replaces MLPs with a parameterized primitive engine using explicit geometric primitives blended via a smooth minimum function, forming a differentiable CSG framework with under 100 parameters.
AI.result: Achieves comparable or superior mIoU to neural baselines with strictly under 100 parameters; inherently resists high-frequency noise where MLPs overfit; enables direct zero-shot user editing of shape features without retraining.
AI.conclusion: Fluid-SDF is uniquely suited for mobile AI, augmented reality, and embedded environments by bypassing expensive on-device gradient updates entirely.

title: One Student, Many Teachers: Multi-Task On-Policy Distillation via Soft-Prompt Privileged Context
summary: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) teaches large language models new skills through a teacher that shares the student's backbone and supervises its own rollouts. Existing teachers either inject privileged context at the input -- inducing post-hoc rationalization -- or fine-tune weights, accumulating drift and forgetting across tasks. We propose \method, whose teacher differs from the student only by a learnable soft prompt: trained on $(x, y_\text{gold})$ pairs with the backbone frozen, the prompt yields a task-specific teacher that preserves the student's exact representational geometry. \method\ extends naturally to multi-task settings by routing each example in a merged corpus to its corresponding soft-prompt teacher, allowing a single student to absorb knowledge from $K$ teachers in parallel; at inference, all prompts are discarded. On Qwen3-1.7B-Base and Phi-4-mini-instruct across four tasks (Science, Tool Use, Biology, Math), the single-task variant (OPD with a PT teacher) matches or exceeds full fine-tuning while training orders of magnitude fewer parameters, and the multi-task variant achieves the best overall average ($56.2$ on Qwen3-1.7B-Base) while preserving general-capability benchmarks -- in contrast to sequential SFT, which degrades both.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes \method, a soft-prompt-based teacher for on-policy self-distillation that preserves student representational geometry, enables multi-task learning via parallel prompt-routing, and matches/exceeds full fine-tuning with far fewer trained parameters across four tasks on two LLM backbones.
AI.motivation: Existing OPSD teachers either inject privileged context (causing post-hoc rationalization) or fine-tune weights (accumulating drift and forgetting), both of which distort the student's representation space.
AI.method: \method uses a learnable soft prompt as the teacher, trained on gold pairs with the backbone frozen. The prompt yields a task-specific teacher that preserves the student's exact representational geometry. Multi-task variant routes each example to its corresponding soft-prompt teacher, enabling parallel knowledge absorption from K teachers.
AI.result: Single-task variant matches/exceeds full fine-tuning while training orders of magnitude fewer parameters. Multi-task variant achieves best overall average (56.2 on Qwen3-1.7B-Base) and preserves general-capability benchmarks, unlike sequential SFT which degrades both.
AI.conclusion: Soft-prompt-based teachers in OPSD offer a parameter-efficient, representation-preserving alternative to fine-tuning for both single and multi-task LLM learning.

title: Probabilistic Concept-Aware Steering for Trustworthy LLM Inference
summary: Steering vectors (SVs), an inference-time intervention technique for large language models (LLMs), guide the generation process by adding a concept-specific direction vector to intermediate activations during inference. However, existing SV methods frequently yield representation-incoherent behaviors that undermine interpretability and fine-grained control, largely because prior work has focused on binary positive-negative steering evaluation while employing discrete clustering metrics that fail to capture the continuous spectrum of semantic alignment. In this work, we present the Probabilistic Concept-Aware Steering (PCS) framework for LLM inference. PCS preserves original task competence while providing controllable, safety-oriented semantic bias through concept-driven steering-vector retrieval and probabilistic strength calibration.

AI.tldr: PCS is a framework for LLM inference that improves steering vector methods by using probabilistic concept-aware steering, enabling controllable semantic bias while maintaining task performance.
AI.motivation: Existing steering vector methods produce representation-incoherent behaviors that undermine interpretability and fine-grained control due to binary positive-negative evaluation and discrete clustering metrics that fail to capture continuous semantic alignment.
AI.method: The Probabilistic Concept-Aware Steering (PCS) framework uses concept-driven steering-vector retrieval and probabilistic strength calibration to guide LLM inference.
AI.result: PCS preserves original task competence while providing controllable, safety-oriented semantic bias.
AI.conclusion: PCS addresses the limitations of existing steering vector methods by enabling more interpretable and fine-grained control over LLM generation through probabilistic calibration.

title: DeforM: Reasoning-Guided Physics-Aware Video Generation via Spatial-Temporal Masking
summary: Video generation models achieve high visual quality but often struggle to generate physics-aware videos. Unlike rigid-body motion, which can be described by explicit trajectories or formulas, complex deformation dynamics remain challenging to synthesize. We observe that a lack of physical reasoning for localizing dynamic areas allows irrelevant regions to dilute the model's attention, leading to generation failure. In this paper, we propose DeforM, a reasoning-guided image-to-video generation framework that directs the model's focus toward physics-critical regions. To reason about and localize these critical regions, we introduce a VLM-guided physical reasoning module, DeforM-Reason, to identify target objects and generate spatial-temporal masks. For physical guidance, we develop two alternative strategies: DeforM-Free for training-free mechanism analysis and DeforM-Injection as a powerful training-based generator. Experimental results demonstrate that DeforM improves the realism of generated deformation scenarios, outperforming baseline models in both visual quality and physical consistency.

AI.tldr: DeforM is a reasoning-guided image-to-video generation framework that uses a VLM-guided physical reasoning module to identify physics-critical regions and generate spatial-temporal masks, improving the realism and physical consistency of deformation dynamics in generated videos through training-free (DeforM-Free) and training-based (DeforM-Injection) guidance strategies.
AI.motivation: Existing video generation models produce high visual quality but fail to generate physics-aware videos, especially for complex deformation dynamics. The lack of physical reasoning for localizing dynamic areas causes irrelevant regions to dilute model attention, resulting in generation failure.
AI.method: DeforM consists of two key components: (1) DeforM-Reason, a VLM-guided physical reasoning module that identifies target objects and generates spatial-temporal masks; (2) two alternative guidance strategies - DeforM-Free (training-free mechanism analysis) and DeforM-Injection (training-based generator) - that direct model focus toward physics-critical regions for deformation dynamics synthesis.
AI.result: DeforM improves the realism of generated deformation scenarios and outperforms baseline models in both visual quality and physical consistency.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach successfully addresses the challenge of synthesizing complex deformation dynamics by incorporating physical reasoning to localize dynamic regions, preventing attention dilution from irrelevant areas and enhancing physical realism in generated videos.

title: Uncertainty Quantification for AI-Driven Crash Simulation Surrogates: A Comparative Study of Monte Carlo Dropout and Deep Ensemble on Open-Source Bumper Beam Benchmark
summary: Machine learning surrogate models are increasingly being explored in engineering product development to augment simulation-driven design, offering near-instantaneous predictions that complement computationally expensive high-fidelity analyses. However, a critical gap limits their adoption in safety-critical workflows: a point prediction without an accompanying uncertainty estimate cannot tell an engineer when the model should not be trusted. This work presents a systematic, head-to-head comparison of two widely used uncertainty quantification approaches -- Monte Carlo Dropout and Deep Ensembles -- applied to an open-source surrogate pipeline built on NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo. A key contribution is the use of concrete dropout, a built-in PhysicsNeMo capability that eliminates the dropout rate as a manual hyperparameter by learning it end-to-end during training, directly addressing the most common criticism of Monte Carlo Dropout-based uncertainty quantification. Automotive crash simulation is used as the application domain, with a steel bumper beam impact problem serving as the benchmark. Both methods are evaluated on identical held-out simulations and compared on point accuracy, uncertainty band calibration, and computational cost. The results reveal a fundamental trade-off between accuracy and calibration that challenges the common assumption that deep ensembles are the default gold standard for surrogate uncertainty quantification. The findings demonstrate that well-calibrated, hyperparameter-free uncertainty estimates are achievable within a fully open-source engineering workflow at a fraction of the computational cost of ensemble approaches.

AI.tldr: This paper compares Monte Carlo Dropout (with concrete dropout) and Deep Ensembles for uncertainty quantification in surrogate models for automotive crash simulation, finding a trade-off between accuracy and calibration, and showing that well-calibrated uncertainty estimates are achievable at lower cost using concrete dropout within the open-source PhysicsNeMo framework.
AI.motivation: Simulation-driven engineering design lacks trustworthy surrogate models because point predictions without uncertainty estimates cannot signal when a model should not be trusted, limiting adoption in safety-critical workflows.
AI.method: A head-to-head comparison of Monte Carlo Dropout (using concrete dropout to learn the dropout rate automatically) and Deep Ensembles for uncertainty quantification, applied to a surrogate pipeline built on NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo and benchmarked on a steel bumper beam impact crash simulation problem.
AI.result: A fundamental trade-off between accuracy and calibration exists, challenging the assumption that Deep Ensembles are the default gold standard. Concrete dropout yields well-calibrated, hyperparameter-free uncertainty estimates at a fraction of the computational cost of ensemble methods.
AI.conclusion: Well-calibrated, hyperparameter-free uncertainty quantification is achievable in a fully open-source engineering workflow, with concrete dropout offering a computationally cheaper alternative to deep ensembles while maintaining calibration quality.

title: FindStatBench: Evaluating Large Language Models on Combinatorial Code Synthesis
summary: We introduce FindStatBench, an execution benchmark for evaluating large language models on combinatorial code synthesis. Built from FindStat, it contains 2,329 tasks across 24 collections and 5.52M hidden instances, covering statistic synthesis, which maps objects to integers, and map synthesis, which maps objects to objects. Each task gives a mathematical description and at most five public input-output examples; a model must emit one Python solve function with no retrieval, tool use, execution feedback, voting, or reranking. Submissions are scored by exact sandboxed execution on held-out combinatorial objects. We evaluate eleven systems: four closed-source production models and seven open-weight models served through one inference provider. FindStatBench reveals three main patterns. First, the strongest open- and closed-source systems converge within 1 pp instance accuracy, and both an oracle over all systems and five-way sampling from one mid-tier model yield only limited task-accuracy gains. Second, examples can hurt: several classical bijections are solved perfectly with zero examples but fail under five-example prompts. Third, some failures reflect output-budget mechanics, as reasoning can exhaust the visible response before code is emitted. Overall, statistic synthesis is much easier than map synthesis, some collections remain near-zero, long prompts cause a sharp accuracy cliff, and exact symbolic rule induction remains brittle.

AI.tldr: FindStatBench evaluates LLMs on combinatorial code synthesis using 2,329 tasks from FindStat, revealing that open- and closed-source systems perform similarly, examples can hinder performance, and statistic synthesis is far easier than map synthesis.
AI.motivation: To systematically benchmark large language models on combinatorial code synthesis—specifically statistic and map synthesis from mathematical descriptions—without retrieval, tool use, or execution feedback, and to understand current limitations in exact symbolic rule induction.
AI.method: Constructed 2,329 tasks from FindStat across 24 collections with 5.52M hidden instances; each task provides a mathematical description and up to five public I/O examples. Models must emit a single Python solve function. Scoring is done via exact sandboxed execution on held-out combinatorial objects. Evaluated 11 systems (4 closed-source, 7 open-weight).
AI.result: Open- and closed-source systems converge within 1 pp instance accuracy; oracle and 5-way sampling yield limited gains. Providing examples can degrade performance on some classical bijections. Some failures stem from output-budget limits (reasoning exhausts space before code). Statistic synthesis is much easier than map synthesis; some collections remain near-zero; long prompts cause sharp accuracy cliffs.
AI.conclusion: Exact symbolic rule induction from descriptions remains brittle for LLMs; examples are not always helpful and can even hurt; output budget mechanics are a practical bottleneck; statistic synthesis is more tractable than map synthesis.

title: Spaghetti Architect: A Contamination-Resistant, By-Construction-Labelled, Multi-Language Code Dataset Generator
comment: 32 pages. Under review at the Journal of Data-centric Machine Learning Research (DMLR). Code: https://github.com/KurathSec/Spaghetti-Architect (artifact archived at doi:10.5281/zenodo.21033174)
summary: Mined code corpora are abundant but uncontrolled: a snippet's semantics, surface "messiness," and difficulty are whatever the wild contained; there is no known-optimal reference to grade against; and any public sample may already sit in a model's training set. We present Spaghetti Architect, a tool that mints code datasets with the control such corpora lack. An anti-optimization transpiler maps a clean, language-agnostic JSON intermediate representation to deliberately redundant, fully-flattened programs in five languages (Python, JavaScript, Go, Java, C++); every program is compiled, run, and checked against a reference oracle, so each instance is correct by construction. The clean IR is a known-optimal reference, messiness is dialed by strictly-nested anti-pattern profiles, each instance is labelled along two orthogonal difficulty axes, intrinsic (problem size) and incidental (presentation at fixed semantics), and contamination is resisted by minting fresh variants from a private held-out seed. We give construct-validity evidence that the quality order moves established complexity and readability metrics, and report baselines on a four-model open ladder: exact match rises with scale, and the intrinsic knob collapses arithmetic-aggregation accuracy of even the strongest model to zero. Further, development-set scores equal freshly re-minted held-out counterparts within $|Δ|\le 0.012$ (comprehension) and $\le 0.011$ (refactoring); on identical programs, refactoring equivalence ($0.73 \rightarrow 0.99$) is scale-invariant while output prediction collapses; and ablating the generator's self-annotations shows they inflate the weakest model an order of magnitude more than the strongest ($-0.173$ vs $-0.017$): the annotated ladder resolves one of three adjacent pairs where the unannotated resolves all three. Open source (MIT), dependency-free, archived under a persistent DOI.

AI.tldr: Spaghetti Architect is a tool that generates clean, controllable code datasets with anti-optimized, redundant programs in five languages, each correct by construction and labeled by difficulty, resisting contamination and providing a known-optimal reference for benchmarking code models.
AI.motivation: Existing mined code corpora lack control over semantics, messiness, difficulty, and have no known-optimal reference for grading; they also risk contamination from public samples in model training sets.
AI.method: An anti-optimization transpiler maps a clean JSON IR to deliberately redundant, fully-flattened programs in Python, JS, Go, Java, C++; each is compiled, run, and checked against a reference oracle. Difficulty is controlled via problem size (intrinsic) and presentation style (incidental), and contamination is resisted by minting fresh variants from a private held-out seed.
AI.result: Quality order aligns with established metrics; model exact match rises with scale; intrinsic difficulty collapses strong model's accuracy to zero; held-out and re-minted scores match within small Δ; refactoring equivalence is scale-invariant; removing self-annotations hurts weakest model far more than strongest; annotated ladder resolves fewer adjacent pairs than unannotated.
AI.conclusion: Spaghetti Architect provides controlled, contamination-resistant code data generation with meaningful difficulty axes, validated by benchmarks across four models and five languages.

title: MissingBench-Verified: Probing Vision-Language Models' Inability to Detect Missing Object Parts
comment: Submitted to the ECCV 2026 Workshop on Explainable Computer Vision (eXCV). 11 pages, 4 figures
summary: Vision Language Models (VLMs) are well known for hallucinating non-existent objects in images. Objects with missing parts present a unique challenge for VLMs, stemming from both real-world knowledge bias and the scarcity of such images in training data. We present MissingBench-Verified, a benchmark designed to evaluate a specific and practically relevant scenario: when vision-language models fail to recognize that an essential component of an object has been removed. Across ten leading models, we observe consistent and significant failure rates that persist even when external tool evidence explicitly contradicts the model's visual perception. We further ask whether granting models access to image processing tools (e.g., cropping, contrast adjustment) enables autonomous inspection to resolve these failures. We find that existing mitigation strategies, including tool-assisted verification, autonomous visual reasoning, longer reasoning durations, and fine-tuning on an easier dataset, provide negligible improvement, indicating that this failure mode cannot be addressed through current prompting or post-hoc correction techniques. Our findings highlight a fundamental limitation of current VLM for inspection and monitoring tasks and underscore the need for architectural or training-level interventions that enable models to override internal expectations when confronted with contradictory evidence.

AI.tldr: VLMs consistently fail to recognize objects with missing parts, and current mitigation strategies (tools, reasoning, fine-tuning) provide negligible improvement.
AI.motivation: VLMs hallucinate non-existent objects, and the specific failure mode of missing object parts is understudied due to real-world knowledge bias and training data scarcity.
AI.method: The authors introduce MissingBench-Verified to evaluate VLMs on recognizing objects with missing essential components, testing 10 models with and without external tool evidence.
AI.result: All 10 models show consistent, significant failure rates; existing mitigation strategies (tool-assisted verification, autonomous reasoning, longer reasoning, fine-tuning) provide negligible improvement.
AI.conclusion: This failure mode is a fundamental limitation of current VLMs, requiring architectural or training-level interventions rather than prompting or post-hoc corrections.

title: On the Limits of Support-Preserving Alignment and Bounded Filtering
summary: We study whether alignment schemes that reshape a base model's output distribution, combined with bounded safety filters, can drive the probability of harmful behavior to zero in modern large language models. Recent research suggests that harmful behaviors can persist under preference-based alignment and that external filtering can be computationally hard in the worst case, but it remains unclear whether practical alignment pipelines that largely preserve internal representations can eliminate harmful behavior entirely rather than merely suppressing its most visible forms. We formalize this setting using support-preserving alignment operators together with bounded filtering algorithms under black-box, white-box, and statistical-query access, and analyze their ability to approximate an ideal eliminator that removes all harmful mass. Building on this framework, we provide computational and information-theoretic arguments indicating that, under these constraints, bounded filtering may fail to eliminate all harmful outputs supported by the base model's distribution. To evaluate these limits empirically, we analyze a range of state-of-the-art open-weight and hosted LLMs accessed via OpenRouter under bounded black-box, white-box, and statistical-query filters on adversarial prompts drawn from curated cybersecurity scenarios and PKU-SafeRLHF. Across models, filter classes, and query budgets, the estimated harmful-output rate decreases with additional filtering compute but consistently plateaus above zero, suggesting a persistent empirical harm floor.

AI.tldr: This paper studies whether alignment schemes with bounded safety filters can eliminate all harmful behaviors in LLMs. Through theoretical analysis and empirical evaluation across multiple state-of-the-art models, the authors find that harmful outputs cannot be fully eliminated—the harm rate plateaus above zero regardless of filtering compute budget, indicating a persistent empirical harm floor.
AI.motivation: To determine whether practical alignment pipelines (with support-preserving operators and bounded filters) can drive the probability of harmful LLM behavior to zero, given that prior work suggests harmful behaviors persist under preference-based alignment and worst-case filtering is computationally hard.
AI.method: Formalizes the setting using support-preserving alignment operators and bounded filtering algorithms under black-box, white-box, and statistical-query access. Provides computational and information-theoretic arguments showing bounded filtering may fail to eliminate all harmful outputs. Empirically evaluates open-weight and hosted LLMs via OpenRouter on adversarial prompts from cybersecurity scenarios and PKU-SafeRLHF across multiple filter classes and query budgets.
AI.result: Across all models, filter classes, and query budgets, the estimated harmful-output rate decreases with additional filtering compute but consistently plateaus above zero, suggesting a persistent empirical harm floor.
AI.conclusion: Under the studied constraints (support-preserving alignment and bounded filtering), harmful behavior cannot be fully eliminated from LLMs; there is a fundamental empirical limit to how much filtering can reduce harmful outputs.

title: When JSON Is Not Enough: Semantic Reliability of Schema-Constrained LLM Ordering Agents
summary: LLM agents are increasingly used as transaction compilers: a user states an intent in natural language, and the model emits a structured object that an API can execute. JSON Schema and provider-level structured-output modes are useful because they remove a large class of parse failures, but they do not by themselves decide whether the object is a safe, faithful transaction. We introduce OrderBench, a deterministic benchmark for restaurant ordering agents that separates syntactic validity, schema validity, status decisions, exact item semantics, constraint preservation, and unsafe acceptances. Across 2,400 Nebius Token Factory calls to four open models in prompt-only and JSON-schema modes, we find that schema-valid output can still have large semantic error rates. In the strongest model, both modes achieve 100% schema validity, yet semantic success remains near 80%; in weaker models, schema-valid unsafe acceptances occur in double digits. The result is a concrete engineering warning: structured output is a necessary interface layer, not a substitute for domain verification and fail-closed execution.

AI.tldr: Structured output modes (JSON Schema) prevent parse failures but do not guarantee semantic correctness; OrderBench benchmark shows schema-valid outputs can have ~20% semantic error rates and double-digit unsafe acceptances in weaker models.
AI.motivation: LLM agents used as transaction compilers need to ensure structured outputs are not only syntactically valid but also safe and faithful to user intent; existing structured-output modes (JSON Schema) only address parse failures, not semantic correctness or safety.
AI.method: Introduced OrderBench, a deterministic benchmark for restaurant ordering agents that separates six evaluation dimensions (syntactic validity, schema validity, status decisions, exact item semantics, constraint preservation, unsafe acceptances). Tested 2,400 calls to four open models in prompt-only and JSON-schema modes.
AI.result: Strongest model achieved 100% schema validity in both modes but only ~80% semantic success; weaker models exhibited double-digit schema-valid unsafe acceptances. Schema validity does not guarantee semantic correctness or safety.
