AI.conclusion: Structured output is a necessary interface layer but not a substitute for domain verification and fail-closed execution; engineering warning that semantic validation remains critical beyond schema compliance.

title: Graph-Based Agentic AI with LangGraph: Workflow Pathways for Long-Running Stateful Business Processes
summary: This paper is a practitioner guide to graph-based workflow pathways for long-running, stateful, multi-step generative AI systems in business processes. Rather than treating LangGraph, a low-level orchestration framework for stateful agents, as a model-quality benchmark target, we present three executable recipes -- SQL analytics with repair loops, agentic retrieval-augmented generation with evidence gating, and human-in-the-loop policy review with interrupt and checkpoint recovery -- to show how typed state, conditional routing, deterministic tools, retries, interrupts, checkpoints, and traces fit together. LangGraph is positioned by workflow-complexity fit, not as a universal default: simpler ReAct-style or plain SDK loops may be better for basic tool use, schema-first tools for structured extraction and validation, and DSPy when prompt or program optimization is the main goal. Each recipe explains when LangGraph is worth the extra structure and which implementation patterns make routes, pauses, and audit trails explicit product behavior rather than hidden prompt logic.

AI.tldr: A practitioner guide demonstrating three executable recipes for using LangGraph to build long-running, stateful, multi-step generative AI workflows, positioning it by workflow-complexity fit rather than as a universal default.
AI.motivation: To provide practical guidance on when and how to use graph-based orchestration (LangGraph) for complex generative AI business workflows, moving beyond naive benchmarking and clarifying its appropriate role relative to simpler alternatives.
AI.method: Three executable LangGraph recipes: (1) SQL analytics with repair loops, (2) agentic RAG with evidence gating, and (3) human-in-the-loop policy review with interrupts/checkpoints. The paper also provides decision criteria comparing LangGraph against ReAct-style loops, plain SDKs, schema-first tools, and DSPy.
AI.result: Demonstrates how typed state, conditional routing, deterministic tools, retries, interrupts, checkpoints, and traces combine in practice; clarifies when LangGraph's extra structure is beneficial versus when simpler alternatives suffice.
AI.conclusion: LangGraph is best suited for complex, stateful, multi-step workflows requiring explicit route/pause/audit patterns; simpler approaches are preferable for basic tool use, structured extraction, or prompt optimization tasks.

title: Cross-Dataset Generalization in Breast MRI Tumor Classification via Class-Wise Dataset Mixing
summary: Breast MRI is highly sensitive for detecting breast tumors, but exams contain many slices and require substantial reading time. Deep learning models often perform well on internal splits but can fail across institutions because of domain shift and dataset-origin bias. We study this failure mode for binary breast MRI tumor classification. EfficientNet-B3 and WaveViT-Small are trained using Duke Breast Cancer MRI and fastMRI, and evaluated only on the independent multi-center MAMA-MIA cohort. In a deliberately confounded setup, where label is perfectly correlated with dataset origin, external accuracy is near chance (0.5048--0.5265), despite very high recall. We then construct a mixed training set in which each class contains samples from both Duke and fastMRI, while preserving patient-level splitting, augmentation, and leakage controls. On MAMA-MIA, dataset mixing improves accuracy/F1 to 0.8463/0.8625 for WaveViT-Small and 0.8884/0.8994 for EfficientNet-B3. These results show that controlling dataset-origin bias is important for reliable breast MRI classification.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that dataset-origin bias severely degrades cross-institution performance of deep learning models for breast MRI tumor classification. When label is perfectly correlated with dataset origin, external accuracy is near chance. However, mixing training data from multiple institutions substantially improves accuracy and F1 scores (up to 0.8884/0.8994) on the independent MAMA-MIA cohort.
AI.motivation: Breast MRI exams are time-consuming due to many slices, and deep learning models often fail across institutions due to domain shift and dataset-origin bias. The authors aim to study and mitigate this failure mode for binary breast MRI tumor classification.
AI.method: EfficientNet-B3 and WaveViT-Small are trained on Duke Breast Cancer MRI and fastMRI datasets, then evaluated on the independent multi-center MAMA-MIA cohort. A deliberately confounded setup is used where label equals dataset origin. A mixed training set is constructed where each class contains samples from both datasets with patient-level splitting, augmentation, and leakage controls.
AI.result: In the confounded setup, external accuracy is near chance (0.5048–0.5265) despite high recall. With dataset mixing, WaveViT-Small achieves 0.8463/0.8625 and EfficientNet-B3 achieves 0.8884/0.8994 (accuracy/F1) on MAMA-MIA.
AI.conclusion: Controlling dataset-origin bias is critical for reliable breast MRI classification. Mixing training data from multiple institutions significantly improves generalization across unseen centers.

title: A Better Start for Language Models: Domain-Conditional Position Offsets
summary: Autoregressive language models are least accurate at the beginning of a sequence, where little context forces reliance on a generic pretraining prior. We show that this cold-start penalty is domain dependent and reduce it with a domain-conditional position offset: a single learned vector added to the embedding activation at the first sequence positions while all model weights remain frozen. The offset trains in minutes on roughly one hundred documents, switches between domains without added sequence state, and has no measurable latency overhead. Across eight Mamba, GPT-NeoX, and Llama models spanning 410M to 8B parameters, it reduces held-out in-domain perplexity by up to 27%; the effect persists at 70B, and one position captures most of the benefit. A matched, converged direct logit-bias correction reaches at most only 7.9% and leaves later-token loss unchanged, showing that the offset propagates through model state rather than merely recalibrating the output prior. A tuned LoRA reaches lower perplexity but uses two to three orders of magnitude more parameters and an active low-rank weight path, while soft prompts add sequence positions. With wrong-domain controls, offsets improve retrieval reranking and domain classification when decisions depend on early in-domain tokens, For the few-shot reasoning whose signal occurs later, the results maintains unchanged. Position-aware prefill application also help generation tasks, whereas naive application at every cached decoding step causes repetition. The offset is therefore not the strongest adapter, but a lightweight, hot switchable tool for short in-domain scoring and calibration.

AI.tldr: A domain-conditional position offset vector added to early token embeddings reduces the cold-start penalty in autoregressive LMs, achieving up to 27% perplexity reduction with minimal cost, no latency overhead, and hot-switchable domain adaptation.
AI.motivation: Autoregressive language models suffer from a cold-start penalty—low accuracy at sequence beginnings—due to reliance on pretraining priors when little context is available. This penalty is domain-dependent and existing adaptation methods (LoRA, soft prompts) are heavyweight.
AI.method: Add a single learned vector (domain-conditional position offset) to embedding activations at the first sequence positions, keeping all model weights frozen. Train on ~100 documents in minutes. Apply during prefill for generation tasks; avoid applying at every cached decoding step (causes repetition).
AI.result: Across 8 models (Mamba, GPT-NeoX, Llama, 410M–8B, and at 70B): in-domain perplexity reduced by up to 27%. Outperforms logit-bias correction (max 7.9% reduction). LoRA achieves lower perplexity but uses 2–3 orders of magnitude more parameters. Offsets improve retrieval reranking and domain classification when decisions depend on early tokens; few-shot reasoning (later signal) unchanged.
AI.conclusion: The position offset is not the strongest adapter overall, but an extremely lightweight, hot-switchable tool for short in-domain scoring and calibration with zero latency overhead.

title: ProbSPARQL: Querying Knowledge Graphs with Multi-dimensional, Uncertain Numeric Data
comment: 18 pages, 5 figures, 1 table. Preprint. Supplementary material and reproducibility artifacts are available online
summary: The SFB 1574 Circular Factory is building a shared knowledge graph infrastructure for integrating data about returned products. A central challenge is that circular-factory data include numeric measurements that (i) originate from sensors or are derived from sensor-based measurements, (ii) are frequently multi-dimensional, and (iii) are inherently uncertain, while downstream triage, validation, reliability-modeling, and reassembly-planning modules require queryable uncertainty representations. Current RDF and SPARQL technologies lack native support for harmonized querying and analysis of such uncertain numeric measurement data. To address this gap, we present ProbSPARQL, an upward-compatible SPARQL extension developed as an early-stage query-layer pilot for this infrastructure. ProbSPARQL models uncertain numeric values as random variables whose distributions are encoded by probabilistic RDF literal datatypes, and supports distribution-aware expressions, probabilistic filters, and divergence-based joins. We implement ProbSPARQL on Apache Jena ARQ and expose it through a Fuseki-compatible execution layer. We assess real-data applicability using project-derived measurement fragments covering GMM-encoded uncertainty and histogram-based empirical roughness distributions, and evaluate scalability separately on controlled ontology-conformant benchmarks with up to 5,000 angle-grinder instances and 1.5M triples. The results show feasible in-engine execution, filter-pushdown speedups over application-layer post-processing, and latency-accuracy trade-offs among divergence-join decision strategies.

AI.tldr: The paper presents ProbSPARQL, a SPARQL extension for querying uncertain numeric measurement data in circular manufacturing knowledge graphs, supporting probabilistic datatypes, distribution-aware filtering, and divergence-based joins.
AI.motivation: Circular factory data includes uncertain, multi-dimensional numeric sensor measurements, but current RDF/SPARQL technologies lack native support for querying such uncertain data, hindering downstream applications like triage and reliability modeling.
AI.method: ProbSPARQL extends SPARQL with probabilistic RDF literal datatypes (random variables with encoded distributions), distribution-aware expressions, probabilistic filters, and divergence-based joins, implemented on Apache Jena ARQ with a Fuseki-compatible layer.
AI.result: Evaluation on real-world data (GMM uncertainty, histogram-based roughness) and controlled benchmarks (up to 5,000 instances, 1.5M triples) shows feasible in-engine execution, filter-pushdown speedups, and latency-accuracy trade-offs in divergence-join strategies.
AI.conclusion: ProbSPARQL enables query-level support for uncertain numeric data in circular manufacturing knowledge graphs, offering practical trade-offs between computational cost and query accuracy.

title: Dual-Edged Homogeneous-Modality Similarity: Towards Visible-Infrared Modality-Incomplete Person Re-Identification with Modality Adaptive Matching
summary: Visible-Infrared Person Re-Identification (VI-ReID) operates under a closed-world assumption, where queries and galleries are from heterogeneous modalities. However, in open-world scenarios, both sets are likely to contain homogeneous and heterogeneous modality images. A query may consist of visible-only, infrared-only, or mixed-modality images, while galleries present multi-modal images over long-term collection. Under these conditions, VI-ReID methods, built on a heterogeneous-modality retrieval paradigm, suffer from three trustworthiness challenges: matching conflicts due to high homogeneous-modality similarity, interference from modality uncertainty, and robustness degradation induced by unknown modality combinations. They fail to meet the requirements of trustworthy visual recognition in reliability, consistency, and dynamic adaptability. To address these challenges, we formalize the Visible-Infrared Modality-Incomplete Re-Identification (VIMI-ReID) task. We reorganize existing datasets to construct the SYSU-VIMI and RegDB-VIMI benchmarks. The unpredictable modality combinations and inherent similarity of homogeneous-modality samples in VIMI-ReID cause a significant performance drop in existing VI-ReID methods. We propose the Modality Adaptive Matching Transformer (MAMT). It employs a Divergence Transformer Module (DTM) and a Shared Transformer Module (STM) to extract modality-specific and modality-shared features, respectively. Guided by a divergence loss, the DTM enriches modality-specific features with modality-style information to enhance discriminability within the same modality. A Modality Adaptive Matching Module (MAM) dynamically fuses features according to the query-gallery modality relationship, enabling stable matching under arbitrary and uncertain modality conditions. Extensive experiments on the VIMI benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness and adaptability of MAMT.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces VIMI-ReID, a more realistic open-world VI-ReID task where queries and galleries can have mixed (homogeneous/heterogeneous) modalities. To address trustworthiness challenges (matching conflicts, modality uncertainty, robustness), the authors propose MAMT with DTM, STM, and MAM modules for modality-adaptive feature extraction and matching. New benchmarks SYSU-VIMI and RegDB-VIMI are constructed, and MAMT shows strong performance.
AI.motivation: Existing VI-ReID methods operate under a closed-world assumption (queries and galleries strictly from heterogeneous modalities), which fails in open-world scenarios where both sets can contain homogeneous and heterogeneous modality images. This leads to three trustworthiness issues: matching conflicts from high homogeneous-modality similarity, interference from modality uncertainty, and robustness degradation from unknown modality combinations. The paper aims to address these challenges by formalizing a new task (VIMI-ReID) and proposing a model that can handle arbitrary modality combinations reliably.
AI.method: The authors propose the Modality Adaptive Matching Transformer (MAMT), which includes: (1) a Divergence Transformer Module (DTM) for modality-specific features with modality-style information, guided by a divergence loss; (2) a Shared Transformer Module (STM) for modality-shared features; and (3) a Modality Adaptive Matching Module (MAM) that dynamically fuses features based on the query-gallery modality relationship. The method is evaluated on newly constructed SYSU-VIMI and RegDB-VIMI benchmarks.
AI.result: Existing VI-ReID methods suffer significant performance drops on the VIMI benchmarks. The proposed MAMT demonstrates effectiveness and adaptability under arbitrary and uncertain modality conditions, outperforming prior methods on the new benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The VIMI-ReID task better reflects real-world open-world scenarios by allowing modality-incomplete query and gallery sets. MAMT effectively addresses the trustworthiness challenges of reliability, consistency, and dynamic adaptability, achieving robust matching under mixed-modality conditions.

title: TD-DPO: Difference-Aware Preference Optimization for Mitigating Sycophancy in Clinical Autism Intervention Dialogue
summary: The sycophancy of large language models can increase the safety risk in intervention dialogue for autistic children. Supervised fine-tuning can somewhat reduce sycophancy, but relying solely on positive examples is often insufficient to identify and correct failure patterns. We observe that sycophancy behaviors can often be localized to a limited span within the model response. In this regime, sequence-level preference optimization can over-update preference-irrelevant tokens and degrade intervention ability. To address this, we propose the \textbf{M}inimal \textbf{E}dit \textbf{D}ata \textbf{A}ugmentation (MEDA) strategy to construct controlled, stable, minimal edit preference pairs and \textbf{T}oken-level \textbf{D}ifference \textbf{D}irect \textbf{P}reference \textbf{O}ptimization (TD-DPO), which upweights difference tokens between chosen and rejected responses while downweighting shared tokens to suppress background drift. Extensive experiments across multiple backbones and evaluators show that TD-DPO achieves a better trade-off between sycophancy mitigation and intervention ability retention in our offline settings, highlighting its potential as a practical alignment approach for autism intervention.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes MEDA and TD-DPO to reduce sycophancy in LLMs used for autism intervention dialogue, achieving better trade-off between sycophancy mitigation and intervention ability retention compared to standard preference optimization.
AI.motivation: Sycophancy in LLMs increases safety risks when used in intervention dialogues for autistic children. Existing methods like supervised fine-tuning are insufficient, and sequence-level preference optimization can over-update irrelevant tokens, degrading intervention ability.
AI.method: The authors propose MEDA (Minimal Edit Data Augmentation) to construct controlled minimal edit preference pairs, and TD-DPO (Token-level Difference Direct Preference Optimization) which upweights difference tokens between chosen and rejected responses while downweighting shared tokens to suppress background drift.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across multiple backbones and evaluators show TD-DPO achieves a better trade-off between sycophancy mitigation and intervention ability retention in offline settings.
AI.conclusion: TD-DPO is a practical alignment approach for reducing sycophancy in autism intervention contexts, outperforming sequence-level preference optimization methods.

title: Position: AI/ML Deepfake Research is Misaligned with AI-Generated Non-Consensual Intimate Imagery (AIG-NCII)
comment: Position paper accepted to ICML 2026, Spotlight
summary: AI-generated non-consensual intimate imagery (AIG-NCII) is not adequately addressed in AI/ML literature regarding AI-generated media, commonly referred to as "deepfakes". While research on deepfakes currently focuses on its epistemic harms -- or harms relating to truth and authenticity -- this is misaligned with the dominant reality of generative AI abuse involving sexualized imagery. We conduct a landscape analysis of highly-cited works to demonstrate that technical interventions addressing deepfakes almost entirely ignore AIG-NCII, limiting the research ecosystem to authenticity detection tools. In this position paper, we argue that existing interventions address viewer-centric epistemic harms, such as fraud or scams, but ignore subject-centric dignity harms, such as AIG-NCII. We illustrate that knowing an image is synthetic does not mitigate harms to subjects and may, in some cases, even exacerbate them. We conclude by offering recommendations to realign the field, including updating threat models to consider subject-centric harms and addressing AIG-NCII in AI safety research. Finally, we caution that researchers should only engage in this high-risk domain if they implement safety guardrails for both subjects and researchers and establish partnerships with domain experts in sexual violence prevention.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that AI/ML research on deepfakes is misaligned with real-world harms, focusing on epistemic (truth/authenticity) issues while neglecting AI-generated non-consensual intimate imagery (AIG-NCII) and its subject-centric dignity harms. The authors call for reorienting the field toward addressing these harms and implementing safety measures.
AI.motivation: Current AI/ML literature on deepfakes inadequately addresses AIG-NCII, focusing instead on epistemic harms (e.g., fraud, scams) that are misaligned with the dominant reality of generative AI abuse involving sexualized imagery and subject-centric dignity harms.
AI.method: Landscape analysis of highly-cited works to demonstrate that technical interventions for deepfakes largely ignore AIG-NCII; position paper arguing for realignment of research priorities.
AI.result: Technical interventions overwhelmingly focus on authenticity detection tools (viewer-centric epistemic harms) while ignoring subject-centric dignity harms like AIG-NCII. Knowing an image is synthetic does not mitigate harms to subjects and may exacerbate them.
AI.conclusion: Recommends updating threat models to consider subject-centric harms, addressing AIG-NCII in AI safety research, and implementing safety guardrails with domain expert partnerships in sexual violence prevention before engaging in this high-risk domain.

title: Attributes Should Come from Images, Not Class Names: Distribution-Conditioned Attribute Selection for Vision-Language Models
summary: A popular route to interpretable zero-shot classification asks a large language model (LLM) to describe each class name and prompts CLIP with the resulting descriptors. We show that these descriptors carry little visual evidence of their own: removing the class name from the prompt collapses ImageNet accuracy from 59.5% to 15.5%. The diagnosis is that the descriptors are conditioned on the label rather than on the images, so they describe the concept in general and mislead exactly when the data shifts; an LLM insists that strawberries are red, but every strawberry in ImageNet-Sketch is a colorless line drawing. We therefore select attributes from the target image collection instead: we score a large attribute pool against the images in CLIP's joint embedding space and keep the top-scoring attributes per class. Selected this way, class-name-free attribute prompts reach 23.8% on ImageNet (against 15.5% for LLM descriptors), the gain holds on four shifted ImageNet variants, and reselecting from the LLM's own pool isolates the selection mechanism as the cause. With one image per class, the selected attributes outperform the prompt-tuning method CoOp by 3 points while fitting in under a minute instead of 14 hours, with no learned soft prompt to obscure the decision. Because the attribute set is chosen by the data, it doubles as a readable summary of a dataset, which we use to describe distribution shift in words.

AI.tldr: LLM-generated class descriptors for zero-shot classification lack visual grounding and fail under distribution shift. Selecting attributes directly from target images instead yields better accuracy, robustness, and interpretability, outperforming prompt-tuning methods while being far more efficient.
AI.motivation: LLM-generated descriptors for CLIP-based zero-shot classification are conditioned on class labels rather than visual data, causing failure under distribution shift. The authors aim to develop a data-driven alternative that selects visually grounded attributes from the target image collection.
AI.method: (1) Score attributes from a large pool against target images in CLIP's joint embedding space; (2) Keep top-scoring attributes per class; (3) Use these attributes as class-name-free prompts for CLIP classification; (4) Evaluate on ImageNet and four shifted variants.
AI.result: Class-name-free attribute prompts reach 23.8% on ImageNet (vs. 15.5% for LLM descriptors). Gains hold across four shifted ImageNet variants. With one image per class, the method outperforms CoOp by 3 points while taking under 1 minute vs. 14 hours.
AI.conclusion: Data-driven attribute selection yields more robust and interpretable zero-shot classification than LLM-generated descriptors. The selected attribute set doubles as a readable summary of a dataset, useful for describing distribution shifts in natural language.

title: The Information Shadow: Measuring Structural Limits on What Language Models Can Learn
summary: Some limits on what language models know are not gaps in data coverage but structural properties of learning from text. We introduce the information shadow: the region of phenomena that a text-trained learner cannot acquire regardless of scale, comprising (I) structures language cannot express, (II) functions that are statistically non-identifiable from the training distribution, and (III) functions that are representable but unreachable by gradient-based training. We give each type a probe that is decisive because the premise of the shadow is, in that setting, provable. For Type I, Language Compression Residuals compare a text learner, which sees only a lossy text-like encoding of the signal, against a full-signal learner, which sees the underlying signal directly. The text learner sits at a computable expressibility ceiling while the full-signal learner pulls away by a gap that stays flat across 300x more data, so the deficit is a property of the channel, not of training. For Type II, the Counterfactual Distinction Test trains models on data exactly consistent with two incompatible rules. Across a provable string task and a language-like agreement task, behavior on counterfactuals is set by the model's inductive bias, while 5% disambiguating data steers the learned rule bidirectionally to either target (r = +/-1.0, p < 1e-10). For Type III, Basin Escape Mapping exhibits a function that is representable at 100% (by hand construction) yet reached 0% of the time by standard training and instantly from a nearby initialization, with width scaling providing no help (p = 1.6 x 10^-14). Each effect is isolated by a control that rules out a capacity or modality artifact. We release the probe suite and discuss implications for benchmark design, capability auditing, and shadow-aware uncertainty.

AI.tldr: Language models have inherent learning limitations (information shadows) beyond data coverage—including inexpressible structures, statistically non-identifiable functions, and unreachable representations—each demonstrated with decisive probes and controls across tasks.
AI.motivation: To show that some limits of language models are not due to insufficient data or scale, but are structural properties of learning from text alone, and to provide a framework for identifying and testing such limitations.
AI.method: Three types of "information shadow" are defined and each is tested with a specific probe: (I) Language Compression Residuals compare text-trained vs. full-signal learners to isolate channel-imposed ceilings; (II) Counterfactual Distinction Test trains models on data consistent with two conflicting rules and tests counterfactual behavior; (III) Basin Escape Mapping tests whether a hand-constructed representable function is reachable by gradient-based training from standard vs. nearby initialization.
AI.result: Type I: text learner hits a fixed ceiling while full-signal learner improves across 300x more data. Type II: counterfactual behavior is dictated by inductive bias, yet 5% disambiguating data can steer learned rules bidirectionally (r = +/-1.0, p < 1e-10). Type III: a representable function is reached 0% of the time by standard training but instantly from a nearby initialization, with width scaling offering no help (p = 1.6e-14).
AI.conclusion: Information shadows are fundamental structural limits of text-trained learners, not data gaps; the probe suite provides tools for benchmark design, capability auditing, and uncertainty quantification in LLMs.

title: MUX: Continuous Reasoning via Multiplexed Tokens
summary: Language models solve complex problems by articulating intermediate reasoning steps in natural language. While effective, this process is computationally bottlenecked: each reasoning step conveys only a single subword, and many are spent expressing a thought instead of carrying out computation. We propose MUX, a simple method for high-bandwidth and compact reasoning based on distillation of discrete reasoning into continuous multiplexed tokens in a latent space. Here, each latent token is trained to represent a weighted linear superposition (multiplexing) of a span of discrete reasoning subwords, where this superposition is lossless by construction and the span can be fully recovered (demultiplexing). We prove that simple position-dependent weightings, such as suitable geometric decay, support lossless multiplexing, which in turn prevents shortcut behaviors caused by latent collapse. We further show that multiplexed reasoning can perform parallel exploration in problems that require search. Across 32 evaluation settings spanning four language models, MUX outperforms strong latent reasoning baselines. Ablation and probing analyses further show that the learned latent tokens encode faithful and interpretable reasoning. Our results suggest that lossless superposition as local learning targets constitutes a sufficient condition for achieving strong and efficient latent continuous reasoning.

AI.tldr: MUX proposes lossless multiplexing of discrete reasoning steps into continuous latent tokens, enabling high-bandwidth and efficient reasoning where each latent token represents a compressed superposition of multiple reasoning subwords.
AI.motivation: Standard language model reasoning is computationally bottlenecked because each step conveys only a single subword, with many tokens spent expressing thoughts rather than carrying out computation.
AI.method: MUX distills discrete reasoning into continuous multiplexed tokens in latent space, where each latent token encodes a weighted linear superposition of a span of discrete reasoning subwords, using position-dependent weightings (e.g., geometric decay) that support lossless reconstruction (demultiplexing).
AI.result: Across 32 evaluation settings with four language models, MUX outperforms strong latent reasoning baselines. Ablation and probing analyses confirm latent tokens encode faithful and interpretable reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Lossless superposition as local learning targets is a sufficient condition for achieving strong and efficient latent continuous reasoning, preventing shortcut behaviors from latent collapse.

title: Decoupled Pipeline with Proposal Reranking and Score Fusion for Positive-Unlabeled Marine Species Detection
summary: The FathomNetCLEF 2026 competition combines underwater object detection and fine-grained marine species classification under a positive-unlabeled evaluation setting. The provided training labels are sparse, while the hidden test set is out-of-distribution relative to the training imagery, creating both annotation incompleteness and source-shift challenges. We describe DS@GT ARC's multi-stage system developed for this setting while keeping model training restricted to the data provided by the competition. The final private-leaderboard model uses a frozen Megalodon YOLOv8x detector as a class-agnostic proposal generator, combines global and tiled inference with tile-edge filtering, classifies expanded proposal crops with a LoRA-finetuned DINOv3 ViT-H classifier, and ranks predictions using weighted geometric fusion of detector and classifier confidence. This system placed 12th out of 102 teams. A closely related variant added a locally trained TTN-inspired validity head as a light reranking signal, improving public-leaderboard and proxy-evaluation performance but slightly reducing private-leaderboard performance. Across experiments, the strongest lesson was that train-derived validation and detector-only metrics were not reliable enough for model selection. Instead, we used proxy datasets only for validation and comparison, and combined those signals with leaderboard feedback and targeted ablations. These experiments showed that reserving proposal recall, avoiding over-aggressive filtering, and improving downstream ranking were more effective than fine-tuning the detector or directly training on noisy pseudo-labels. Code: https://github.com/dsgt-arc/fathomnetclef-2026.

AI.tldr: DS@GT ARC developed a multi-stage system for FathomNetCLEF 2026 that uses a frozen YOLOv8x detector as a class-agnostic proposal generator, global+tiled inference with edge filtering, a LoRA-finetuned DINOv3 ViT-H classifier, and weighted geometric fusion for ranking, achieving 12th out of 102 teams. Key findings: train-derived validation metrics were unreliable, and improving recall/ranking was more effective than fine-tuning detectors or training on noisy pseudo-labels.
AI.motivation: The competition combines underwater object detection and fine-grained marine species classification under a positive-unlabeled setting with sparse training labels and out-of-distribution test data, creating annotation incompleteness and source-shift challenges that require a robust multi-stage approach.
AI.method: Frozen Megalodon YOLOv8x detector (class-agnostic proposal generator) → global + tiled inference with tile-edge filtering → LoRA-finetuned DINOv3 ViT-H classifier on expanded proposal crops → weighted geometric fusion of detector and classifier confidence. A variant added a TTN-inspired validity head for light reranking.
AI.result: Placed 12th out of 102 teams. The TTN-inspired reranking variant improved public-leaderboard and proxy-evaluation performance but slightly reduced private-leaderboard performance.
AI.conclusion: Train-derived validation and detector-only metrics were unreliable for model selection; proxy datasets with leaderboard feedback and targeted ablations were necessary. Reserving proposal recall, avoiding aggressive filtering, and improving downstream ranking were more effective than fine-tuning the detector or training on noisy pseudo-labels.

title: Gradient-Energy Guided Block-Wise Perturbations for Sharpness-Aware Minimization
summary: Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) improves generalization by minimizing the worst-case loss in a local parameter neighborhood. Standard SAM implicitly allocates its global perturbation budget across parameter blocks according to instantaneous minibatch gradient norms. Such an allocation can be noisy and may not reflect the sensitivity that blocks accumulate throughout training. We propose Gradient-Energy Adaptive Radius SAM (GEAR-SAM), which maintains an exponential moving average (EMA) of squared block gradients as a lightweight, curvature-related sensitivity signal and allocates the fixed SAM budget through a closed-form constrained optimization. GEAR-SAM preserves the global SAM radius, requires no Hessian-vector products or explicit Fisher estimation, and adds only scalar state beyond SAM. Experiments on image classification, transfer learning, noisy-label learning, and partition studies demonstrate improved generalization and robustness across architectures and tasks. More broadly, GEAR-SAM provides a dynamic view of sharpness-aware optimization: a fixed perturbation budget should be redistributed as the sensitivity of functional network blocks evolves during training.

AI.tldr: GEAR-SAM improves generalization by dynamically redistributing the SAM perturbation budget across parameter blocks using EMA of squared gradients, outperforming standard SAM across multiple tasks.
AI.motivation: Standard SAM allocates perturbation budget based on noisy minibatch gradient norms, which may not reflect true block sensitivity; this leads to suboptimal generalization.
AI.method: GEAR-SAM maintains an exponential moving average (EMA) of squared block gradients as a lightweight sensitivity signal, then allocates the fixed SAM budget via closed-form constrained optimization—no Hessian-vector products or Fisher estimation needed.
AI.result: Improved generalization and robustness across image classification, transfer learning, noisy-label learning, and partition studies, with only scalar state added beyond SAM.
AI.conclusion: A fixed SAM perturbation budget should be dynamically redistributed as block sensitivity evolves during training; GEAR-SAM provides a principled, efficient way to achieve this.

title: State Compression in Two-Agent LLM Relays: A Closed-World Study of Constraint Preservation
summary: Long-running Large Language Model (LLM)-based agents often accumulate large intermediate traces containing audits, eliminations, and numeric calculations. In practice, this state is compressed before handing it to a downstream decision step, creating an information bottleneck in which small omissions can break strict numeric or categorical constraints. This paper evaluates hand-off compression in a closed-world travel-planning relay with two LLM agents. A Researcher audits a fixed inventory of hotels and flights for 50 goal instances, and a Booker selects a hotel--flight pair using only the goal and the hand-off payload, with the inventory withheld. We compare four hand-off conditions: no compression, narrative summarization, schema-constrained JSON extraction, and embedding-based pruning. Exhaustive enumeration over the fixed inventory provides exact feasible and optimal labels. Results show that hand-off representation strongly affects downstream feasibility under a small decision model. JSON extraction achieves the highest feasibility accuracy at 0.96, while narrative summarization, despite producing the smallest compressed hand-off payload, degrades feasibility to 0.48. Embedding-based pruning matches the uncompressed control on feasibility at 0.88 without an additional generative compression call. These findings indicate that constraint checking benefits from structured and auditable hand-off representations rather than relying on brevity alone.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates four hand-off compression methods (no compression, narrative summarization, JSON extraction, embedding-based pruning) in a travel-planning relay between two LLM agents. JSON extraction achieves the highest feasibility accuracy (0.96), while narrative summarization degrades performance (0.48) despite being smallest. Embedding-based pruning matches the uncompressed control (0.88) without extra generative calls.
AI.motivation: Long-running LLM agents accumulate large intermediate traces, and compressing these traces before downstream decision steps creates information bottlenecks that can break strict numeric or categorical constraints, motivating a need to evaluate how hand-off compression affects feasibility.
AI.method: Closed-world travel-planning relay with two LLM agents (Researcher audits inventory, Booker selects hotel-flight pair from hand-off payload); compared four hand-off conditions: no compression, narrative summarization, schema-constrained JSON extraction, and embedding-based pruning; exhaustive enumeration provides ground-truth feasible/optimal labels.
AI.result: JSON extraction achieved highest feasibility accuracy (0.96); narrative summarization degraded to 0.48 despite smallest payload; embedding-based pruning matched uncompressed control at 0.88 without extra generative compression calls.
AI.conclusion: Constraint checking benefits from structured and auditable hand-off representations rather than relying on brevity alone for compression.

title: Generative World Renderer at the Speed of Play
summary: Generative world renderer AlayaRenderer receives structured world states exported from physics engines and synthesizes RGB frames. Unlike models that generate frames from text/control-hints prompts, AlayaRenderer preserves scene structure without altering the underlying world dynamics. This demonstrates an alternative path toward interactive world modeling and user-controllable play. However, the original AlayaRenderer is too computationally expensive for real-time deployment. This technical report introduces AlayaRenderer-Flash, a real-time-oriented generative forward world renderer that pushes AlayaRenderer from 0.56 FPS to 31.54 FPS, reaching the speed of play. AlayaRenderer-Flash reformulates the original renderer as a few-step autoregressive streaming model and introduces lightweight distilled codecs for efficient latent encoding and frame reconstruction. It retains the teacher model's G-buffer and text-prompt interfaces while enabling continuous rendering over input streams of unbounded length. We evaluate AlayaRenderer-Flash on G-buffer streams across content preservation, temporal consistency, cross-window stability, prompt controllability, and runtime efficiency. Our results show that AlayaRenderer-Flash substantially reduces inference cost while preserving the core rendering capabilities of the teacher model. By integrating AlayaRenderer-Flash with a physics engine, we build a fully playable generative world running at 30 FPS.

AI.tldr: AlayaRenderer-Flash is a real-time generative world renderer that achieves 31.54 FPS (up from 0.56 FPS) by reformulating the original AlayaRenderer as a few-step autoregressive streaming model with lightweight distilled codecs, enabling continuous, physics-driven interactive play.
AI.motivation: The original AlayaRenderer, while capable of preserving scene structure and world dynamics, is too computationally expensive for real-time deployment (0.56 FPS), limiting its use in interactive world modeling and user-controllable play.
AI.method: AlayaRenderer-Flash reformulates the original renderer as a few-step autoregressive streaming model and introduces lightweight distilled codecs for efficient latent encoding and frame reconstruction, enabling continuous rendering over unbounded input streams.
AI.result: AlayaRenderer-Flash pushes rendering speed from 0.56 FPS to 31.54 FPS, achieving real-time performance while preserving the teacher model's core rendering capabilities, including G-buffer and text-prompt interfaces.
AI.conclusion: AlayaRenderer-Flash substantially reduces inference cost while maintaining content preservation, temporal consistency, cross-window stability, and prompt controllability, enabling a fully playable generative world running at 30 FPS when integrated with a physics engine.

title: Agentic Calibration of Grey-Box Simulation Models: An LLM-Driven Alternative
comment: Manuscript: 19 pages, 2 figures. Appendix: 11 pages, 1 figure
summary: Calibration of grey-box simulation models is a constrained optimization problem in which model evaluations are expensive, the parameter space can be high-dimensional, and the search must respect plausibility constraints. Although the simulation code is fully available to the analyst, the joint effect of multiple parameters remains difficult to predict analytically. Classical optimizers such as Nelder--Mead (NM) are simple to deploy but sample-inefficient, particularly under constraints. Modern Bayesian Optimization methods achieve competitive solutions with far fewer evaluations but require non-trivial modeling machinery for constraint handling. We introduce an agentic calibration method in which a large language model acts as the optimizer, with constraints incorporated as a plain-language section of the system prompt. We evaluate the agentic method, NM, and Bayesian Optimization (BO) on an anal cancer simulation model under both unconstrained and clinically constrained calibration. Under unconstrained calibration, the agentic method achieves substantially lower best error than BO and NM, while requiring fewer model evaluations. Under constrained calibration, the agentic method reaches comparable error levels and both outperform NM. These results are obtained at the cost of increased inference time per iteration. Agentic calibration achieves competitive performance with substantially fewer model evaluations, and constraint handling is essentially free at the modeller-facing interface through simple textual specifications rather than additional modelling machinery. The main trade-off lies in increased per-iteration inference cost, making the approach particularly suitable when simulation time dominates. Beyond performance, the per-iteration rationale makes the search auditable and explainable, so its decisions can be scrutinised and justified to third parties.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces an agentic calibration method using LLMs as optimizers for grey-box simulation models, achieving competitive or better error than Nelder-Mead and Bayesian Optimization with fewer model evaluations and simpler constraint handling via plain-language prompts, at the cost of increased per-iteration inference time.
AI.motivation: Grey-box simulation model calibration is expensive, high-dimensional, and constrained; classical optimizers like Nelder-Mead are sample-inefficient, while Bayesian Optimization requires complex machinery for constraint handling.
AI.method: An LLM acts as the optimizer (agentic calibration) with constraints specified in plain language within the system prompt, evaluated against Nelder-Mead and Bayesian Optimization on an anal cancer simulation model under both unconstrained and clinically constrained settings.
AI.result: Under unconstrained calibration, agentic method achieves substantially lower best error than BO and NM with fewer evaluations. Under constrained calibration, agentic matches BO error and both outperform NM. The trade-off is increased inference time per iteration.
AI.conclusion: Agentic calibration offers competitive performance with fewer model evaluations and simpler constraint handling (via text specifications) than existing methods, most suitable when simulation time dominates over inference cost, with added benefits of auditability and explainability.

title: Structured Synthetic Reasoning Data for Arithmetic Fine-Tuning of Small Language Models
summary: Small language models are attractive for local deployment, but they often struggle with multi-step arithmetic reasoning. We study whether structured synthetic reasoning data can improve this behaviour under consumer-hardware constraints. Starting from GSM8K, we generated a 21,250-example corpus of grade-school arithmetic word-problem variants using GPT-5-mini, combining natural-language solution traces, light Socratic-style cues, structural variation, and irrelevant distractor context. We then fine-tuned Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B with LoRA on consumer hardware (Apple M4, 16 GB RAM). Exact-match accuracy on GSM8K improved from 36.5% to 49.1% for Qwen3-0.6B and from 53.5% to 66.5% for Qwen3-1.7B. For Qwen3-1.7B, transfer to related arithmetic benchmarks was stronger, reaching 98.9% on MultiArith and 73.0% on SVAMP, compared with 54.4% and 45.3% for the base model. Qualitative analysis suggests that fine-tuned models produce shorter reasoning traces, make fewer arithmetic and distractor-use errors, and benefit more consistently from self-consistency sampling. These results show that low-cost synthetic data design can materially improve arithmetic adaptation in small language models. Because the intervention combines Socratic-style cues with other data-design choices, we interpret the gains as evidence for structured synthetic reasoning data rather than as a causal test of Socratic guidance alone.

AI.tldr: Fine-tuning small language models (Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B) with structured synthetic reasoning data (21,250 examples generated from GSM8K using GPT-5-mini, combining solution traces, Socratic cues, structural variation, and distractors) on consumer hardware (Apple M4, 16GB RAM) improves arithmetic reasoning, with Qwen3-1.7B reaching 66.5% on GSM8K, 98.9% on MultiArith, and 73.0% on SVAMP.
AI.motivation: Small language models struggle with multi-step arithmetic reasoning, and we investigate whether structured synthetic reasoning data can improve this under consumer-hardware constraints.
AI.method: Generated a 21,250-example corpus of grade-school arithmetic word-problem variants from GSM8K using GPT-5-mini, incorporating natural-language solution traces, Socratic-style cues, structural variation, and irrelevant distractors. Fine-tuned Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B with LoRA on Apple M4 (16GB RAM).
AI.result: Exact-match accuracy improved from 36.5% to 49.1% (Qwen3-0.6B) and 53.5% to 66.5% (Qwen3-1.7B) on GSM8K. Qwen3-1.7B transferred well: 98.9% on MultiArith, 73.0% on SVAMP. Fine-tuned models produced shorter reasoning traces with fewer arithmetic and distractor-use errors.
AI.conclusion: Low-cost synthetic data design can materially improve arithmetic adaptation in small language models under consumer hardware constraints.

title: Continual Video-MLLM Adaptation over Evolving Domains
summary: Video multimodal large language models have shown strong capability in video understanding, yet their adaptation to sequentially evolving domains remains underexplored. In real-world deployments, video data often arrives continuously from heterogeneous domains, requiring the model to acquire new domain-specific knowledge without overwriting previously learned capabilities. Existing continual learning methods typically rely on shared adaptation spaces, which can induce severe cross-domain interference and catastrophic forgetting. We propose Distribution-Aware Expert Routing, a parameter-efficient framework for continual Video-MLLM adaptation over evolving domains. DAER maintains domain-isolated lightweight experts while keeping the pretrained Video-MLLM backbone frozen, thereby decoupling domain-specific adaptation from the general multimodal knowledge of the pretrained model. To enable fine-grained specialization, we introduce an intra-domain distribution-aware routing mechanism that matches each input to expert-level prototype reservoirs using MMD. To address the absence of task identities at inference time, we further propose an inter-domain routing mechanism that performs prototype matching in a discriminative subspace for robust domain identification. In addition, we introduce adaptive domain merging to improve parameter scalability and adopt a two-stage optimization strategy to stabilize expert specialization during continual learning. We evaluate DAER by curating a domain-incremental benchmark built from ten VidQA datasets covering diverse visual environments and reasoning demands. Experiments on two strong Video-MLLM backbones show that DAER consistently outperforms prior methods.

AI.tldr: DAER is a parameter-efficient continual learning framework for Video-MLLMs that uses distribution-aware expert routing with domain-isolated experts, MMD-based prototype matching, and adaptive domain merging to prevent catastrophic forgetting when adapting to sequentially evolving video domains.
AI.motivation: Video-MLLMs struggle with continual learning in real-world deployments where video data arrives continuously from heterogeneous domains, as existing continual learning methods relying on shared adaptation spaces induce cross-domain interference and catastrophic forgetting.
AI.method: DAER maintains domain-isolated lightweight experts with a frozen Video-MLLM backbone, uses intra-domain distribution-aware routing (MMD-based prototype matching to expert-level reservoirs) and inter-domain routing (prototype matching in a discriminative subspace for domain identification without task identities), plus adaptive domain merging for scalability and two-stage optimization for expert specialization.
AI.result: Evaluated on a domain-incremental benchmark built from ten VidQA datasets covering diverse visual environments and reasoning demands, DAER consistently outperforms prior methods on two strong Video-MLLM backbones.
AI.conclusion: DAER effectively enables continual Video-MLLM adaptation over evolving domains by decoupling domain-specific adaptation from general multimodal knowledge, demonstrating superior performance in mitigating catastrophic forgetting compared to existing approaches.

title: Spatio-Temporal Prediction of Unsteady Airfoil Aerodynamics Using Augmented Graph Neural Ordinary Differential Equations with Exogenous Controls
comment: 27 pages, 18 figures, submitted to Computers & Fluids
summary: Unsteady aerodynamic phenomena, such as gusts, turbulence, and fluid-structure interactions affect an aircraft during flight. For design, optimisation and certification, it is indispensable to quantify such unsteady aerodynamic effects. Industry-standard computational fluid dynamics methods, such as solving the unsteady Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes equations or the linearized frequency domain method, are either computationally expensive or restricted by assumptions like linearity. Once trained, machine learning methods are capable of computing non-linear relationships very fast, making them suitable as surrogate models. By autoregressively applying graph neural networks (GNNs), operating on a discretised spatial domain, spatio-temporal predictions can be made. However, autoregressive GNNs suffer from error accumulation leading to unstable rollouts over time. Here we show that combining GNNs with augmented Neural Ordinary Differential Equations yields temporally stable predictions of the surface forces on a pitching airfoil. We found that our approach, called GNODE, based on Graph Neural Ordinary Differential Equations, provides temporally more stable, spatially smoother, and overall more accurate results than an autoregressive GNN baseline. Tests are conducted on a dataset consisting of a simulations of a pitching airfoil, including transonic shocks, transient behaviour and dynamic non-linearities. Augmenting GNODEs with additional latent dimensions improves the expressivity and accuracy by capturing underlying history effects. The developed method demonstrates an approach that is suitable to model non-linear spatio-temporal systems with exogenous inputs.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes GNODE, a method combining graph neural networks with augmented Neural ODEs, to produce temporally stable and accurate predictions of unsteady aerodynamic forces (surface forces on a pitching airfoil), outperforming autoregressive GNN baselines by mitigating error accumulation.
AI.motivation: Unsteady aerodynamic phenomena (gusts, turbulence, fluid-structure interactions) are critical for aircraft design and certification, but existing methods (URANS, linearized frequency domain) are either computationally expensive or limited by linearity assumptions. Machine learning surrogate models offer speed but suffer from error accumulation in autoregressive spatio-temporal predictions.
AI.method: The GNODE approach integrates graph neural networks (GNNs) operating on discretised spatial domains with augmented Neural Ordinary Differential Equations (NODEs) to make spatio-temporal predictions. Additional latent dimensions are used to capture history effects and improve expressivity.
AI.result: GNODE provides temporally more stable, spatially smoother, and overall more accurate surface force predictions on a pitching airfoil compared to an autoregressive GNN baseline, tested on simulations including transonic shocks, transient behaviour, and dynamic non-linearities.
AI.conclusion: Combining GNNs with augmented NODEs is a suitable approach for modeling non-linear spatio-temporal systems with exogenous inputs, effectively addressing the instability issue in autoregressive GNNs.

title: Fence: Specialized SLM Guardrails for LLM Applications
summary: Real-world applications that use closed-source large language models (LLMs) need advanced safety measures that go beyond the basic content filters. Content moderation filters such as toxicity and bias have relatively standard definitions where as application specific guardrails like hallucination, topic drift and behaviour deviation are more difficult to model and can vary by use case. Additionally, data scarcity and annotation costs, make the process of creating and testing specialized guardrails challenging. In this work, we propose using Small Language Models (SLMs) trained on synthetic data as specialized guardrails for LLM applications. We introduce a novel synthetic data generation method inspired by the design of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to generate high quality synthetic data samples which can be used to train SLMs to encode use case specific guardrail information and hence function as specialized guardrails. Our experiments demonstrate that SLM guardrails trained on high quality synthetic data show performance gains over prompt based LLM guardrails.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using Small Language Models (SLMs) trained on GAN-inspired synthetic data as specialized guardrails for LLM applications, outperforming prompt-based LLM guardrails.
AI.motivation: Real-world closed-source LLM applications need advanced safety measures beyond basic content filters. Specialized guardrails like hallucination, topic drift, and behavior deviation are difficult to model and vary by use case. Data scarcity and high annotation costs further complicate creating and testing these guardrails.
AI.method: The authors propose training Small Language Models (SLMs) on synthetic data as specialized guardrails. A novel synthetic data generation method inspired by Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) is introduced to produce high-quality synthetic samples. These samples are used to train SLMs to encode use-case-specific guardrail information.
AI.result: SLM guardrails trained on high-quality synthetic data demonstrate performance gains over prompt-based LLM guardrails.
AI.conclusion: SLMs trained with GAN-inspired synthetic data generation are an effective and scalable approach for creating specialized guardrails, addressing data scarcity and cost challenges while outperforming prompt-based methods.

title: SkyEV: RGB-Event UAV detection and tracking dataset and baseline
summary: Detecting UAVs in air spaces has become increasingly important due to UAVs widespread availability and easy usage. However, due to their small size, they are typically difficult to detect at a sufficient range. For the training of optimized detection algorithms, datasets have been published, covering optical sensing methods ranging from infrared to regular RGB to event-sensor-based. However, these datasets often fail to reflect realistic counter-UAV scenarios, lacking critical factors such as camera ego-motion, extremely small target scales, and diverse lens configurations, and introduce compression artefacts on the frame images. To address this gap, we introduce SkyEV, an open-source dataset featuring highly synchronized uncompressed RGB and event-based data. SkyEV distinguishes itself by capturing complex real-world conditions, including significant camera motion and varied optical setups, which are essential for testing the fundamental trade-off between Field of View and detection range. Furthermore, we provide a unified data loader and establish an experimental baseline using a multi-modal architecture, demonstrating the dataset's efficacy in detecting challenging, small-scale targets.

AI.tldr: SkyEV is a new open-source dataset with synchronized uncompressed RGB and event-based data for UAV detection, designed to address limitations of existing datasets by including real-world challenges like camera ego-motion, extremely small targets, diverse lens configurations, and varying Field of View vs. detection range trade-offs.
AI.motivation: Existing UAV detection datasets fail to reflect realistic counter-UAV scenarios, lacking critical factors such as camera ego-motion, extremely small target scales, diverse lens configurations, and introduce compression artifacts. SkyEV addresses this gap.
AI.method: The authors introduce SkyEV, an open-source dataset featuring highly synchronized uncompressed RGB and event-based data. It captures complex real-world conditions including significant camera motion and varied optical setups. They also provide a unified data loader and establish an experimental baseline using a multi-modal architecture.
AI.result: The dataset demonstrates efficacy in detecting challenging, small-scale targets through baseline experiments with a multi-modal architecture.
AI.conclusion: SkyEV fills a critical gap in UAV detection datasets by providing realistic, high-quality synchronized RGB-event data that enables testing of the fundamental trade-off between Field of View and detection range in real-world counter-UAV scenarios.

title: Interactive Training 2: Auditable Control Plane for Live Model Training
summary: Experiment trackers show how training is progressing, but changing a live run still usually requires trainer-specific code. We present Interactive Training 2, an open-source control plane for steering training through a shared protocol. Training applications declare which settings and actions they expose, humans and automated controllers submit requests through the same interface, and the training loop validates and applies them at safe control points. A customized Aim workspace combines live metrics and controls with a chronological record of requests and outcomes. We demonstrate the system across five NLP and reinforcement-learning workflows. The released code and traces provide a reusable foundation for auditable human- and agent-guided training.

AI.tldr: Interactive Training 2 is an open-source control plane that enables real-time steering of training runs through a shared protocol, demonstrated across NLP and RL workflows.
AI.motivation: Changing live training runs typically requires trainer-specific code, limiting flexibility and human-in-the-loop control.
AI.method: The system uses a shared protocol where training applications declare exposed settings/actions, humans and automated controllers submit requests via the same interface, and the training loop validates/applies changes at safe control points, integrated with a customized Aim workspace for live metrics and audit trails.
AI.result: Demonstrated across five NLP and reinforcement-learning workflows; released code and traces provide a reusable foundation.
AI.conclusion: Interactive Training 2 enables auditable, human- and agent-guided training without requiring trainer-specific code modifications.

title: Wisdom of LLM Crowds: Aggregation and Contamination in Language Model Ensembles
summary: The wisdom of crowds -- the finding that aggregating judgments across individuals often outperforms the best individual -- has been extensively studied with human forecasters. Whether the same phenomenon emerges when the ``crowd'' consists of large language models (LLMs) is an open question with both theoretical and practical implications. We elicited probability estimates from 15 LLMs on 254 binary prediction market questions and evaluated classical and learned aggregation methods. Learned aggregators -- a multilayer perceptron and a logistic regression -- outperformed all individual models and classical methods. The logistic regression was found to match the neural network, suggesting that the benefit of learned aggregation derives from learning a linear combination of diverse model outputs rather than from nonlinear interactions. Symbolic regression applied to the neural network's learned mapping recovered a pure model-disagreement signal as the lowest-complexity useful formula on the Pareto frontier, further supporting this interpretation. Training cutoff contamination proved a pervasive confound: the apparent capability gap between frontier cloud models and smaller local models collapsed from 35.8% to 8.9% on a clean subset of questions resolving after all models' training cutoffs, and individual model rankings showed only moderate stability. Even when the prediction market is evaluated at each model's training cutoff, LLMs remained substantially less accurate, indicating a genuine gap in collective information aggregation. These findings suggest that LLM crowds can exhibit wisdom-of-crowds effects, but that contamination-free evaluation is essential for reliable assessment.

AI.tldr: The study investigates whether the "wisdom of crowds" effect emerges when aggregating predictions from multiple LLMs on binary prediction market questions. Learned aggregation methods (MLP and logistic regression) outperformed individual models and classical methods, with logistic regression matching the neural network, suggesting the benefit comes from linear combination of diverse outputs rather than nonlinear interactions. Training cutoff contamination was a significant confound, collapsing the performance gap between frontier and local models from 35.8% to 8.9% on clean data.
AI.motivation: To determine whether the wisdom-of-crowds phenomenon, well-established with human forecasters, extends to crowds of LLMs, and to assess the role of contamination in LLM evaluation.
AI.method: Elicited probability estimates from 15 LLMs on 254 binary prediction market questions, evaluated classical aggregation methods (e.g., averaging) vs. learned aggregation (MLP, logistic regression), applied symbolic regression to interpret the neural network's mapping, and analyzed contamination effects using training cutoff information.
AI.result: Learned aggregators outperformed all individual models; logistic regression matched MLP performance; symbolic regression recovered a pure model-disagreement signal as the simplest useful formula; contamination collapsed the frontier-vs-local model gap from 35.8% to 8.9%; individual model rankings showed only moderate stability.
AI.conclusion: LLM crowds exhibit wisdom-of-crowds effects, but the benefit of learned aggregation is primarily from linear combination of diverse outputs. Contamination-free evaluation is critical for reliable assessment, and a genuine capability gap remains even after controlling for contamination.

title: Weakly Supervised Pathology-Informed Representation Learning for PET-Based Content Retrieval of Intra-Tumour Heterogeneity
summary: We propose a weakly supervised 18FFDG PET representation-learning framework for content based medical image retrieval, using H&E derived information during training while preserving PET-only inference. The proposed method was designed to use H&E derived information during training while maintaining PET only inference. A teacher student training strategy was used to learn the PET tumour derived voxel representations, from which global and hotspot conditioned embeddings were generated along with maps of intra tumour heterogeneity in our oesophegeal cancer test case. A progressive ablation strategy was used to evaluate the contribution of different supervision mechanisms. Retrieval performance was assessed across cross-validation folds using metrics including mean average precision, normalised discounted cumulative gain and mean reciprocal rank. Additional analyses evaluated ablation performance, hotspot faithfulness through perturbation/deletion experiments, prototype-specific PET uptake behaviour and indirect patient level concordance between learned PET prototype classes and selected histomic features. Progressive introduction of pathology informed supervision and hotspot modelling improved PET retrieval performance compared with global PET representations and conventional PET baselines. Across the ablation ladder, PET hotspot conditioned representations consistently provided stronger retrieval than global embeddings, indicating that focusing on informative tumour subregions improved sensitivity to intra tumour heterogeneity. Histopathology concordance further showed that the learned classes were not simply high uptake PET regions; instead, they demonstrated distinct heterogeneity in 18F FDG uptake.

AI.tldr: A weakly supervised PET representation-learning framework using H&E pathology information during training enables PET-only content-based medical image retrieval, with hotspot-conditioned embeddings outperforming global representations by capturing intra-tumor heterogeneity.
AI.motivation: To improve content-based medical image retrieval for PET by leveraging H&E pathology information during training while preserving PET-only inference, enabling better capture of intra-tumor heterogeneity.
AI.method: Teacher-student training strategy using H&E-derived information, with global and hotspot-conditioned embeddings generated from PET tumor voxel representations; progressive ablation across supervision mechanisms; perturbation/deletion experiments for hotspot faithfulness.
AI.result: Pathology-informed supervision and hotspot modeling improved PET retrieval over global representations and conventional PET baselines; hotspot-conditioned embeddings consistently outperformed global embeddings; learned classes showed distinct FDG uptake heterogeneity beyond high-uptake regions.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating histopathology-derived supervision and focusing on tumor subregions via hotspot modeling enhances PET retrieval by improving sensitivity to intra-tumor heterogeneity, and learned representations are clinically meaningful beyond simple uptake patterns.

title: Cost Accounting for Reactive Computational Graphs: Exhaustive Sweeps, Sequential Mutation, and the Backward-Locality Gap
comment: Companion paper: "Exact Network Surgery: Functional Invariance and Gradient Plasticity in Reactive Computational Graphs" (submitted concurrently)
summary: Exhaustive site-by-site interventions on a neural network's computational graph -- activation-patching sweeps, circuit-discovery searches, systematic ablation studies -- mutate the graph at every candidate site, and their cost is dominated by recomputation after each mutation. On a reactive graph engine whose invalidation provably touches exactly the downstream cone of a mutated node, we give a complete cost accounting for such workloads. First, the aggregate speedup of an exhaustive sweep over independent full recomputations is not a universal constant: if per-layer weight varies regularly with depth at Karamata index q, the ratio converges to (q+2)/(q+1) when weight concentrates near the output and to q+2 near the input, recovering 2 only in the depth-uniform case; a wall-clock corollary predicts a ceiling of about 1.79, below 2, until interpreter overhead is compiled away. Second, we prove the exact cost of a sequence of persistent mutations, never undone between insertions: the interleaved cost exceeds the isolated sum by an exact overcount summed over comparable site pairs, with closed-form extremes over insertion orders, while batched application is order-independent and sub-additive, costing exactly the union of the sites' cones plus the fresh nodes. Third, we prove the exact mirror of forward locality for the backward pass, showing it collapses the aggregate speedup to 1 under backpropagation on architectures without long skip connections. Every identity is validated on NeuroDSL, a reactive graph engine in Julia: measured sweep ratios converge to the predicted limits under four cost profiles; the training-mode ratio collapses to 1 at the predicted rate; and all 18 per-graft sequential costs and the batched total match the closed forms at zero tolerance across three insertion orders.

AI.tldr: This paper provides a complete cost accounting for exhaustive site-by-site neural network interventions (activation patching, circuit discovery, ablation studies) using a reactive graph engine. It derives analytical speedup limits (~1.79 ceiling), proves exact costs for sequential mutations and batched application, and shows backward-pass collapses speedup to 1 without long skip connections, validated on NeuroDSL in Julia.
AI.motivation: Exhaustive site-by-site interventions on neural networks (activation patching, circuit searches, ablation studies) are computationally expensive due to repeated recomputation after each mutation. Prior work lacks a rigorous cost model for these workloads, making it unclear what speedups are achievable and how to optimally schedule mutations.
AI.method: The authors formalize a reactive graph engine where invalidation provably touches exactly the downstream cone of a mutated node. They derive analytical expressions for (1) aggregate speedup of sweeping vs. independent recomputation as a function of per-layer weight distribution (Karamata index q), (2) exact cost of sequential persistent mutations with overcount terms and order-dependent closed forms, (3) batched application cost as union of sites' cones plus fresh nodes, and (4) backward-pass mirror showing speedup collapse to 1. All identities are validated on NeuroDSL (Julia-based reactive graph engine).
AI.result: The sweep speedup converges to (q+2)/(q+1) near output and q+2 near input, recovering 2 only in the depth-uniform case; wall-clock ceiling ~1.79. Training-mode ratio collapses to 1 at the predicted rate. All 18 per-graft sequential costs and batched total match closed forms at zero tolerance across three insertion orders.
AI.conclusion: The reactive graph engine provides provably optimal recomputation for intervention workloads. Practical speedups are bounded below 2x unless interpreter overhead is compiled away. The backward pass offers no speedup benefit, and batched mutations are order-independent and sub-additive. These results enable principled optimization of mechanistic interpretability and ablation workflows.

title: Trajectory-Aware Clinical Risk Prediction via Severity-Grounded Knowledge Graphs and Retrieval-Augmented Generation
summary: While Electronic Health Records (EHRs) offer a wealth of clinical data, effectively augmenting a patient's records with heterogeneous external knowledge to predict the patient's clinical risk remains a significant challenge. Existing methods fail to capture disease severity, treatment responses, and nuanced clinical progression, due to data sparsity and the underutilization of unstructured clinical notes. To address these challenges, we propose TRACER (a trajectory-aware and clinically grounded prediction framework) that (1) constructs a medical knowledge graph enriched with severity information from medical literature, (2) retrieves clinically relevant, severity-weighted paths of a patient's progression from the knowledge graph, (3) extracts clinically relevant events from unstructured clinical notes, and (4) augments patient context with similar peer cases. Experiments on the MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV datasets demonstrate large gains over state-of-the-art baselines, with up to 28.5% increase in Macro F1 score for the mortality prediction task, and 19.7% increase for the readmission prediction task.

AI.tldr: TRACER is a trajectory-aware clinical prediction framework that augments EHR data with severity-weighted medical knowledge graphs, clinical notes, and peer cases, achieving up to 28.5% improvement in mortality prediction and 19.7% in readmission prediction on MIMIC-III/IV.
AI.motivation: Existing EHR-based methods fail to capture disease severity, treatment responses, and nuanced clinical progression due to data sparsity and underutilization of unstructured clinical notes, motivating the need for a framework that integrates heterogeneous external knowledge.
AI.method: TRACER (1) constructs a medical knowledge graph enriched with severity information from literature, (2) retrieves severity-weighted progression paths, (3) extracts clinically relevant events from unstructured notes, and (4) augments patient context with similar peer cases.
AI.result: On MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV, TRACER achieves up to 28.5% Macro F1 improvement for mortality prediction and 19.7% improvement for readmission prediction over state-of-the-art baselines.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating severity-weighted knowledge graphs, clinical notes, and peer case augmentation significantly enhances clinical risk prediction accuracy.

title: Posterior Samplings are Missing Modalities Generators for Medical Image Translation
summary: Magnetic resonance imaging comes in various modality contrasts that provide complementary anatomical and pathological information. Complete multimodal acquisitions are often unavailable due to time and protocol constraints. This leads to real-world datasets with missing modalities, where conventional medical image translation methods are typically limited to fixed source-target settings or require retraining for each observed source-target pair. We propose a unified framework that formulates missing-modality generation as a linear inverse problem under a joint distribution and solves it via posterior sampling with a flow matching model. By learning a joint prior over the complete modality set, our method can reconstruct arbitrary missing modalities at inference time by guiding the sampling trajectory to enforce measurement consistency with observed modalities. We further mitigate inter-modality error propagation in multi-target generation by adopting a many-to-one sampling strategy. Experiments on BraTS and IXI datasets show that our method achieves the best performance over baselines across most missing-modality scenarios. In downstream tumor segmentation, synthesized images from our method result in higher segmentation performance, indicating better preservation of clinically relevant structures.

AI.tldr: A unified flow matching framework for generating arbitrary missing MRI modalities from any subset of observed modalities by formulating it as a linear inverse problem with posterior sampling.
AI.motivation: Real-world medical imaging datasets often have incomplete multimodal MRI acquisitions due to time and protocol constraints, and existing methods are limited to fixed source-target pairs or require retraining for each scenario.
AI.method: Formulates missing-modality generation as a linear inverse problem under a joint distribution, solved via posterior sampling with a flow matching model. Uses a many-to-one sampling strategy to mitigate inter-modality error propagation in multi-target generation.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art performance on BraTS and IXI datasets across most missing-modality scenarios, and yields higher downstream tumor segmentation performance.
AI.conclusion: The unified framework effectively handles arbitrary missing-modality generation without retraining, and better preserves clinically relevant structures for downstream tasks.

title: Dynamic Loss Balancing for Joint SOH and RUL Prediction of Lithium-Ion Batteries via a Rotary SOH-Injected Prior Battery Transformer
summary: The deployment of reliable lithium-ion battery management systems is crucial for accelerating electrification, yet the joint prognosis of State of Health (SOH) and Remaining Useful Life (RUL) remains severely hindered by task heteroscedasticity. Conventional multi-task learning frameworks fail to balance the bounded, low-variance noise of SOH estimation with the unbounded, nonlinearly expanding uncertainty of long-term RUL predictions. Here, we present the Rotary SOH-Injected Prior Battery Transformer (RoSIP-Batt), a unified co-estimation framework that resolves these optimization conflicts. By formulating joint prediction as a Bayesian multi-task objective, RoSIP-Batt introduces a homoscedastic uncertainty weighting mechanism to dynamically scale task-specific gradients based on learned residual noise levels. The architecture leverages decoupled dual classification tokens and a per-dimension gated fusion mechanism, secured by a gradient-detachment operator to prevent high-variance RUL updates from corrupting the stable SOH representation space.
