To capture electrochemical degradation patterns without relying on absolute cycle steps, Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) is incorporated into a shared Transformer backbone to model translation-invariant relative temporal profiles. Crucially, the intermediate SOH estimate is directly injected into the RUL regression head as a physical degradation prior. Evaluations across the NASA, MIT-Stanford, and HUST datasets show that RoSIP-Batt significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, reducing SOH estimation error to 1.994% MAE on NASA and restricting RUL prediction error to 62.85 cycles on Stanford. These findings establish RoSIP-Batt as a highly generalizable, computationally efficient solution suitable for real-time embedded BMS deployment.

AI.tldr: RoSIP-Batt is a unified Bayesian multi-task framework for joint SOH and RUL prediction of lithium-ion batteries, using homoscedastic uncertainty weighting, decoupled dual classification tokens, gated fusion with gradient detachment, and Rotary Position Embedding, achieving state-of-the-art results on NASA, MIT-Stanford, and HUST datasets.
AI.motivation: Joint SOH and RUL prognosis is hindered by task heteroscedasticity—bounded low-variance noise in SOH vs. unbounded expanding uncertainty in long-term RUL—which conventional multi-task learning fails to balance.
AI.method: Formulates joint prediction as a Bayesian multi-task objective with homoscedastic uncertainty weighting for dynamic gradient scaling; decoupled dual classification tokens; per-dimension gated fusion with gradient-detachment operator to protect SOH representation; Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) for translation-invariant temporal modeling; and injection of intermediate SOH estimate into RUL head as physical degradation prior.
AI.result: SOH MAE of 1.994% on NASA dataset; RUL error of 62.85 cycles on MIT-Stanford dataset; consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across all three benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: RoSIP-Batt is a highly generalizable, computationally efficient solution suitable for real-time embedded BMS deployment.

title: Using LLMs for Explainable, Data-Driven Insight Generation from Time Series
summary:
Time series forecasts are widely used in decision-critical domains, where they are rarely consumed without accompanying explanations. Producing such explanations is usually a manual and costly process, and attempts to automate it using large language models often suffer from hallucination when applied to temporal data. We propose a domain-agnostic framework for grounded natural language explanation generation for time series forecasts, illustrated in Figure 1. The framework consists of three components: (i) extraction of structured explanatory factors from historical analyst-written explanations, (ii) evidence-conditioned explanation generation, and (iii) scalable evaluation for readability, logical consistency, and persuasiveness. The design explicitly constrains generation to verifiable evidence, reducing unsupported claims.
  We evaluate the framework on a financial forecasting case study involving the NASDAQ-100 index and a freight pricing case study using data from Vortexa. Results show that generated explanations approached analyst-written explanations in terms of readability, consistency and persuasiveness. These findings demonstrate that grounded explanation generation for time series forecasting can be achieved at scale without domain-specific fine-tuning.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a domain-agnostic framework for generating grounded natural language explanations for time series forecasts, consisting of structured factor extraction, evidence-conditioned generation, and scalable evaluation. The framework reduces hallucination by constraining generation to verifiable evidence, and is validated on NASDAQ-100 and freight pricing case studies.
AI.motivation: Time series forecasts in decision-critical domains require accompanying explanations, but manual explanation generation is costly, and existing LLM-based automation suffers from hallucination when applied to temporal data.
AI.method: A three-component domain-agnostic framework: (i) extraction of structured explanatory factors from historical analyst-written explanations, (ii) evidence-conditioned explanation generation constrained to verifiable evidence, and (iii) scalable evaluation for readability, logical consistency, and persuasiveness.
AI.result: On NASDAQ-100 and freight pricing case studies, generated explanations approached analyst-written explanations in readability, consistency, and persuasiveness.
AI.conclusion: Grounded explanation generation for time series forecasting can be achieved at scale without domain-specific fine-tuning, reducing unsupported claims through evidence-constrained generation.

title: Bounding Boxes to Improve Small Language Model Performance on Vision-Based Grading Tasks
comment: Accepted for 1st Workshop on Small Language Models for Education (SLM4ED '26) at AIED 2026
summary: The deployment of Small Language Models (SLMs) in educational settings offers significant advantages in terms of privacy, cost, and scalability. However, SLMs often struggle with complex vision-based tasks, such as grading handwritten student exams, due to the high computational cost of processing large images and the visual distractions present on a full page. In this paper, we investigate whether cropping student responses using bounding boxes can improve the accuracy and computational efficiency of SLMs on a short-answer grading task. Using a dataset of scanned handwritten responses from the 2025 Australian Physics Olympiad, we evaluate the performance of several models ranging from 4B to 72B parameters under varying conditions of Chain of Thought (CoT) prompting and image cropping. Our results demonstrate that using bounding boxes significantly improves grading accuracy and reduces computational cost (FLOPs) across models. We conclude that bounding boxes are a crucial pre-processing step for deploying SLMs in large-scale, vision-based educational assessments.

AI.tldr: Using bounding boxes to crop student responses significantly improves the accuracy and computational efficiency of Small Language Models (SLMs) for grading handwritten exams, tested on Australian Physics Olympiad data.
AI.motivation: SLMs offer privacy, cost, and scalability benefits for education, but struggle with complex vision-based tasks like grading handwritten exams due to high computational cost and visual distractions in full-page images.
AI.method: Cropped student responses using bounding boxes on a dataset of scanned handwritten answers from the 2025 Australian Physics Olympiad; evaluated models from 4B to 72B parameters with varying Chain of Thought (CoT) prompting and image cropping conditions.
AI.result: Bounding boxes significantly improve grading accuracy and reduce computational cost (FLOPs) across all model sizes.
AI.conclusion: Bounding boxes are a crucial pre-processing step for deploying SLMs in large-scale, vision-based educational assessments.

title: Deep Reinforcement Learning to Master the Asymmetric Strategy of Baghchal
summary: Baghchal is a two-player asymmetric board game with Nepali origins where four tigers are to capture goats and twenty goats desire to keep tigers in immobility. Although Baghchal has a complex structure which is strategic, has perfect information structure, and has cultural meaning, it has not been adequately covered in deep reinforcement learning (RL) literature. This paper gives a systematic exploration of four deep RL solutions Deep Q-Network (DQN), REINFORCE, Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) and MuZero that are trained on one side of the asymmetric gameplay of Baghchal and then evaluated on the other side. The algorithms are rated based on win rate, draw rate, average captures, training convergence and computational cost. It is experimentally found that MuZero generates the best performance in both tasks, achieving 86 percent win over these Tiger and 62 percent win over these Goat and the ability to do so is due to the model-based planning machine through the Monte Carlo Tree Search. PPO is the most realistic algorithm and is provided to be competitive over both asymmetric tasks with significantly reduced computational costs compared to MuZero. Emergent strategic behavior analysis shows that model-based strategies are optimal over long-horizon planning, whereas value-based counterparts like DQN are more biased up towards the Tiger role owing to the more substantial reward signal.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically compares four deep RL algorithms (DQN, REINFORCE, PPO, MuZero) on the asymmetric board game Baghchal, finding MuZero achieves the highest win rates (86% as Tiger, 62% as Goat) due to model-based MCTS planning, while PPO offers a computationally efficient competitive alternative.
AI.motivation: Baghchal is a strategically complex, perfect-information asymmetric board game with cultural significance that has been inadequately explored in deep reinforcement learning literature.
AI.method: Four deep RL solutions (DQN, REINFORCE, PPO, MuZero) are trained on one side of asymmetric gameplay and evaluated on the other side, rated by win rate, draw rate, average captures, training convergence, and computational cost.
AI.result: MuZero achieves the best performance (86% win rate as Tiger, 62% as Goat) attributed to model-based MCTS planning. PPO is the most practical computationally-efficient competitive alternative. DQN exhibits bias toward the Tiger role due to stronger reward signals.
AI.conclusion: Model-based strategies (MuZero) excel in long-horizon planning for asymmetric games, while value-based methods like DQN show role-dependent bias. PPO strikes the best balance between performance and computational cost.

title: Cross-Modal UAV Object Tracking: State-Aware Representation Learning and A Unified Benchmark
summary: Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) object tracking has emerged as a popular research field with broad practical applications. Modern UAVs are increasingly equipped with both visible light and thermal infrared sensors. However, due to constraints in communication bandwidth, computational resources and power consumption, current systems often activate one modality and switch between modalities to maintain robust tracking in complex scenarios. Such modality switch inevitably leads to significant appearance change and sudden spatial shift, posing great challenges for existing tracking algorithms. To handle this problem, we propose a novel State-Aware Representation Learning Approach called SARLA, which perceives the inconsistent modality states of current frame with template and last frame in the target representations to adapt to the sudden changes in both appearance and position, for robust cross-modal object tracking. In particular, we propose the Modality State Aware Representation Module (MSARM) and Spatial State Aware Representation Module (SSARM). MSARM guides the model to learn appearance correlation, bridging the modality gap, while SSARM models cross-frame spatial correlation to mitigate sudden spatial shift impacts. In addition, we design a spatial shift prediction loss to further handle the effects of spatial variation caused by modality switch. To promote the development of this research field, we establish a large-scale video benchmark called CM-UOT, which consists of 1079 cross-modal sequences with an average video length greater than 621 frames and encompasses over 671K frames in total. Extensive experiments on CM-UOT dataset demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed SARLA against 20 excellent tracking methods. The source code, datasets, and evaluation protocols associated with this work are publicly available at: https://github.com/hongsmile365/sarla-.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes SARLA, a State-Aware Representation Learning Approach for cross-modal UAV object tracking that handles sudden appearance and spatial changes caused by modality switching between visible and thermal infrared sensors. It introduces MSARM and SSARM modules, a spatial shift prediction loss, and a new benchmark dataset CM-UOT with 1079 sequences (671K+ frames). Experiments show SARLA outperforms 20 existing methods.
AI.motivation: Existing UAV tracking systems switch between visible and thermal infrared modalities due to resource constraints, causing sudden appearance changes and spatial shifts that challenge current tracking algorithms. There is a need for an approach that can robustly handle these modality switch-induced inconsistencies.
AI.method: The paper proposes SARLA with two key modules: (1) Modality State Aware Representation Module (MSARM) for learning appearance correlation and bridging modality gaps, and (2) Spatial State Aware Representation Module (SSARM) for modeling cross-frame spatial correlation to mitigate sudden spatial shifts. A spatial shift prediction loss is also designed to further handle spatial variation effects. Additionally, a large-scale CM-UOT benchmark dataset is constructed.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on the CM-UOT dataset demonstrate SARLA achieves superior performance compared to 20 state-of-the-art tracking methods. The dataset comprises 1079 cross-modal sequences with over 671K frames.
AI.conclusion: SARLA effectively addresses cross-modal UAV object tracking challenges caused by modality switching through state-aware representation learning. The public release of code, datasets, and evaluation protocols aims to advance research in this field.

title: ChemHyperMag: Physics-informed magnetic hypergraph learning improves molecular ADMET prediction
comment: Accepted by Proceedings of the AI4Physics Workshop at the 43 rd International Conference on Machine Learning (AI4Physics@ICML 2026)
summary: Accurate prediction of ADMET (Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism, Excretion, and Toxicity) is important for drug discovery. Most predictors use undirected molecular graphs and pairwise edges. This choice misses asymmetric interactions, nonreversible dynamics, and motif level effects from functional groups and ring systems. We propose ChemHyperMag for multitask ADMET prediction under missing labels. ChemHyperMag builds a functional group hypergraph from rings, BRICS fragments, Bemis-Murcko scaffolds, and bonds. It also defines a potential driven nonreversible flow guided by electronegativity and Gasteiger partial charges. The resulting circulation is encoded by a Hermitian magnetic Laplacian and processed with a magnetic Chebyshev encoder. We perturb magnetic phases to form stochastic views and train with an InfoNCE objective. Experiments on multiple ADMET benchmarks show improvements over recent methods with fewer labeled samples and no conformers. ChemHyperMag is scalable and provides interpretable directional signals through its magnetic phases.

AI.tldr: ChemHyperMag is a multitask ADMET predictor that uses functional group hypergraphs and magnetic Chebyshev encoders with nonreversible flow dynamics, achieving state-of-the-art results with fewer labels and no conformers.
AI.motivation: Existing ADMET predictors rely on undirected molecular graphs with pairwise edges, which fail to capture asymmetric interactions, nonreversible dynamics, and motif-level effects from functional groups and ring systems.
AI.method: ChemHyperMag constructs a functional group hypergraph from rings, BRICS fragments, Bemis-Murcko scaffolds, and bonds; defines potential-driven nonreversible flow guided by electronegativity and Gasteiger charges; encodes this using a Hermitian magnetic Laplacian with a magnetic Chebyshev encoder; and uses perturbed magnetic phases for stochastic views trained with an InfoNCE objective.
AI.result: Outperforms recent methods on multiple ADMET benchmarks with fewer labeled samples and without requiring conformer information; provides interpretable directional signals through magnetic phases.
AI.conclusion: ChemHyperMag offers a scalable, interpretable, and label-efficient approach to multitask ADMET prediction by modeling asymmetric interactions and nonreversible flow via magnetic graph representations.

title: Operational Hallucination and Safety Drift in AI Agents
summary: Large language models (LLMs) serving as planners in tool-using autonomous agents introduce dynamic reliability risks in multi-turn execution. While single-turn safety mechanisms are relatively mature, extended interactions reveal structural vulnerabilities where initial alignment degrades over time. This paper empirically characterizes two observed failure modes across multiple state-of-the-art LLMs: Safety Drift, the gradual erosion of declared safety intent leading to constraint-violating actions (e.g., textual refusal followed by reconnaissance and unsafe execution), and Operational Hallucination, persistent repetitive tool calls indicative of flawed state perception (e.g., livelocks even in legitimate tasks). Through controlled multi-turn evaluation on high-stakes ethical dilemmas, malicious requests, and benign controls, we quantify these phenomena using declaration-action gap and livelock metrics, demonstrating their cross-model prevalence under direct execution protocols. Root-cause analysis attributes the instabilities to the decoupling of reasoning context from execution state in current agent loops. We propose an Action-Aware Supervision Layer - a lightweight, plug-and-play architectural blueprint incorporating intent-action consistency checks, runtime state tracking, and forced termination primitives. Post-hoc simulation on captured failure trajectories shows the layer can intercept observed violations without false positives on benign cases. This work advances agent reliability by shifting focus from linguistic safeguards to enforceable architectural mechanisms for responsible agentic AI.

AI.tldr: LLMs used as planners in multi-turn tool-using agents exhibit two failure modes: Safety Drift (gradual erosion of safety alignment) and Operational Hallucination (persistent repetitive tool calls). The paper proposes an Action-Aware Supervision Layer with intent-action consistency checks, runtime state tracking, and forced termination to intercept these violations.
AI.motivation: While single-turn safety for LLMs is mature, multi-turn agentic interactions reveal structural vulnerabilities where initial alignment degrades over time, creating dynamic reliability risks that existing safety mechanisms fail to address.
AI.method: Empirical characterization of Safety Drift and Operational Hallucination via controlled multi-turn evaluation across state-of-the-art LLMs on high-stakes ethical dilemmas, malicious requests, and benign controls, quantified using declaration-action gap and livelock metrics. Root-cause analysis identifies reasoning-execution decoupling. Proposes an Action-Aware Supervision Layer with post-hoc simulation on captured failure trajectories.
AI.result: Both failure modes are cross-model prevalent under direct execution protocols. The proposed Action-Aware Supervision Layer intercepts observed violations without false positives on benign cases.
AI.conclusion: Agent reliability can be improved by shifting from linguistic safeguards to enforceable architectural mechanisms for responsible agentic AI.

title: Privileged Lesion-Context Relational Distillation for Mask-Free Skin Lesion Classification
comment: Manuscript submitted for consideration. The paper presents a mask-free skin lesion classification framework evaluated on HAM10000 and externally validated on ISIC 2018
summary: Accurate skin lesion classification can benefit from lesion segmentation masks, but requiring masks or an auxiliary segmentation model during inference reduces clinical practicality and increases computational complexity. This work introduces Privileged Lesion-Context Relational Distillation (PLCRD), a teacher-student framework that exploits lesion masks exclusively during training while preserving image-only inference. The privileged teacher jointly analyzes the original dermoscopic image and its mask-guided lesion region to learn lesion-specific and contextual diagnostic representations. An image-only student is then trained through complementary knowledge-transfer mechanisms that convey the teacher's diagnostic distribution, lesion-focused attention, inter-lesion relational geometry, and lesion-context structure. PLCRD decomposes deep representations into lesion and contextual embeddings and transfers their relational organization through inter-lesion similarity alignment, lesion-context affinity matching, separation regularization, and class-aware relational learning. This formulation avoids direct feature matching between heterogeneous teacher and student architectures and enables the student to internalize mask-informed diagnostic structure without accessing masks at deployment. The framework was evaluated on HAM10000 using lesion-disjoint data partitioning and externally validated on ISIC 2018 without retraining. PLCRD achieved a lesion-level macro-F1 of 0.773 +/- 0.018, balanced accuracy of 0.764 +/- 0.023, and macro-AUROC of 0.976 +/- 0.002 on HAM10000, together with a macro-F1 of 0.732 +/- 0.008 on ISIC 2018. The results indicate that privileged lesion annotations can be transformed into transferable relational knowledge, yielding a practical and interpretable approach to mask-free skin lesion classification.

AI.tldr: PLCRD is a teacher-student framework that uses lesion segmentation masks only during training to teach an image-only student model, achieving strong skin lesion classification without requiring masks at inference.
AI.motivation: Skin lesion classification benefits from segmentation masks, but requiring masks or an auxiliary segmentation model during inference reduces clinical practicality and increases computational complexity. The goal is to leverage mask information during training while keeping inference mask-free.
AI.method: A privileged teacher jointly analyzes dermoscopic images and mask-guided lesion regions. An image-only student is trained via complementary knowledge transfer: diagnostic distribution, lesion-focused attention, inter-lesion relational geometry, and lesion-context structure. The framework decomposes representations into lesion and contextual embeddings and transfers relational organization through inter-lesion similarity alignment, lesion-context affinity matching, separation regularization, and class-aware relational learning.
AI.result: On HAM10000: lesion-level macro-F1 0.773±0.018, balanced accuracy 0.764±0.023, macro-AUROC 0.976±0.002. On ISIC 2018 (external validation): macro-F1 0.732±0.008.
AI.conclusion: Privileged lesion annotations can be transformed into transferable relational knowledge, yielding a practical and interpretable mask-free skin lesion classification approach.

title: Federated Lightweight Fine-Tuning
comment: 22 pages, 10 figures, 6 tables. Extended preprint with appendix. Under review at ACCV 2026
summary: Federated fine-tuning is bottlenecked by communication: FedAvg and pseudo-gradient schemes transmit a payload that scales with the model, and gradient compression shrinks it by only a constant factor. We take a different lever. Mapping networks generate a network's weights from a small trainable latent through a frozen affine projection; because the map is shared and affine, averaging latents is exactly averaging the generated weights. We turn this into a practical low-bandwidth federated channel with two changes: a low-rank, seed-regenerable factorisation of the projection (cutting generator memory from ~80 GB to ~10 MB), and a delta formulation $θ= θ^{\mathrm{pre}} + U V^{\top} z$ that learns an additive correction around a shared centrally-pretrained base -- federated fine-tuning, which is what makes the method work at scale. A frozen orthogonal classifier head further removes the head from the payload while improving accuracy. On CIFAR-100 with ResNet-18+GroupNorm, our method (FLITE, Federated Low-rank Iterative Training Engine) communicates 1,280 floats (~5 KB) per client per round -- an 8718x reduction -- and reaches 74.67%, within ~0.5 pp of full-weight FedAvg. The averaging identity holds to floating-point precision ($6 \times 10^{-8}$); the method sits one to two orders of magnitude below PowerSGD and top-k on the bandwidth-accuracy Pareto; it matches or exceeds full-weight FedAvg under strong non-IID skew. int4 latents reach 648 bytes per round at unchanged accuracy, whereas int4 full-weight FedAvg collapses to chance.

AI.tldr: FLITE achieves extreme communication reduction (8,718x, ~5 KB/round) in federated fine-tuning by using a frozen affine projection that maps small trainable latents to network weights, where averaging latents exactly equals averaging generated weights.
AI.motivation: Federated fine-tuning is bottlenecked by communication: existing methods (FedAvg, pseudo-gradient schemes, gradient compression) either scale payload with model size or achieve only constant-factor reductions.
AI.method: Uses mapping networks with a frozen affine projection to generate weights from small trainable latents; employs low-rank seed-regenerable factorization (reducing generator memory from ~80 GB to ~10 MB) and a delta formulation θ = θ^pre + UVᵀz for additive correction around a shared pretrained base; uses a frozen orthogonal classifier head.
AI.result: On CIFAR-100 ResNet-18+GroupNorm: 1,280 floats (~5 KB) per client per round (8,718x reduction), 74.67% accuracy (~0.5 pp of FedAvg). Averaging identity holds to 6×10⁻⁸ precision. Outperforms PowerSGD and top-k on bandwidth-accuracy Pareto. Int4 latents: 648 bytes/round with unchanged accuracy.
AI.conclusion: FLITE demonstrates that mapping networks with affine projections enable extreme communication efficiency in federated fine-tuning while maintaining accuracy, outperforming existing compression methods on the bandwidth-accuracy Pareto frontier.

title: AlayaWorld: Interactive Long-Horizon World Modeling -- Full Technical Report
comment: Authors are listed alphabetically by the first name and their role. See the contribution section for details
summary: Unlike conventional video game development, which relies on labor-intensive pipelines for asset production, animation, physics, and programming, video world models generate interactive environments from user inputs instantly. It enable us to create customized, explorable, and continuously evolving virtual world from text, an image, or video. Realizing this vision requires four tightly coupled capabilities: interaction, persistent spatiotemporal consistency, stable long-horizon generation, and efficient response. We present AlayaWorld, an interactive long-horizon video world model that generates 24-fps video at 540p and 720p. Built on a 15B video diffusion transformer, AlayaWorld generates short latent chunks autoregressively under camera trajectories and switchable text prompts. Its bounded visual context combines a persistent sink frame, compressed temporal history, geometry-aligned spatial memory, and recent-frame conditioning. To reduce long-term drift, the model is trained with corrupted histories and prediction residuals collected from its own roll-outs. We further introduce a discrete autoregressive distillation formulation that combines distribution-matching distillation, self-forcing++, and consistency distillation, reducing inference from approximately 30 sampling steps to four steps per chunk. On iWorld-Bench, AlayaWorld achieves the best performance over long-horizon generation. Conceived as a full-stack, open-source, and long-term project, AlayaWorld is intended to provide an extensible foundation for future research on interactive video world models.

AI.tldr: AlayaWorld is an interactive long-horizon video world model that generates 24-fps video at 540p/720p using a 15B video diffusion transformer with autoregressive latent chunk generation, bounded visual context (persistent sink frame, compressed temporal history, geometry-aligned spatial memory, recent-frame conditioning), and discrete autoregressive distillation for efficient 4-step inference, achieving state-of-the-art performance on iWorld-Bench.
AI.motivation: To overcome the labor-intensive pipelines of traditional video game development by enabling instant generation of interactive, customizable, and continuously evolving virtual worlds from text, images, or video inputs.
AI.method: Built on a 15B video diffusion transformer that autoregressively generates short latent chunks under camera trajectories and switchable text prompts, with bounded visual context combining persistent sink frame, compressed temporal history, geometry-aligned spatial memory, and recent-frame conditioning. Trained with corrupted histories and prediction residuals from own roll-outs to reduce drift. Uses discrete autoregressive distillation (distribution-matching distillation, self-forcing++, consistency distillation) to reduce inference from ~30 to 4 sampling steps per chunk.
AI.result: Achieves best performance on iWorld-Bench for long-horizon generation, generating 24-fps video at 540p and 720p resolution.
AI.conclusion: AlayaWorld provides an extensible, full-stack, open-source foundation for future research on interactive video world models.

title: CGMap: A Geospatially Aware Deep Learning Framework for Crop Gap Mapping Using UAV
summary: In India, crop germination is primarily monitored by visual inspection and manual counting, which are prone to errors, despite their crucial role in determining eventual yield potential. This paper highlights a deep learning based pipeline which uses object detection methods and drone imagery to assess and provide a precise count of sugarcane germination in fields. The approch uses a pre-trained AI model to find germinated plant sampling and identify gaps, also known as ``bald spots'', which restricts field productivity. The techniques used here relies on the YOLOV8 architecture, which was trained on a carefully selected dataset of UAV photos taken in various agroclimatic zones of India. Here, we bring upon a novel orientation-normalization technique that uses minimum Spanning Trees (MST) to account for variations in planting geometry, allowing for dependable row and column extraction across a variety of field layouts. By converting detected seedlings into spatial point clouds, emergence gaps can be inferred from the anticipated spacing between plants. A geospatial germination map exported in Well-Known Text (WKT) format is the end result, and it can be easily incorporated into GIS platforms used by sugar mills and agronomists to direct transplant initiatives. Timely interventions based on the insights provided by the algorithm can significantly increase yield, resulting in higher profits. Hence, support proper allocation of resources, avoid wastage, and enhance long-term sustainability.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a YOLOV8-based deep learning pipeline using drone imagery to automate sugarcane germination monitoring in India, featuring a novel MST-based orientation-normalization technique for row/column extraction and generating geospatial germination maps in WKT format for GIS integration.
AI.motivation: Traditional manual visual inspection and counting of sugarcane germination are error-prone yet critical for yield estimation; there is a need for automated, precise, and scalable assessment.
AI.method: A deep learning pipeline using YOLOV8 object detection on UAV imagery, trained on a dataset from diverse Indian agroclimatic zones, with a novel orientation-normalization technique using Minimum Spanning Trees (MST) to handle varying planting geometries and enable robust row/column extraction; detected seedlings are converted to spatial point clouds to infer emergence gaps.
AI.result: A geospatial germination map in Well-Known Text (WKT) format is produced, which can be directly integrated into GIS platforms for downstream use by sugar mills and agronomists.
AI.conclusion: The approach enables timely, data-driven interventions to improve yield, optimize resource allocation, reduce waste, and enhance long-term sustainability in sugarcane farming.

title: An Analysis of Residual-Stream Geometry Across Transformer Depth
summary: We propose a transition-centred geometric analysis of transformer residual streams. Relative displacement measures how \emph{far} representations move between consecutive layers, and orthogonal Procrustes analysis separates each transition into a rigid rotation and a non-rigid residual. Across six instruction-tuned models, on code generation and cross-lingual translation, these measurements reveal reproducible depth regularities. Relative displacement is strongly layer-dependent; typically larger early and late, with a quieter middle third; and nearly invariant across conditions within each model. Rotation magnitude is nearly constant across depth, while Procrustes residual and angle concentration remain depth-modulated, with residual peaking at the final transition. During generation, non-English targets show larger final-layer displacement and residual than English targets. We present these as descriptive geometric regularities, not as measures of computational effort or causal explanations. The contribution is a measurement framework for residual-stream transitions and evidence that, in the settings studied here, depth curves are model-dependent and largely condition-stable.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a geometric analysis of transformer residual streams using relative displacement and orthogonal Procrustes analysis, revealing depth-dependent regularities (e.g., U-shaped displacement, constant rotation, depth-modulated residual) that are model-dependent but condition-stable across instruction-tuned models on code generation and cross-lingual translation.
AI.motivation: To understand and characterize the geometric behavior of residual stream transitions in transformer models across layers, particularly how representations move between consecutive layers in a depth-dependent manner.
AI.method: Relative displacement measures movement magnitude between layers; orthogonal Procrustes analysis decomposes each transition into rigid rotation and non-rigid residual components. Applied to six instruction-tuned models on code generation and cross-lingual translation tasks.
AI.result: Displacement is U-shaped (large early/late, quieter middle third); rotation magnitude is nearly constant; Procrustes residual and angle concentration are depth-modulated, with residual peaking at the final transition. Non-English targets show larger final-layer displacement/residual than English.
AI.conclusion: These are descriptive geometric regularities, not causal measures; depth curves are model-dependent and largely condition-stable, providing a general measurement framework for residual-stream analysis.

title: Neuro-Symbolic Meta-Policies for Temporal Knowledge-Graph Memory under Partial Observability
summary: Partially observable reinforcement learning requires deciding what to retain, retrieve, and forget over time. We introduce a neuro-symbolic meta-policy that learns which symbolic memory heuristic to apply at each decision point while keeping execution symbolic. Our setting uses temporal knowledge-graph memory in RoomKG, where hidden state and observations are represented as Resource Description Framework (RDF) graphs and memory is augmented with temporal RDF triple annotations. The model combines knowledge-graph encoding of memory contents with value heads for question answering, exploration, and forgetting, yielding a controller that is both adaptive and inspectable. This gives the work a direct Semantic Web grounding through RDF-based representation, annotation-compatible graph semantics, and graph-based symbolic operations over explicit memory state. On train/test room splits at long-term memory capacity of 512, the qualifier-aware StarE-GNN configuration achieves the best held-out performance among the compared symbolic, neural, and neuro-symbolic systems while preserving step-level traceability of memory-management decisions.

AI.tldr: A neuro-symbolic meta-policy for partially observable RL learns to select symbolic memory heuristics (retain, retrieve, forget) at each step, using temporal RDF knowledge-graph memory in RoomKG. The StarE-GNN model with qualifier-aware encoding achieves best held-out performance at 512 memory capacity while maintaining full decision traceability.
AI.motivation: Partially observable RL requires effective memory management (what to retain, retrieve, and forget over time), but existing approaches lack interpretability and explicit control over memory operations.
AI.method: A neuro-symbolic meta-policy selects symbolic memory heuristics per decision point. Memory is stored as temporal RDF graphs (RoomKG) with temporal triple annotations. A knowledge-graph encoder (StarE-GNN) combined with value heads for question answering, exploration, and forgetting produces an adaptive, inspectable controller.
AI.result: At long-term memory capacity of 512, the qualifier-aware StarE-GNN configuration achieves the best held-out performance among symbolic, neural, and neuro-symbolic baselines, while preserving step-level traceability of memory-management decisions.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates that neuro-symbolic memory control with explicit RDF-based graph representations yields both strong performance and full inspectability in partially observable RL, providing a direct Semantic Web grounding.

title: Image Editing Models are Numerical Solvers
summary: We investigate whether a pretrained generative image-editing model can provide a common interface for numerical simulation. Physical inputs and solutions are rendered as images, while scalar quantities such as material properties, diffusivity, and loading parameters enter through lightweight adapters. Using established numerical and analytic solvers for supervision, we apply the same architecture and training protocol to heterogeneous elliptic equations, forced heat and Burgers evolution, complex Ginzburg-Landau dynamics, two-dimensional Navier-Stokes prediction, potential flow, elasticity, eikonal travel time, phase-field fracture, and entropic optimal transport. The results show that a pretrained image model can represent diverse static and time-dependent physical mappings, including unstable and shock-like behavior, when each task is expressed through a suitable visual encoding. This work is a capability study rather than an attempt to surpass specialized solvers. It also identifies fundamental constraints: image and latent representations complicate numerical range selection and direct enforcement of governing equations or invariants, while a failed Kuramoto-Sivashinsky experiment indicates that representation errors prevent meaningful long-horizon simulation of chaotic systems.

AI.tldr: The paper explores using a pretrained generative image-editing model as a common interface for various numerical simulations (PDEs, elasticity, transport, etc.) by rendering physical inputs/solutions as images and using lightweight adapters for scalar parameters. While the approach works for many static and time-dependent physical mappings, it faces fundamental limitations in numerical range handling, constraint enforcement, and chaotic system simulation (e.g., Kuramoto-Sivashinsky fails).
AI.motivation: To investigate whether a single pretrained generative image-editing model can serve as a unified interface for diverse numerical simulations, potentially offering an alternative to specialized solvers.
AI.method: Physical inputs and solutions are rendered as images; scalar quantities (material properties, diffusivity, loading parameters) enter through lightweight adapters. The same architecture and training protocol are applied across heterogeneous elliptic equations, forced heat/Burgers evolution, complex Ginzburg-Landau, 2D Navier-Stokes, potential flow, elasticity, eikonal travel time, phase-field fracture, and entropic optimal transport, using established solvers for supervision.
AI.result: The pretrained image model can represent diverse static and time-dependent physical mappings (including unstable and shock-like behavior) when each task is encoded visually. However, image/latent representations complicate numerical range selection and direct enforcement of governing equations/invariants, and the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky experiment failed due to representation errors preventing meaningful long-horizon chaotic simulation.
AI.conclusion: This is a capability study showing feasibility for many PDE/physics tasks but not surpassing specialized solvers. Fundamental constraints exist around numerical range handling, constraint enforcement, and chaotic system simulation, indicating clear limitations of this image-based approach.

title: MambaLSTM: A Spatio-Temporal Framework for Enhanced Traffic Accident Risk Prediction
summary: In traffic accident risk prediction, most studies overlook the extra noise that could be incorporated when fusing temporal features into spatial features, and some models struggle to capture global correlations among spatial regions. To address these challenges, we propose a novel traffic accident risk prediction framework named MambaLSTM. First, we develop a squeeze-and-excitation temporal feature fusion module to integrate temporal information without compromising spatio-temporal integrity. Second, we introduce a new patch embedding module for effectively capturing semantic relationships among spatially adjacent regions. Additionally, we introduce a Mamba block based on state-space models to model global spatial semantics in urban regions. Finally, we propose a MambaLSTM unit to efficiently capture long- and short-term temporal dependencies for identifying dynamic risk patterns. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate the proposed model's superiority over state-of-the-art methods. The code is released at https://github.com/Zhenzovo/MambaLSTM.

AI.tldr: MambaLSTM is a traffic accident risk prediction framework that addresses noise from temporal-spatial fusion and limited global spatial correlation capture. It uses squeeze-and-excitation temporal fusion, patch embedding for spatial semantics, Mamba state-space blocks for global spatial modeling, and MambaLSTM units for temporal dependencies, outperforming state-of-the-art methods on real-world datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing traffic accident risk prediction models either introduce extra noise when fusing temporal features into spatial features or fail to capture global correlations among spatial regions.
AI.method: (1) Squeeze-and-excitation temporal feature fusion module for noise-robust temporal integration; (2) Patch embedding module for spatial region semantics; (3) Mamba block (state-space model) for global spatial modeling; (4) MambaLSTM unit for long- and short-term temporal dependency capture.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on real-world datasets show MambaLSTM outperforms state-of-the-art methods.
AI.conclusion: The proposed MambaLSTM framework effectively addresses temporal-spatial fusion noise and global spatial correlation limitations, achieving superior traffic accident risk prediction performance.

title: MAGE: Human-Like Macro Placement via Agentic Multimodal Reasoning
summary: Macro placement still requires substantial manual refinement in industrial physical design flows. We present MAGE (Macro Placement Agentic Engine), a multimodal multi-agent framework for macro placement refinement. MAGE decomposes the macro placement task into a six-phase workflow that combines structured floorplanning rules, visual checks, and iterative refinement. Expert floorplanning knowledge is encoded through natural-language directives and validation criteria, rather than learned from labeled placement data. A tournament-style refinement mode evaluates multiple candidate placements and propagates feedback from higher-quality solutions. We also introduce four metrics for quantifying human-likeness in macro placement: notch score, whitespace score, pocket score, and alignment score. These metrics capture structural properties used by expert designers but not directly measured by conventional PPA metrics. Across nine designs in NanGate45 and GlobalFoundries 12nm enablements, MAGE achieves geometric-mean improvements of 11.1%-19.3% in WNS and 70.0%-74.0% in TNS over commercial macro placers. On the three NanGate45 designs, for which human-expert and Hier-RTLMP baselines are available, MAGE improves WNS and TNS by 18.3% and 72.5% over the human expert, and by 47.0% and 80.4% over Hier-RTLMP, with comparable wirelength and power. On human-likeness metrics, MAGE improves the overall score by 6%-48% over all baselines. Additional case studies on anonymized netlists, unseen designs, dense rectilinear floorplans, and high-utilization settings show that the framework transfers to new placement settings without design-specific retraining.

AI.tldr: MAGE is a multimodal multi-agent framework for macro placement refinement that uses a six-phase workflow combining floorplanning rules, visual checks, and iterative refinement, achieving 11.1%-19.3% WNS and 70.0%-74.0% TNS improvements over commercial macro placers across nine designs, and outperforming human experts by 18.3% WNS and 72.5% TNS.
AI.motivation: Macro placement still requires substantial manual refinement in industrial physical design flows, motivating an automated approach that incorporates expert knowledge without relying on labeled placement data.
AI.method: MAGE decomposes macro placement into a six-phase workflow combining structured floorplanning rules, visual checks, and iterative refinement using natural-language directives and validation criteria. A tournament-style refinement mode evaluates multiple candidate placements and propagates feedback. Four human-likeness metrics (notch, whitespace, pocket, alignment scores) are introduced to capture structural properties not measured by conventional PPA metrics.
AI.result: Across nine designs in NanGate45 and GlobalFoundries 12nm, MAGE achieves 11.1%-19.3% geometric-mean improvement in WNS and 70.0%-74.0% in TNS over commercial macro placers. Over human expert: 18.3% WNS and 72.5% TNS improvement. Over Hier-RTLMP: 47.0% WNS and 80.4% TNS improvement. Human-likeness metrics improve by 6%-48% over all baselines.
AI.conclusion: MAGE demonstrates that combining multimodal multi-agent frameworks with structured expert knowledge can effectively automate macro placement refinement, achieving superior timing results and human-like placement quality without retraining on new designs.

title: Moving Alphabet: A Controlled Study of Training Data for Text-to-Video Generation
summary: Text-to-video generation has advanced significantly over the past five years through scaling of model size, data, and compute. Unlike model architecture, training data is often underexplored. Real-world data curation is complex and non-trivial, involving clip selection from raw videos and captioning to create video-text pairs for learning text-to-video mappings. We study how data distribution and caption quality impact text-to-video models. To enable controlled experiments, we introduce Moving Alphabet, a procedural testbed that renders letters with varying fonts, colors, sizes, and positions, moving in different directions and speeds against a black background. This design allows precise control over data distribution and caption quality by corrupting ground-truth metadata. Our experiments yield three findings: a) a diverse and balanced distribution of video content and duration is critical for generalization; b) caption quality significantly affects both model performance and training efficiency, suggesting that text-to-video models are bounded by video understanding capabilities; and c) classifier-free guidance and fine-tuning on high-quality data provide partial recovery from models trained on corrupted captions, but cannot fully compensate for poor pre-training data. We believe these insights can inform the development of large-scale text-to-video models, and we advocate for greater attention to the science of pre-training data.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Moving Alphabet, a procedural testbed for controlled experiments on how data distribution and caption quality impact text-to-video generation models. Key findings: (1) diverse and balanced video content/duration distribution is critical for generalization; (2) caption quality significantly affects model performance and training efficiency; (3) classifier-free guidance and fine-tuning on high-quality data cannot fully compensate for poor pre-training data.
AI.motivation: To systematically study how data distribution and caption quality impact text-to-video models through controlled experiments, as real-world data curation is complex and often underexplored compared to model architecture scaling.
AI.method: Introduced Moving Alphabet, a procedural testbed that renders letters with varying visual attributes (fonts, colors, sizes, positions) moving in different directions/speeds against black backgrounds, enabling precise control over data distribution and caption quality via corrupting ground-truth metadata.
AI.result: Three findings: a) diverse and balanced distribution of video content and duration is critical for generalization; b) caption quality significantly affects both model performance and training efficiency, suggesting models are bounded by video understanding capabilities; c) classifier-free guidance and fine-tuning on high-quality data provide only partial recovery from corrupted caption training.
AI.conclusion: These insights can inform development of large-scale text-to-video models, advocating for greater attention to the science of pre-training data.

title: Multi-layer MIMO Relay as Deep Physical Neural Networks: Power Amplifiers as Activation Functions
summary: Wireless physical neural networks (WPNNs) embed neural computation directly into analog hardware, offering lower energy consumption and latency than conventional digital implementations. In this paper, we propose a deep WPNN in which nonlinear activations are realized by a multi-hop multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) relay network, in which each relay implements a trainable complex linear gain and bias, followed by the power amplifier's intrinsic nonlinearity acting as an activation function. The cascade of multiple relays therefore realizes an over-the-air fully connected network whose parameters can be trained end-to-end. We develop two transceiver designs for different channel state information (CSI) availability scenarios: a least squares (LS)-based scheme requiring only receiver-side CSI, and a singular-value-decomposition (SVD)-based scheme requiring both transmitter-side and receiver-side CSI. Simulation results show that the proposed architecture enables accurate over-the-air inference for image classification. In particular, the results highlight the advantage of exploiting hardware nonlinearity for enhanced inference capability.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a deep wireless physical neural network (WPNN) using multi-hop MIMO relays with trainable gains and biases, where power amplifier nonlinearity serves as activation functions. Two transceiver designs (LS-based and SVD-based) are developed for different CSI scenarios, and simulations show accurate over-the-air image classification with benefits from hardware nonlinearity.
AI.motivation: To embed neural computation directly into analog hardware for lower energy consumption and latency compared to digital implementations, leveraging wireless channels as a computational substrate.
AI.method: A deep WPNN architecture using cascaded multi-hop MIMO relays where each relay applies a trainable complex linear gain and bias, followed by the power amplifier's intrinsic nonlinearity as an activation function. Two transceiver designs: LS-based (receiver-side CSI only) and SVD-based (both transmitter- and receiver-side CSI).
AI.result: The proposed architecture achieves accurate over-the-air inference for image classification. Hardware nonlinearity enhances inference capability.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting intrinsic hardware nonlinearity as activation functions in over-the-air MIMO relay networks enables effective deep WPNN implementations for classification tasks, with design trade-offs depending on CSI availability.

title: Engineering Trustworthy Agentic AI for Critical Systems
comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication
summary: Agentic artificial intelligence systems, capable of autonomous perception, planning, tool use, and multi-step action, are increasingly proposed for critical engineering domains where decisions carry physical, operational, or economic consequences. This survey addresses a gap in current literature by treating trustworthiness, whether agentic behavior can be verified, audited, and trusted under the constraints that engineering practice actually requires, as a first-class engineering property, rather than evaluating agentic AI by task capability alone. The study adopts a trustworthiness model organized around five cross-cutting dimensions: safety and constraint satisfaction; robustness and reliability; transparency and interpretability; accountability and auditability; and privacy and security. This is mapped onto an agentic assurance workflow spanning perception through audit. Building on this foundation, agentic systems architectures, threats, concrete trust mechanisms, and quantitative metrics are surveyed for direct application in agentic systems development and evaluation. These principles are then examined across four constraint-bound engineering domains: power systems, autonomous vehicles/robotics/UAVs, high-performance computing, and communication networks, identifying recurring design patterns, shared failure modes, and domain-specific gaps. Synthesizing across those domains, agentic AI trustworthiness is shown to be a single problem, with a path outlined toward a reusable, cross-domain assurance framework analogous to the graded certification regimes used by mature safety-critical engineering fields.

AI.tldr: This survey argues that trustworthiness (safety, robustness, transparency, accountability, privacy) should be a first-class engineering property for agentic AI systems, proposes a cross-dimensional trustworthiness model mapped to an assurance workflow, surveys concrete mechanisms and metrics, examines four engineering domains (power systems, autonomous vehicles, HPC, communication networks), and outlines a path toward a reusable cross-domain assurance framework akin to safety-critical certification regimes.
AI.motivation: Current literature evaluates agentic AI primarily by task capability, but critical engineering domains require trustworthiness as a first-class property—agentic behavior must be verifiable, auditable, and trustworthy under real engineering constraints.
AI.method: The paper organizes trustworthiness around five dimensions (safety, robustness, transparency, accountability, privacy) mapped onto an assurance workflow (perception through audit). It surveys architectures, threats, trust mechanisms, and metrics, then examines four constraint-bound engineering domains to identify patterns, failure modes, and gaps.
AI.result: Agentic AI trustworthiness is shown to be a single, cross-cutting problem rather than domain-specific, with recurring design patterns and shared failure modes across power systems, autonomous vehicles/robotics/UAVs, HPC, and communication networks.
AI.conclusion: A path is outlined toward a reusable, cross-domain assurance framework analogous to graded certification regimes used in mature safety-critical engineering fields.

title: STS-NET: Spatio-Temporal Stress Network for Self-Supervised Crop Stress Detection using Satellite Image Time Series
summary: Early and accurate detection of crop stress is essential to improve agricultural productivity and ensure global food security. However, collecting a large labeled crop stress dataset is a challenging task. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel spatial-temporal stress network (STS-NET), built on a self-supervised 3D-convolutional autoencoder (3D-CAE), designed to utilize Satellite Image Time Series (SITS) data for crop stress detection. STS-NET exploits four vegetation indices: Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (GNDVI), Red-Edge Chlorophyll Index (RECI) and Normalized Difference Red-Edge Index (NDRE) obtained from high resolution Planetscope imagery to capture spatiotemporal stress patterns. The model is trained on our BSPT (Barnala Spatial-Temporal) dataset and evaluated on a real-world sugarcane dataset collected over a year from a 2.5-acre test plot located in Lakhimpur-Kheri (LK) district in Uttar Pradesh in India. STS-NET achieved a precision of 97. 98\% for water stress, 85.08\% for nitrogen stress, and 83.47\% for combined stress. The results demonstrate the potential of STS-NET in effectively detecting stress in sugarcane crops with minimal reliance on labeled data. Furthermore, STS-NET can serve as a robust feature extractor for simpler models.

AI.tldr: STS-NET, a self-supervised 3D convolutional autoencoder using satellite image time series and four vegetation indices, detects crop stress (water, nitrogen, combined) in sugarcane with high precision (up to 97.98%) while minimizing reliance on labeled data.
AI.motivation: Early and accurate crop stress detection is critical for agricultural productivity and food security, but collecting large labeled crop stress datasets is challenging.
AI.method: A self-supervised 3D-convolutional autoencoder (3D-CAE) called STS-NET processes Satellite Image Time Series (SITS) data using four vegetation indices (NDVI, GNDVI, RECI, NDRE) from high-resolution PlanetScope imagery to capture spatiotemporal stress patterns.
AI.result: On a real-world sugarcane dataset, STS-NET achieved 97.98% precision for water stress, 85.08% for nitrogen stress, and 83.47% for combined stress.
AI.conclusion: STS-NET effectively detects sugarcane crop stress with minimal labeled data and can serve as a robust feature extractor for simpler models.

title: Physical Self-Supervised Learning: IMU Sensing without Manual Labels
comment: 15 pages, 20 figures. Published in ACM MobiSys 2026
summary: Deep neural networks have become a promising approach for IMU-based sensing, but their scalability is fundamentally limited by costly labeled data and poor robustness to heterogeneous devices, placements, and users. Existing unsupervised and self-supervised methods reduce but do not remove this dependence, still requiring labeled data for domain adaptation and largely ignoring known physical structure. We propose physical self-supervised learning, an autoencoder-style paradigm for label-free IMU sensing. We replace the conventional neural decoder with an auto-adaptive physics decoder, a learnable family of kinematic equations that enforces explicit physical structure while adapting across environments, and adopt a hybrid two-stage IMU encoder with reconstruction in a structured latent space to mitigate sensor noise. Our framework further introduces probabilistic frequency-spatial constraints to disentangle sensor and object motion, a multi-view kinematic tree to exploit sparse physical self-supervised signals, and an uncertainty-aware formulation to handle the inherent ambiguity of IMU inference. Evaluated on inertial tracking and full-body motion capture over public datasets and realistic deployments, physical self-supervised learning reduces errors by up to 5x for tracking and 4x for motion capture in challenging generalization scenarios, consistently outperforming state-of-the-art supervised and self-supervised baselines without any labels.

AI.tldr: Physical self-supervised learning (PSSL) is an autoencoder-style, label-free framework for IMU sensing that replaces the neural decoder with an auto-adaptive physics decoder and hybrid IMU encoder, achieving up to 5x error reduction in tracking and 4x in motion capture without any labels.
AI.motivation: Deep neural networks for IMU sensing are limited by costly labeled data and poor robustness to heterogeneous devices, placements, and users. Existing unsupervised/self-supervised methods still require labeled data for domain adaptation and ignore known physical structure.
AI.method: Proposes physical self-supervised learning (PSSL) with: (1) auto-adaptive physics decoder replacing conventional neural decoder with learnable kinematic equations; (2) hybrid two-stage IMU encoder with structured latent space reconstruction; (3) probabilistic frequency-spatial constraints to disentangle sensor and object motion; (4) multi-view kinematic tree for sparse self-supervised signals; (5) uncertainty-aware formulation for handling IMU inference ambiguity.
AI.result: Reduces errors by up to 5x for tracking and 4x for full-body motion capture on public datasets and realistic deployments, consistently outperforming state-of-the-art supervised and self-supervised baselines without any labels.
AI.conclusion: Physical self-supervised learning demonstrates that incorporating explicit physical structure (kinematic equations) into self-supervised learning can eliminate the need for labeled data in IMU sensing while achieving superior generalization and performance compared to both supervised and self-supervised methods.

title: Attacking Graph Foundation Models Through Their Shared Representation
summary: A graph foundation model generalizes across graph domains by mapping every input into one shared representation before any task reasoning. We call this map the alignment layer, the component that separates a graph foundation model from a graph neural network, and we show it is a distinct attack surface that prior work has not studied. We attack it at inference time, with no access to training, on six public models spanning spectral tokenizers, text embedding spaces, and a discrete codebook. A directed representation-space perturbation collapses every model, but at a budget comparable to the representation norm a plain graph network also needs, with one exception: OpenGraph, whose spectral tokenizer collapses at a fifth of that budget, an alignment-specific fragility a plain network does not share and which a same-representation control traces to the tokenizer rather than the decoder. A realizable input-space attack that edits edges, features, or text removes at least half the correct predictions on three of the six models at peak. How much of this fragility an input-access attacker realizes tracks how directly the decoder reads the representation, and not the clean accuracy a task leaves; we measure this carrier gain structurally from the decoder's local Lipschitz sensitivity, and report clean-accuracy headroom as a within-model ordering heuristic that does not survive on realizable attacks.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies the alignment layer (which maps diverse graph inputs into a shared representation) as a distinct attack surface in graph foundation models, shows it exhibits unique fragility not present in plain graph neural networks, demonstrates both representation-space and input-space attacks that significantly degrade performance, and proposes decoder Lipschitz sensitivity as a structural measure of this vulnerability.
AI.motivation: Prior work has not studied the alignment layer — the key component that distinguishes graph foundation models from graph neural networks — as a distinct attack surface at inference time.
AI.method: The authors attack the alignment layer at inference time (no training access) on six public graph foundation models (spectral tokenizers, text embedding spaces, discrete codebooks). They conduct representation-space perturbations and realizable input-space attacks (editing edges, features, or text), and analyze decoder Lipschitz sensitivity as a structural measure of fragility.
AI.result: Representation-space perturbation collapses all models; OpenGraph's spectral tokenizer collapses at 1/5 the budget of plain networks (alignment-specific fragility). Input-space attacks remove ≥50% correct predictions on 3/6 models. Fragility tracks decoder's local Lipschitz sensitivity, not clean accuracy.
AI.conclusion: The alignment layer is a uniquely vulnerable component in graph foundation models. Clean accuracy is a poor heuristic for attack robustness; decoder Lipschitz sensitivity better predicts realizable attack success.

title: A Controlled Study of Attention-Only Transformers
summary: Feed-forward networks hold two thirds of a transformer's non-embedding parameters, yet the architecture has not received a necessity test that controls parameters, compute, and depth at once. We pretrain attention-only decoder transformers (Simple Attention Networks, SANs) against standard transformers matched separately for parameter count, training FLOPs, and depth (2 to 48 layers), for up to 105B tokens at 6M to 87M parameters. Deleting feed-forward layers in place is costly: the standard transformer leads by 0.47 nats at matched depth and 0.26 nats at matched FLOPs. Reallocating the freed budget into attention depth closes the gap: at matched parameters the difference is 0.006 nats (0.27 percent of loss), reproducible to one part in ten thousand across seed pairs, shrinking across 5B, 30B, and 105B budgets, and holding near 0.02 nats across a 29x size range. Three measurements localize the remaining gap to parametric recall: attention-only models are better on context-grounded answers and worse where knowledge must come from weights. Weight spectra show why: routing matrices (Q/K) crystallize early, content matrices accumulate rank slowly, and removing feed-forward layers relocates this accumulation to the attention output projection. QK-normalization, not feed-forward layers or residual gating, keeps 48-layer attention-only stacks trainable. The deficit concentrates on low-context query prediction and localizes there entirely by the largest budget. A pre-registered test confirms the account: it predicts a 0.02 to 0.05 nat gap on knowledge-dense web text; a matched pair trained on fineweb-edu measures 0.040. Within the tested regime, attention does the rest.

AI.tldr: Attention-only transformers (SANs) nearly match standard transformers when controlling for parameters, FLOPs, and depth, with a residual gap of ~0.02 nats attributed to parametric recall—knowledge stored in weights rather than context. The deficit concentrates on low-context knowledge-dense predictions and is confirmed by a pre-registered test on FineWeb-Edu (0.040 nat gap).
AI.motivation: To test whether feed-forward layers in transformers are necessary, by controlling for parameters, compute, and depth simultaneously—a combined control not previously performed.
AI.method: Pretrain attention-only decoder transformers (SANs) and standard transformers matched for parameter count, training FLOPs, and depth (2–48 layers) at scales from 6M to 87M parameters and up to 105B tokens. Reallocate freed FFN budget into additional attention depth. Use weight spectra analysis, QK-normalization, and pre-registered testing on FineWeb-Edu.
AI.result: At matched parameters, attention-only models lag by just 0.006 nats (0.27% of loss); at matched depth the gap is 0.47 nats, and at matched FLOPs it is 0.26 nats. The small remaining gap (~0.02 nats) is attributed to parametric recall, concentrated on low-context knowledge-dense predictions. A pre-registered test on FineWeb-Edu measured a 0.040 nat gap.
AI.conclusion: Within the tested regime (up to 87M params, 105B tokens), attention alone can perform nearly all the work of standard transformers. Feed-forward layers primarily contribute parametric recall (memorized knowledge), while attention handles context-dependent reasoning. QK-normalization is essential for training deep (48-layer) attention-only stacks.

title: When Does Machine Learning Beat Value Sorting? A Three-Dataset Diagnostic of Exposure-Weighted Shipment Prioritization
comment: 9 pages, 1 figure, 4 tables, accepted for presentation at AIIIP 2026
summary: Delay-risk models are usually judged by predictive accuracy. What matters in practice is narrower: with capacity to review only a few shipments, which ones should a manager check first? We evaluate whether machine learning clears a demanding no-model baseline: inspect the highest-value shipments first. Across three real supply-chain contexts: SCMS procurement, DataCo logistics, and Olist e-commerce, we use leakage-controlled rolling-origin evaluation and 1000-sample paired bootstrap confidence intervals. Ranking by predicted delay severity times known value (M1) beats severity-only ranking in all three datasets, yet it does not generally beat value sorting. At a 10% review budget, M1 minus VALUE_ONLY is -5.5 percentage points (pp) for SCMS, +10.1 pp for DataCo, and -4.9 pp for Olist. The divide is consistent with severity learnability: DataCo has R^2 = 0.27 and calibration bias of +0.01 days, whereas SCMS and Olist have R^2 of approximately -0.02 and negative calibration bias. Nested-CV cost-sensitive retraining does not deliver a stable improvement over M1. Rather than proposing a new learning algorithm, this paper presents a deployment diagnostic and evaluation protocol. Value sorting should remain a permanent benchmark, and ML should be deployed only after severity learnability and calibration have been audited and the model clears that gate under leakage-controlled rolling-origin evaluation.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates whether ML-based delay-risk models outperform a simple baseline of sorting shipments by value for deciding which shipments managers should inspect. Across three real supply-chain datasets, value sorting often matches or beats ML predictions, and ML only adds value when delay severity is highly learnable. The paper proposes a deployment diagnostic and evaluation protocol rather than a new algorithm.
AI.motivation: Delay-risk models are typically judged by predictive accuracy, but in practice managers can only review a limited number of shipments. The key question is which shipments to inspect first, and existing metrics of model performance do not directly address this operational constraint.
AI.method: The authors compare ranking by predicted delay severity times known value (M1) against severity-only ranking and value-only sorting across three datasets (SCMS, DataCo, Olist). They use leakage-controlled rolling-origin evaluation and 1000-sample paired bootstrap confidence intervals. They also test nested-CV cost-sensitive retraining.
AI.result: M1 outperforms severity-only ranking across all three datasets but does not generally beat value sorting. At a 10% review budget, M1 minus VALUE_ONLY yields -5.5 pp (SCMS), +10.1 pp (DataCo), and -4.9 pp (Olist). The divide aligns with severity learnability: DataCo has R²=0.27 and calibration bias +0.01 days; SCMS and Olist have negative R² and negative calibration bias. Cost-sensitive retraining does not improve over M1.
AI.conclusion: Value sorting should remain a permanent benchmark for shipment inspection decisions. ML should only be deployed after auditing severity learnability and calibration under leakage-controlled rolling-origin evaluation. The paper provides a deployment diagnostic and evaluation protocol rather than a new learning algorithm.

title: ZeroSplat: Generalized Referring Segmentation in 3D Gaussian Splatting
summary: Recent advancements in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) have enabled language-guided scene understanding. However, existing Referring 3D Gaussian Splatting (R3DGS) methods are fundamentally restricted to single-target queries. To reflect the ambiguity of real-world instructions, we introduce the Generalized Referring 3D Gaussian Splatting Segmentation (GR3DGS) task, which requires dynamically segmenting an arbitrary number of targets (0, 1, or $N$). To facilitate comprehensive evaluation of this new task, we construct two new benchmarks: GR-LERF and GR-ScanNet. Crucially, existing R3DGS paradigms exhibit fundamental technical bottlenecks that severely limit their performance on the GR3DGS task: they lack intrinsic 3D point-level understanding by operating merely on 2D rendered pixels, and they incur prohibitive computational overhead by requiring per-scene optimization to embed heavy semantic features. To dismantle these bottlenecks, we propose ZeroSplat, a novel training-free and zero-feature framework. ZeroSplat lifts 2D Vision-Language Model (VLM) priors into 3D space through robust multi-view geometric constraints. This strategy enables intrinsic point-level understanding without incurring any additional feature storage. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ZeroSplat significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods across generalized and single-target scenarios while maintaining exceptional efficiency. Project Page: https://inkmind-ai.github.io/ZeroSplat

AI.tldr: ZeroSplat is a training-free, zero-feature framework for Generalized Referring 3D Gaussian Splatting Segmentation (GR3DGS) that lifts 2D VLM priors into 3D space via multi-view geometric constraints, enabling arbitrary-number target segmentation without per-scene optimization or heavy feature storage, outperforming existing methods on new benchmarks GR-LERF and GR-ScanNet.
AI.motivation: Existing R3DGS methods are limited to single-target queries and lack intrinsic 3D point-level understanding while incurring prohibitive computational overhead from per-scene optimization of heavy semantic features. The paper introduces the GR3DGS task to handle real-world ambiguity with arbitrary numbers of targets (0, 1, or N).
AI.method: ZeroSplat lifts 2D Vision-Language Model (VLM) priors into 3D space using robust multi-view geometric constraints, enabling intrinsic point-level understanding without additional feature storage or per-scene training.
AI.result: ZeroSplat significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods across both generalized (multi-target) and single-target scenarios while maintaining exceptional efficiency.
AI.conclusion: The work dismantles key bottlenecks (lack of 3D point-level understanding and prohibitive computational overhead) in existing R3DGS paradigms, establishing a new benchmark and framework for generalized referring 3D scene understanding.

title: Scalable and Efficient Joint Spiking Embedding Predictive Architecture for Large-Scale Dynamic Graphs
summary: Dynamic graph learning aims to capture evolving structural and semantic patterns in real-world systems, such as fraud detection and recommender systems. Due to the scarcity of labeled data in real-world dynamic graphs, recent studies have introduced generative or contrastive paradigms (e.g., masked graph autoencoders or graph contrastive learning) to generate task-agnostic graph embeddings. However, these methods typically rely on complex edge-level reconstruction objectives and tailored graph augmentation strategies. This incurs substantial computational overhead when scaling to large-scale dynamic graphs. In this paper, we propose SG-JEPA, a joint spiking embedding predictive architecture for large-scale dynamic graphs. In contrast to existing self-supervised methods, SG-JEPA partitions nodes into context and target sets along the temporal dimension to learn embeddings that are predictive of each other via additional spatial-temporal information. Furthermore, through encoding sequential inputs into coarse-to-fine spike count embeddings, spiking neurons enable SG-JEPA to adapt to the varying computational constraints of downstream tasks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SG-JEPA achieves competitive or even superior performance over discriminative baselines on node classification, while effectively scaling to the dynamic graph with 13 million edges. SG-JEPA avoids the complex machinery (negative sampling, graph augmentations, edge-level reconstruction, etc.), resulting in superior training efficiency and memory scalability compared with prior self-supervised dynamic graph baselines.

AI.tldr: SG-JEPA proposes a joint spiking embedding predictive architecture for self-supervised learning on large-scale dynamic graphs, using predictive node embeddings across temporal dimensions and spike-based encoding to avoid costly reconstruction or contrastive objectives, achieving competitive node classification performance and superior efficiency on graphs with up to 13 million edges.
AI.motivation: Existing self-supervised dynamic graph learning methods (masked graph autoencoders, graph contrastive learning) suffer from high computational overhead due to complex edge-level reconstruction and tailored graph augmentations, making scaling to large-scale dynamic graphs challenging.
AI.method: SG-JEPA partitions nodes into context and target sets along the temporal dimension, learns predictive embeddings via spatiotemporal information, and uses spiking neurons to encode sequential inputs into coarse-to-fine spike count embeddings, enabling adaptive computational efficiency.
AI.result: SG-JEPA achieves competitive or superior node classification performance compared to discriminative baselines, scales to dynamic graphs with 13 million edges, and demonstrates superior training efficiency and memory scalability by avoiding negative sampling, graph augmentations, and edge-level reconstruction.
AI.conclusion: SG-JEPA offers an efficient and scalable alternative to prior self-supervised dynamic graph methods, effectively balancing representation quality with computational constraints.

title: SciHazard: A Benchmark for Measuring Scientific Safety Risks with Decomposed Harm Scoring
summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly support science, but they can also convert hazardous scientific knowledge into actionable misuse guidance. Existing benchmarks often rely on templated queries disconnected from real-world hazards, and employ LLM-as-a-Judge paradigms without domain grounding. To address this, we introduce SciHazard, a real-world-grounded benchmark for scientific risks and a dataset agnostic evaluation framework for measuring harmfulness. SciHazard contains 2400 hazardous questions and 600 oversafety questions across 12 disciplines, with both queries grounded in regulated entities and documented failure scenarios. To compute \textsc{DeHarm-Score} , we develop a decomposed evaluating procedure that combines query hazard severity, refusal behavior, and response-level risk. For non-refused responses, it further decomposes response-level harm into \textsc{Executability}, quantified via dynamic checklists with importance weighting, and \textsc{Net-new risk}, assessed through retrieval-augmented claim extraction and synthesis-barrier verification. An expert-validation study shows that \textsc{DeHarm-Score} improves agreement with expert annotations by 90.17\% over the strongest baseline. We benchmark 31 frontier LLMs and deep research agents in an extensive scientific safety evaluation. Notably, deep research agents yield 32.3\% higher mean \textsc{DeHarm-Score} than standard LLMs, exposing autonomous agents as a critical blind spot in current safety defenses. Code and dataset are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/DeharmScore-7B55.
