AI.tldr: SciHazard is a real-world-grounded benchmark for evaluating scientific risks in LLMs, containing 2400 hazardous and 600 oversafety questions across 12 disciplines, along with a DeHarm-Score evaluation framework that decomposes harm into query severity, refusal behavior, executability, and net-new risk. Experiments show DeHarm-Score improves expert agreement by 90.17%, and deep research agents expose 32.3% higher risk than standard LLMs.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks rely on templated queries disconnected from real-world hazards and use LLM-as-a-Judge paradigms without domain grounding, making them insufficient for measuring actual scientific misuse risks from LLMs.
AI.method: The authors construct SciHazard with 2400 hazardous and 600 oversafety questions grounded in regulated entities and documented failures across 12 disciplines. They propose DeHarm-Score, which decomposes evaluation into query hazard severity, refusal behavior, and response-level risk—further splitting non-refused responses into Executability (dynamic checklists with importance weighting) and Net-new risk (retrieval-augmented claim extraction with synthesis-barrier verification).
AI.result: DeHarm-Score improves agreement with expert annotations by 90.17% over the strongest baseline. Deep research agents yield 32.3% higher mean DeHarm-Score than standard LLMs across 31 tested frontier models.
AI.conclusion: SciHazard and DeHarm-Score provide more accurate, domain-grounded safety evaluation for scientific LLM misuse. Autonomous agents represent a critical blind spot in current safety defenses, warranting further attention.

title: In-Context Learning for Wound Classification with Small Multimodal Language Models
summary: Wound image classification is often treated as a task-specific supervised learning problem, requiring substantial amounts of manually labelled data and retraining when the label space or deployment setting changes. This study evaluated whether small multimodal language models (SMLMs) can provide a training-free alternative for wound classification through retrieval-based in-context learning (ICL). Experiments used two public wound-image datasets: the Kaggle wound dataset (1469 images, 10 classes) and the Medetec dataset (560 images, 9 classes). Eleven SMLMs from the Qwen 3.5, Ministral 3, and Gemma 4 families were evaluated under zero-shot prompting and few-shot prompting with random support examples, embedding-based k-nearest-neighbour (kNN) retrieval, and kNN retrieval followed by maximal marginal relevance reranking (MMR). Retrieval-only weighted-kNN controls, support-set reduction experiments, and support-context size sweeps were used to assess the effects of retrieval, model scale, and prompt length. Query-conditioned ICL consistently outperformed zero-shot and random few-shot prompting. On the Kaggle dataset, the best result was achieved by Qwen 3.5 27B with kNN+MMR, reaching 0.872 accuracy and 0.871 F1 score. On Medetec, Qwen 3.5 27B with kNN+MMR reached 0.678 accuracy and 0.670 F1. Larger models exceeded matched weighted-kNN controls, indicating use of retrieved examples beyond nearest-neighbour voting. Retrieval-based ICL degraded modestly under support-set reduction, and most gains saturated with 8-10 support images. Retrieval-based ICL allows SMLMs to perform adaptable wound image classification without task-specific retraining. Compact retrieved contexts may support practical and privacy-conscious deployment, although performance remains dependent on model scale, retrieval strategy, and dataset difficulty.

AI.tldr: This study evaluates whether small multimodal language models (SMLMs) can perform wound image classification without training, using retrieval-based in-context learning. On two public datasets, query-conditioned ICL with kNN+MMR retrieval consistently outperformed zero-shot and random few-shot prompting, with Qwen 3.5 27B achieving best results (0.872 accuracy on Kaggle, 0.678 on Medetec). Performance depends on model scale, retrieval strategy, and dataset difficulty, but offers a training-free, privacy-conscious deployment alternative.
AI.motivation: To explore whether small multimodal language models can serve as a training-free alternative for wound classification, avoiding the need for substantial manually labeled data and model retraining when label spaces or deployment settings change.
AI.method: Evaluated 11 SMLMs (Qwen 3.5, Ministral 3, Gemma 4 families) on two wound datasets (Kaggle: 1469 images/10 classes; Medetec: 560 images/9 classes) under zero-shot prompting, random few-shot prompting, embedding-based kNN retrieval, and kNN+MMR retrieval. Included weighted-kNN controls, support-set reduction experiments, and prompt length sweeps.
AI.result: Query-conditioned ICL outperformed zero-shot and random few-shot prompting. Qwen 3.5 27B with kNN+MMR achieved best results: 0.872 accuracy/0.871 F1 on Kaggle; 0.678 accuracy/0.670 F1 on Medetec. Larger models exceeded weighted-kNN controls. Gains saturated with 8-10 support images; performance degraded modestly under support-set reduction.
AI.conclusion: Retrieval-based ICL enables SMLMs to perform adaptable wound classification without task-specific retraining. Compact retrieved contexts support practical, privacy-conscious deployment, though performance remains contingent on model scale, retrieval strategy, and dataset difficulty.

title: PAC--Bayes Bounds on Quotient Parameter Spaces: Geometry-induced Implicit-Bias Priors
summary:
Overparameterized models often have continuous parameter symmetries, so different parameters define the same predictor. We show that PAC--Bayesian analysis should be performed on the quotient predictor space: pushing a prior and posterior to the quotient preserves the empirical and population Gibbs risks while removing the nonnegative KL contribution caused solely by how the two distributions differ among parameterizations of the same predictor.
  Quotienting alone does not determine which prior to use. We construct a canonical choice of one parameterization for each predictor and account for the geometric volume of its equivalent parameterizations. This transforms a neutral reference prior into a data-independent prior that reflects the model's implicit bias. It approximates the ideal but inadmissible posterior-matched prior, which would minimize the KL term by depending on the training data. The resulting certificate is tighter exactly when this geometry-induced prior has smaller KL divergence from the learned quotient posterior than the neutral prior.
  We test this prediction in Fourier regression with a Hadamard parameterization and in Query-Key attention, using ordinary SGD without an explicit regularizer. The implicit-bias prior reduces the mean quotient-space KL by \(40.69\%\) and the mean PAC--Bayes certificate by \(21.40\%\) in the Fourier-Hadamard experiment. The smaller, prior-scale-dependent improvement in Query-Key attention confirms the predicted conditional nature of the effect.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes performing PAC-Bayesian analysis on the quotient predictor space (factoring out parameter symmetries) and introduces a data-independent prior that captures the model's implicit bias by accounting for the geometric volume of equivalent parameterizations. This yields tighter generalization certificates, demonstrated in Fourier-Hadamard regression and Query-Key attention experiments.
AI.motivation: Overparameterized models have continuous parameter symmetries where different parameters define the same predictor, causing the KL divergence term in PAC-Bayes bounds to capture spurious differences due to parameterization choice rather than predictor differences. The authors aim to remove this artifact and construct a principled prior reflecting implicit bias.
AI.method: (1) Push prior and posterior to the quotient predictor space to remove KL contribution from parameterization redundancies. (2) Construct a canonical choice of one parameterization per predictor and account for the geometric volume of its equivalent parameterizations, transforming a neutral reference prior into a data-independent prior that reflects the model's implicit bias. (3) Approximate the ideal but inadmissible posterior-matched prior.
AI.result: Fourier-Hadamard experiment: mean quotient-space KL reduced by 40.69%, mean PAC-Bayes certificate reduced by 21.40%. Query-Key attention: smaller, prior-scale-dependent improvement, confirming the predicted conditional nature of the effect.
AI.conclusion: Quotienting out parameter symmetries and using a geometry-informed prior that captures implicit bias leads to tighter PAC-Bayes certificates, with the improvement being conditional on the relationship between the geometry-induced prior and the learned posterior.

title: Semantic Primes as Explanans for Emotion in Large Language Models
summary: Progresses have been made on understanding emotion mechanisms of large language models (LLMs). However, how to explain emotion in LLMs, or even what constitutes good explanations, are less clear. Emotion representations, components, circuits are widely recoverable, but as explanations of a model's own computation they are circular; the emotion space dimensions tend to be arbitrary and non-terminating. A pressing question to ask is whether a more primitive set of internal variables does the work: the semantic primes of the Natural Semantic Metalanguage (NSM). Across four instruction-tuned LLMs (Llama-1B, Gemma-2B, Gemma-9B, OLMo-7B), experiments show that the NSM primes are (1) recoverable internal elements; and (2) on the reference model, intervening with a prime based direction controls emotion about three times as strongly, and twice as selectively, as the best appraisal based direction; and (3) the model treats a prime based explication as interchangeable with the corresponding emotion. These evidences suggest that NSM primes seem to be better explanans for emotion in LLMs than many alternative options according to scientific explanations criteria.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes that Natural Semantic Metalanguage (NSM) primes serve as better fundamental explanatory units for emotions in LLMs than emotion concepts themselves, showing across four models that NSM primes are recoverable, provide stronger control over emotions, and are treated as interchangeable with emotions.
AI.motivation: Current approaches to explaining emotions in LLMs—using emotion representations, components, or circuits—are circular (they rely on the model's own emotion concepts) and suffer from arbitrary, non-terminating emotion space dimensions. The authors seek a more primitive, grounded set of internal variables to explain LLM emotions.
AI.method: The authors test Natural Semantic Metalanguage (NSM) primes (e.g., GOOD, BAD, FEEL) as explanatory primitives across four instruction-tuned LLMs (Llama-1B, Gemma-2B, Gemma-9B, OLMo-7B). They evaluate (1) recoverability of NSM prime representations, (2) causal intervention strength and selectivity of NSM-based directions vs. appraisal-based directions for controlling emotion, and (3) interchangeability between NSM-based explications and corresponding emotions in model behavior.
AI.result: NSM primes are (1) recoverable internal elements in all tested models; (2) intervening with NSM prime-based directions controls emotion ~3x more strongly and ~2x more selectively than the best appraisal-based direction; (3) models treat NSM-based explications as interchangeable with the corresponding emotion concepts.
AI.conclusion: NSM primes appear to be better explanans (explanatory variables) for emotion in LLMs than alternative options (e.g., appraisal dimensions), according to standard criteria for scientific explanations.

title: Open-Vocabulary Gaze Object Prediction: Benchmark and Method
summary: Gaze Object Prediction (GOP) aims to localize and recognize the objects humans attend to, a task crucial for understanding human-centric interactions. However, existing methods are typically trained under a closed-vocabulary paradigm with a fixed label space and evaluated on scene-specific datasets, limiting their applicability to real-world scenarios where gaze targets often follow a long-tail distribution or belong to unseen categories. To address this gap, we introduce Diverse Scenes for Gaze object prediction (DiSG), a benchmark containing 86 in-the-wild categories that facilitates the evaluation of Open-Vocabulary GOP (OVGOP). Building on DiSG, we propose a framework that leverages text-driven object discovery to localize potential gaze candidates, with a gaze-guided selection module to pinpoint the intended target from the candidate objects. Furthermore, to better capture semantic knowledge across diverse in-the-wild categories, we introduce Gradient-Informed Selection Tuning (GIST) to selectively update parameters most relevant to a given class vocabulary. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our proposed model performs effectively in open-vocabulary settings and also outperforms existing methods in the conventional closed-vocabulary setting. The benchmark and code is available at https://github.com/sensniu/ovgop.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces DiSG, a benchmark for Open-Vocabulary Gaze Object Prediction (OVGOP), and proposes a framework combining text-driven object discovery, gaze-guided selection, and Gradient-Informed Selection Tuning (GIST) to handle unseen and long-tail gaze target categories in real-world scenarios.
AI.motivation: Existing GOP methods rely on closed-vocabulary paradigms with fixed label spaces and scene-specific datasets, failing in real-world scenarios where gaze targets follow long-tail distributions or belong to unseen categories.
AI.method: Proposes DiSG benchmark (86 in-the-wild categories) for OVGOP evaluation; a framework with text-driven object discovery for candidate localization, gaze-guided selection for target identification, and GIST for selectively updating parameters relevant to class vocabulary.
AI.result: The proposed model performs effectively in open-vocabulary settings and outperforms existing methods in conventional closed-vocabulary settings.
AI.conclusion: DiSG and the proposed framework enable effective open-vocabulary gaze object prediction, demonstrating strong generalization to unseen and long-tail categories.

title: Intelligence from Learnable Novelty
summary: Intelligence appears under different names in different fields: as data compression in statistics and machine learning, as universal computation in dynamical systems, and as adaptive behavior in agents. Each field carries its own objective, and the two most influential drives often fail in mirror image: novelty search, which seeks surprise, is transfixed by a noisy television screen, while the free-energy principle, which avoids surprise, is most content in a dark room. Both failures have a single cause: each objective treats as one quantity the surprise a learner can convert into knowledge and the surprise it never can. Here we show that the learnable part of that information, which we call learnable novelty, yields the seemingly disparate projections of intelligence, and we give a closed-form estimator of it built on a cheap and differentiable reservoir computer. Used as a measure, with no supervision of any kind, the estimator recovers decades of complexity classification, ranking the Turing-complete rule~110 highest among the elementary cellular automata. Used as an objective, its gradient carries a neural cellular automaton from simple dynamics into a regime of solitons, the traveling, colliding structures by which rule~110 computes, as well as organizes the representation of an image encoder around the ten digit classes of MNIST, fully unsupervised: no label ever enters training. Handed to a reinforcement-learning agent as an intrinsic reward, it supplies the exploration that task rewards lack, improving on the task baseline in nine of ten environments and collapsing in none. Complexity generation, abstraction, and exploration, ordinarily pursued with unrelated objectives in separate fields, thus emerge from ascent on one differentiable quantity, and the projections of intelligence gain a common quantitative footing.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "learnable novelty" — a unified quantity that bridges data compression, computation, and adaptive behavior — and provides a closed-form, differentiable estimator that recovers complexity rankings, enables unsupervised organization (e.g., MNIST digit clustering), generates soliton dynamics in neural cellular automata, and improves reinforcement learning exploration across 9/10 environments.
AI.motivation: Existing drives for intelligence — novelty search (maximizing surprise) and the free-energy principle (minimizing surprise) — fail symmetrically because they treat all surprise equally, failing to distinguish between learnable (convertible to knowledge) and irreducible surprise. A unified objective is needed.
AI.method: The authors define "learnable novelty" as the learnable portion of information, and build a closed-form estimator using a cheap, differentiable reservoir computer (echo-state network). This estimator is used both as a static measure and as a gradient-based objective for unsupervised learning in neural cellular automata, image encoders, and reinforcement learning agents.
AI.result: The measure recovers decades of complexity classification, ranking rule 110 (Turing-complete) highest among elementary cellular automata. As an objective, it drives a neural cellular automaton into soliton dynamics, organizes an image encoder's representations around MNIST digit classes without labels, and serves as an intrinsic reward that improves exploration in 9/10 RL environments without collapsing.
AI.conclusion: Complexity generation, abstraction, and exploration — traditionally pursued with separate objectives in different fields — all emerge from ascending a single differentiable quantity (learnable novelty), providing a common quantitative foundation for disparate projections of intelligence.

title: Do AI-Native Biotechs Need Departments? Benchmarking Company World Models for AI-Driven Drug Development
comment: Working paper. Includes public no-label benchmark cases and dry-lab evaluation artifacts. No wet-lab, patient-level, clinical, regulatory, or investment validation is claimed
summary: AI-native biotechnology companies are often designed by copying human biotech org charts into agent roles. We argue for a different abstraction: a Company World Model, defined as a persistent asset-to-value state representation with transition models, explicit value functions, planning, and updating across scientific, regulatory, BD, commercial, financial, and execution constraints. We introduce a dry-lab benchmark for testing whether AI-agent organizations should mimic departments or operate around such a world model. The benchmark contains 45 retrospective public-information decision cases with strict time cutoffs, hidden outcomes, common schemas, automatic scoring, and blinded pairwise judging. We compare human-org-mimic, stronger human-org-mimic-plus, AI-native asset-centric, and AI-native value-conversion architectures. The value-conversion architecture is a prompt-level approximation of a Company World Model: a Live Asset Value Record updated by Deal, Approval, Revenue, and Investment Arbiter loops. Under a success function defined by external BD, regulatory approval and launch, and revenue discipline, it achieved the highest automatic value-conversion score and was strongly preferred over the original baselines by value-specific blinded judges. Stress tests narrowed the claim: a stronger human baseline remained competitive, and a neutral judge did not show robust value-conversion dominance. Codex-only mechanistic ablations suggest that Revenue Room, Deal Room, and Approval Room carry useful work under the target objective. The central finding is objective-sensitive: departments may remain useful governance views, but the core AI-native operating primitive should be a shared, predictive asset-to-value state rather than a static human org chart. The study is dry-lab only and does not establish real-world drug success, clinical benefit, or revenue prediction accuracy.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Company World Model—a persistent asset-to-value state representation—as a better abstraction for AI-native biotech companies than simply copying human org charts. The authors introduce a dry-lab benchmark with 45 retrospective cases and compare four architectures. The value-conversion architecture (a prompt-level approximation of the Company World Model) achieved the highest automatic score and was preferred by value-specific judges, though human baselines remained competitive. The findings suggest the core AI-native operating primitive should be a shared, predictive asset-to-value state rather than a static human org chart.
AI.motivation: Current AI-native biotech companies often simply replicate human organizational structures (org charts) into agent roles, which may not be optimal for AI-driven operations. The authors argue for a fundamental rethinking: instead of mimicking human departments, AI systems should operate around a shared, predictive state representation that captures the full asset-to-value lifecycle.
AI.method: The authors constructed a dry-lab benchmark containing 45 retrospective decision cases from public information, with strict time cutoffs and hidden outcomes. They compared four architectures: human-org-mimic, stronger human-org-mimic-plus, AI-native asset-centric, and AI-native value-conversion. The value-conversion architecture approximates a Company World Model using a Live Asset Value Record updated by Deal, Approval, Revenue, and Investment Arbiter loops. Evaluation used automatic scoring and blinded pairwise judging.
AI.result: The value-conversion architecture achieved the highest automatic value-conversion score and was strongly preferred by value-specific blinded judges over baselines. Stress tests showed a stronger human baseline remained competitive, and a neutral judge did not show robust value-conversion dominance. Codex-only mechanistic ablations indicated that Revenue Room, Deal Room, and Approval Room components carry useful work under the target objective.
AI.conclusion: The core AI-native operating primitive should be a shared, predictive asset-to-value state rather than a static human org chart. However, departments may remain useful as governance views, and the finding is objective-sensitive. The study is dry-lab only and does not establish real-world drug success, clinical benefit, or revenue prediction accuracy.

title: OPD-IAD: From Language Judgment to Industrial Anomaly Detection via On-Policy Self-Distillation
summary: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) have recently shown strong potential for industrial anomaly detection (IAD) by providing image-level anomaly judgments and interpretable defect reasoning. However, current LVLM-based IAD methods still struggle to produce precise pixel-level anomaly maps from generated language judgments. We aim to achieve precise pixel-level localization while using language as guidance rather than letting it dominate the visual response. Specifically, we propose \textbf{OPD-IAD}, an evidence-privileged dense on-policy self-distillation framework for LVLM-based IAD. OPD-IAD distills privileged defect evidence onto the model's own on-policy judgment trajectory, enabling the final generated judgment to be learned under dense supervision rather than treated only as a textual answer. The resulting judgment serves as a semantic condition for dense anomaly perception. To turn this condition into dense visual evidence, we introduce \textbf{Language-guided Visual Anchoring}, which uses a judgment reforward to re-encode the image and question under the final-judgment condition into semantic anchors and contrasts them with dense visual features through a contrastive heatmap head to generate anomaly maps. The language judgment therefore provides compact semantic guidance, while dense visual features remain the basis for pixel-level scoring, allowing language to guide anomaly localization without letting language quality directly dictate the pixel-level response. Extensive experiments show that OPD-IAD achieves the best overall performance among LVLM-based IAD methods, leading on most image-level, pixel-level, and QA metrics.

AI.tldr: OPD-IAD is a framework that uses privileged self-distillation and language-guided visual anchoring to achieve precise pixel-level anomaly localization in LVLM-based industrial anomaly detection, where language guides but does not dominate the visual response.
AI.motivation: Current LVLM-based IAD methods struggle to produce precise pixel-level anomaly maps from generated language judgments, as language judgments tend to dominate rather than guide the visual response for dense localization.
AI.method: (1) Evidence-privileged dense on-policy self-distillation: distills privileged defect evidence onto the model's own on-policy judgment trajectory for dense supervision. (2) Language-guided Visual Anchoring: re-encodes image and question under the final-judgment condition into semantic anchors, then contrasts them with dense visual features via a contrastive heatmap head.
AI.result: OPD-IAD achieves the best overall performance among LVLM-based IAD methods, leading on most image-level, pixel-level, and QA metrics.
AI.conclusion: Language can effectively guide anomaly localization without directly dictating pixel-level responses, enabling precise pixel-level anomaly maps from LVLM-based judgments.

title: CANDOR: Chance-Calibrated Discordance in Frozen Foundation Encoders
summary: Frozen encoders are chosen by how well a lightweight head reads a finding from their features, not whether the geometry separates it. Nearest-neighbor discordance does, but with unequal banks the opposite-label neighbor wins on density, not geometry, so prevalence alone makes an uninformed encoder look blind. We introduce CANDOR, a discordance measure whose equal-size banks are symmetric under a label swap, fixing its chance level at exactly one half. Across 22 encoders, 20 datasets from 7 domains, and 605,443 images, this correction reverses the conclusion. Collapse falls below chance almost everywhere, so no encoder is blind, yet all are weak: the best chest model reads pneumothorax at 84.5 AUROC and still places 18.4% of those positives nearer an opposite-label film than its own kind in the same hospital. The same encoder that resolves bird species at 4.5 leaves chest findings at 42.8 and glaucoma at 49.8, at chance and worse than random weights. Such a case caps the normalized margin of any Lipschitz head, yet some head among eleven is correct on all but 2.8% of cases where one head misses 35.9%: the deficit is selection, not information. Erasure retention is associated with collapse; we detect no association with the objective, scale, recency, or size of the finding. Because the chance level is fixed, CANDOR can be read before any head is trained, flagging which findings a frozen encoder supports poorly.

AI.tldr: CANDOR is a symmetric discordance measure that fixes chance level at exactly 0.5, revealing that no frozen encoder is truly blind across 22 encoders and 605K images, but all show weak representation for various medical findings; the bottleneck is selection of the correct head, not missing information.
AI.motivation: Existing discordance measures are asymmetric under label swap (unequal bank sizes), causing prevalence alone to make uninformed encoders appear blind; a corrected measure is needed to fairly evaluate frozen encoder quality.
AI.method: Introduces CANDOR, a discordance measure with equal-size banks that is symmetric under label swap, fixing chance level at exactly 0.5. Evaluated across 22 encoders, 20 datasets (7 domains), and 605,443 images.
AI.result: Correction reverses prior conclusions: collapse below chance almost everywhere (no encoder is blind). Best chest model achieves 84.5 AUROC but 18.4% of positives are nearer an opposite label. Same encoder resolves birds at 4.5 but chest at 42.8 and glaucoma at 49.8 (at chance or worse). Erasure retention associated with collapse, no association with objective, scale, recency, or size.
AI.conclusion: The deficit is selection (picking the correct head), not information. CANDOR can flag poor encoder support before any head is trained, due to fixed chance level.

title: DWM: Separating World Effects from Actions in Latent World Models
summary:
Latent world models underpin much of modern model-based control, yet current action-conditioned formulations supervise
  the next-latent transition with a single, undifferentiated target, forcing a monolithic learning signal to absorb every
  source of state change. In real world, however, transitions arise from two heterogeneous sources: an action-driven
  component induced by the agent, and an action-invariant world effect -- the change that would still occur under a null
  action, dictated by the environment's intrinsic dynamics (e.g., gravity-driven sliding, inertia, contact rebound, and
  persistent drift). Fusing them into a single target entangles the two inside the latent transition, prevents the model
  from attributing observed changes to their underlying causes, and undermines the transferability of the learned
  dynamics. We introduce DWM (Decomposed World Model), a supervision-level framework that operationalizes this
  decomposition. DWM augments the predictor of a latent world model with an auxiliary world head, regularized by a
  normalized world-contrastive objective to be action-invariant, while the original pred head is coupled to it via an
  orthogonality constraint; together, the two signals induce an explicit additive decomposition of the predicted
  transition into an action-invariant and a complementary action-driven component, without altering the underlying
  architecture or inference pipeline. To evaluate DWM under persistent world effects, we construct W-variants of three
  standard control benchmarks -- PushT-W, Reacher-W, and TwoRoom-W -- each instantiating a distinct action-invariant
  dynamic. DWM matches strong baselines on the flat counterparts and delivers a mean absolute improvement of 13.1% in CEM
  planning success across the W-variants.

AI.tldr: DWM (Decomposed World Model) is a supervision-level framework that decomposes latent world model transitions into action-driven and action-invariant components using an auxiliary world head, orthogonality constraint, and world-contrastive objective, achieving 13.1% mean improvement in CEM planning success on W-variant benchmarks with persistent world dynamics.
AI.motivation: Current action-conditioned latent world models supervise next-latent transitions with a single undifferentiated target, fusing action-driven and action-invariant (e.g., gravity, inertia) components. This entanglement prevents attributing observed changes to their causes, undermines model transferability, and limits performance under persistent world dynamics.
AI.method: DWM augments the latent world model predictor with an auxiliary "world head" regularized by a normalized world-contrastive objective to enforce action-invariance, while coupling it to the original prediction head via an orthogonality constraint, inducing explicit additive decomposition into action-invariant and action-driven components without altering architecture or inference.
AI.result: DWM matches strong baselines on flat benchmarks and achieves a mean absolute improvement of 13.1% in CEM planning success across three W-variant benchmarks (PushT-W, Reacher-W, TwoRoom-W), each instantiating a distinct action-invariant dynamic.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly decomposing latent transitions into action-driven and action-invariant components via an auxiliary head and orthogonality constraint improves world model performance under persistent environment dynamics, without requiring architectural changes at inference time.

title: Think Sparse, Predict Dense: Continuous Thought Machines for Image Super-Resolution
summary: Continuous Thought Machines introduce an internal temporal dimension in which neuron-level histories and synchronization-derived representations evolve over a sequence of thought ticks. Extending this mechanism to dense visual prediction is non-trivial, because tasks such as image super-resolution require spatial evidence to remain available at every output location rather than being compressed into a single global representation. In the proposed window-level use of CTM, the thought dynamics produce a compact summary representation for each local window. DQ-CTM transforms this compact thought representation into window-aligned dense queries through a structured low-rank, parameter-efficient compact-to-dense query mechanism. Each position within a window receives its own query, while shared thought dynamics progressively refine the dense representation across ticks. In its super-resolution instantiation, termed ThinkSR, encoded feature maps are partitioned into local visual windows without token pooling, restored to the original feature field after shared refinement, and decoded into a high-resolution image. Preliminary experiments under a fixed four-tick training horizon reveal a progressive reconstruction trajectory. PSNR-Y increases from 28.1045 dB at $T=0$ to 30.2817 dB at $T=4$, while PSNR-RGB increases from 26.6271 dB to 28.7781 dB and the mean $\ell_1$ error decreases from 0.034602 to 0.023545. All 100 evaluated images improve from $T=1$ to $T=4$. These initial results establish the feasibility of sparse latent thought for dense spatial reconstruction and motivate broader continuous-thought architectures for dense vision.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces DQ-CTM, a continuous thought machine extended to dense visual prediction (super-resolution) via a compact-to-dense query mechanism operating on local windows, achieving progressive improvement over thought ticks in ThinkSR.
AI.motivation: Extending Continuous Thought Machines (CTMs) with internal temporal dynamics to dense visual prediction tasks like image super-resolution is non-trivial because spatial evidence must remain available at every output location rather than being compressed into a single global representation.
AI.method: DQ-CTM uses window-level CTM thought dynamics to produce compact summaries per local window, then transforms them into window-aligned dense queries via a low-rank, parameter-efficient compact-to-dense mechanism. In ThinkSR, encoded feature maps are partitioned into local windows (no token pooling), refined across thought ticks, restored to original field, and decoded to high-resolution.
AI.result: Under a fixed four-tick training horizon, PSNR-Y increases from 28.1045 dB (T=0) to 30.2817 dB (T=4); PSNR-RGB from 26.6271 dB to 28.7781 dB; mean ℓ1 error decreases from 0.034602 to 0.023545. All 100 evaluated images improved from T=1 to T=4.
AI.conclusion: The results establish feasibility of sparse latent thought for dense spatial reconstruction and motivate broader continuous-thought architectures for dense vision tasks.

title: Estimating Rare Events in Language Models with Proper Evaluation
summary: Quantifying the risk of rare failures in language models, such as those triggered by adversarial distribution shifts or very large-scale deployments, requires estimating probabilities far too small for random sampling. While recent work has formalized Low Probability Estimation, existing pipelines remain fragile in the rarest regimes: estimators can suffer zero-estimate collapse or systematic bias, and standard evaluation losses can become unstable or poorly matched to asymmetric safety costs. In this work, we introduce Gradient Activation Adaptive Multi-Level Splitting (GA-AMLS), which adapts rare-event Monte Carlo methods to the continuous activation space of language models. Specifically, GA-AMLS uses a gradient-based MCMC kernel to navigate activation space, eliminating the zero-estimate collapse of input-space search and replacing the independence assumptions of prior activation-space estimators with conditional sampling under an explicit, heavier-tailed activation prior. We also propose the Shifted-Power Bregman (SPB) Loss, a proper scoring rule that remains finite for zero-estimates and offers tunable asymmetry between underestimation and overestimation penalties. Experiments on small transformer models reveal a bias-variance tradeoff: GA-AMLS achieves the lowest loss under symmetric evaluation, reducing average log-space squared error relative to the strongest baseline across model sizes, while methods with overestimation bias prevail under asymmetric penalties. Our findings highlight that estimator choice should be matched to deployment context. More broadly, our work establishes activation space as a tractable domain for rare-event estimation in language models, circumventing the brittleness of discrete input-space search.

AI.tldr: Introduces GA-AMLS, a method adapting rare-event Monte Carlo to continuous activation space of language models for estimating extremely low failure probabilities, along with SPB Loss for handling zero-estimate collapse and asymmetric safety costs.
AI.motivation: Quantifying rare failures in language models (e.g., from adversarial shifts or large-scale deployment) requires estimating probabilities too small for random sampling; existing low-probability estimation pipelines suffer from zero-estimate collapse, systematic bias, and unstable loss functions poorly matched to asymmetric safety costs.
AI.method: GA-AMLS uses a gradient-based MCMC kernel to navigate continuous activation space, eliminating zero-estimate collapse of input-space search and replacing independence assumptions of prior activation-space estimators with conditional sampling under an explicit, heavier-tailed activation prior. Also proposes SPB Loss, a proper scoring rule that remains finite for zero-estimates with tunable asymmetry.
AI.result: On small transformer models, GA-AMLS achieves lowest loss under symmetric evaluation, reducing average log-space squared error relative to the strongest baseline across model sizes. Methods with overestimation bias prevail under asymmetric penalties, revealing a bias-variance tradeoff tied to deployment context.
AI.conclusion: Estimator choice should be matched to deployment context. Establishes activation space as a tractable domain for rare-event estimation in language models, circumventing brittleness of discrete input-space search.

title: One Rewrite to Fix Them All? Type-Aware Repair Allocation for Text-to-Image Prompt Optimization
summary: Text-to-image (T2I) generators often fail to follow their prompts faithfully, producing wrong counts, swapped attributes, ambiguous relations, and illegible text. Prompt optimization repairs such failures by rewriting the user prompt, requiring no generator retraining, and has yielded promising results. However, existing optimizers absorb heterogeneous failures into one uniform prompt expansion, even though each calls for different repair language. We formulate semantic prompt optimization as atomic repair allocation: each failed proposition is routed to a type-conditioned repair operator before the resulting local constraints are compiled into one executable prompt. We instantiate this formulation in the training-free Type-Aware Repair Allocation (TARA) framework, which separates diagnosis, allocation, compilation, and a semantic repair gate, an accept-or-revert controller over exactly one prescribed repair that prevents semantic regressions. Extensive experiments on DSG and TIFA across four frozen generators demonstrate that TARA achieves the best semantic accuracy in all eight benchmark-generator cells, improving over VisualPrompter by 5.6 and 2.6 points on DSG and TIFA, respectively, while maintaining image quality and running fastest in our matched local setting at 16.0 seconds versus 20.0 seconds per prompt.

AI.tldr: TARA is a training-free, type-aware prompt optimization framework that decomposes T2I failures into atomic repairs, assigns each to specialized operators, and uses a semantic gate to accept or revert changes, achieving state-of-the-art semantic accuracy across multiple benchmarks and generators while running faster than prior methods.
AI.motivation: Existing prompt optimizers treat all T2I failures (wrong counts, swapped attributes, etc.) uniformly with one prompt expansion, even though different failure types require different repair strategies. The authors aim to formulate a decomposed, type-aware approach to semantic prompt optimization.
AI.method: TARA (Type-Aware Repair Allocation) is a training-free framework with four components: (1) diagnosis of failed propositions in the prompt, (2) allocation of each failure to a type-conditioned repair operator, (3) compilation of local constraints into an executable prompt, and (4) a semantic repair gate that accepts or reverts repairs to prevent semantic regression.
AI.result: On DSG and TIFA benchmarks across four frozen generators, TARA achieves the best semantic accuracy in all eight benchmark-generator cells, improving over VisualPrompter by 5.6 points on DSG and 2.6 points on TIFA, while maintaining image quality and running faster (16.0s vs 20.0s per prompt).
AI.conclusion: Atomic repair allocation with type-conditioned operators and a semantic gating mechanism effectively improves prompt faithfulness in T2I generation without retraining, outperforming uniform expansion methods in both accuracy and efficiency.

title: Reliability-Aware 3D Geometric Injection for Universal Person Re-identification
summary: Universal person re-identification (ReID) aims to retrieve pedestrian identities across diverse real-world scenarios, including severe occlusions, clothing changes, and cross-modality shifts, within a unified model. However, existing 2D representations fundamentally struggle with spatial ambiguities due to a lack of depth and topological awareness, while naively introducing monocular 3D priors often causes severe negative transfer due to geometric estimation noise under extreme visual degradation. To safely harness the clothing-invariant and canonical structural properties of 3D geometry, we propose UniGeo, a Universal Monocular 3D-Enhanced ReID framework driven by a Consistency-Aware Reliability Gate and Dual-Stream Residual Fusion. Specifically, the processing of 3D information is strategically decoupled into geometric extraction and dynamic utilization. To provide pure structural compensation, we project monocular 3D parameters into kinematic joint representations, explicitly capturing instance-level geometric topology to resolve appearance-based ambiguities. To robustly incorporate these cues without perturbing the reliable 2D feature space, we isolate the 3D prior as a late-stage structural residual; modulated by the consistency-aware gate, this mechanism adaptively filters geometric noise and enables controlled fallback to the pure 2D baseline. Extensive experiments show that our method improves challenging, structure-sensitive scenarios while preserving competitive performance on clean domains. Code is available at https://github.com/BohanSu/UniGeo.

AI.tldr: UniGeo is a universal person re-identification framework that safely integrates monocular 3D geometry (via kinematic joint representations) into 2D ReID using a Consistency-Aware Reliability Gate and Dual-Stream Residual Fusion. This decouples 3D extraction from dynamic utilization, using late-stage structural residuals to filter geometric noise, improving performance under occlusions, clothing changes, and cross-modality shifts without degrading clean-domain results.
AI.motivation: Existing 2D person ReID representations suffer from spatial ambiguities due to lack of depth and topological awareness, while naive introduction of monocular 3D priors causes negative transfer from geometric estimation noise under extreme visual degradation.
AI.method: Proposes UniGeo with (1) decoupled geometric extraction and dynamic utilization; (2) projection of monocular 3D parameters into kinematic joint representations for instance-level geometric topology; (3) late-stage structural residual injection via a Consistency-Aware Reliability Gate that adaptively filters geometric noise and allows fallback to pure 2D baseline.
AI.result: The method improves challenging, structure-sensitive scenarios (occlusions, clothing changes, cross-modality shifts) while preserving competitive performance on clean domains.
AI.conclusion: Safely harnessing clothing-invariant and canonical structural properties of 3D geometry via consistency-gated residual fusion enables universal ReID without negative transfer.

title: AHEAD: Advancing Multi-Class Label Aggregation with Interpretable Cross-Annotator Modeling
summary: Crowdsourced labeling provides valuable labeled data for domains across natural language processing, computer vision, and video. Label aggregation aims to infer latent true labels from noisy and biased annotations, with the key lying in annotator reliability estimation. Despite promising progress, existing approaches struggle with one real-world bottleneck: most individual annotators label only a small subset of tasks, making accurate annotator estimation highly intractable. In this paper, we focus on the considerably more challenging multi-class label aggregation and propose AHEAD (cross-Annotator learning and High-confidEnce Annotator-guideD label aggregation), a cross-annotator learning framework that advances annotator reliability estimation by leveraging the population-level data. Specifically, AHEAD first learns high-dimensional cross-annotator contexts via a graph neural network, deriving multi-view, complementary annotator embeddings by aggregating individual-level annotator features with contextual information. These embeddings are then decoded into interpretable annotator-specific confusion matrices to fit the observed labels. We formulate a composite objective incorporating high-confidence annotators to alleviate the unsupervised training issues faced by prior models. Experiments on 10 real-world datasets spanning NLP, CV, Video, and Audio show that AHEAD substantially improves label accuracy, increasing average accuracy from 68.75% to 73.23%, with gains of up to 14.9% in the best case. Meanwhile, scalability experiments on the largest dataset further demonstrate the overall superiority of our method.

AI.tldr: AHEAD is a cross-annotator learning framework for multi-class label aggregation that uses graph neural networks to learn annotator embeddings from population-level data, incorporating high-confidence annotator guidance to improve reliability estimation and label accuracy, achieving 68.75% to 73.23% average accuracy across 10 datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing label aggregation methods struggle with accurate annotator reliability estimation because individual annotators typically label only a small subset of tasks, making estimation highly intractable.
AI.method: AHEAD learns high-dimensional cross-annotator contexts via a graph neural network, generates multi-view complementary annotator embeddings by aggregating individual-level features with contextual information, decodes embeddings into interpretable annotator-specific confusion matrices, and uses a composite objective incorporating high-confidence annotators to address unsupervised training issues.
AI.result: On 10 real-world datasets spanning NLP, CV, Video, and Audio, AHEAD increased average label accuracy from 68.75% to 73.23%, with gains up to 14.9% in the best case. Scalability experiments on the largest dataset also demonstrated superiority.
AI.conclusion: AHEAD substantially improves multi-class label aggregation by leveraging cross-annotator population-level information and high-confidence annotator guidance, outperforming prior methods across diverse domains.

title: AgentDebugX: An Open-Source Toolkit for Failure Observability, Attribution, and Recovery in LLM Agents
summary: LLM agent failures are difficult to debug because the step where an error surfaces is often not the one that caused it. Existing observability tools replay execution traces but provide little support for identifying the root cause or translating diagnosis into recovery. We present AgentDebugX, an open-source debugging framework that organizes debugging as a closed loop of Detect, Attribute, Recover, and Rerun. At its core, DeepDebug performs multi-turn root-cause diagnosis through global trajectory understanding, structure-guided investigation, and cross-examination. On the Who and When benchmark, DeepDebug achieves the best strict attribution accuracy among the evaluated methods on both tested open-weight backbones, reaching 28.8 percent exact agent-and-step accuracy on qwen3.5-9b versus 21.7 percent for the strongest single-pass baseline. On GAIA, DeepDebug repairs 13 of 73 failed tasks in a single rerun, compared with 4 to 6 for three decoupled self-correction baselines, improving overall accuracy from 55.8 percent to 63.6 percent. AgentDebugX exposes this workflow through a Python library, CLI, web console, and installable agentic skill, and provides an opt-in Error Hub for sharing scrubbed failure-diagnosis-repair bundles and reusing them as debugging memory.

AI.tldr: AgentDebugX is an open-source debugging framework for LLM agents that organizes debugging as a closed loop (Detect-Attribute-Recover-Rerun), powered by DeepDebug for multi-turn root-cause diagnosis. It achieves 28.8% strict attribution accuracy on Who/When benchmark and repairs 13/73 failed tasks on GAIA, improving accuracy from 55.8% to 63.6%.
AI.motivation: LLM agent failures are difficult to debug because the step where an error surfaces is often not the one that caused it, and existing observability tools provide little support for root-cause identification or translating diagnosis into recovery.
AI.method: AgentDebugX organizes debugging as a closed loop of Detect, Attribute, Recover, and Rerun. Its core component, DeepDebug, performs multi-turn root-cause diagnosis through global trajectory understanding, structure-guided investigation, and cross-examination. The framework is exposed via Python library, CLI, web console, and installable agentic skill, with an opt-in Error Hub for sharing failure-diagnosis-repair bundles.
AI.result: On the Who and When benchmark, DeepDebug achieves 28.8% exact agent-and-step accuracy on qwen3.5-9b versus 21.7% for the strongest single-pass baseline. On GAIA, DeepDebug repairs 13 of 73 failed tasks in a single rerun, compared with 4 to 6 for three decoupled self-correction baselines, improving overall accuracy from 55.8% to 63.6%.
AI.conclusion: AgentDebugX provides an effective closed-loop debugging framework for LLM agents with superior root-cause attribution and repair capabilities, and introduces a community-driven Error Hub for sharing and reusing debugging knowledge.

title: Wave2Body: Rethinking mmWave Human Pose Estimation as Radar-to-Body Token Translation
summary: Millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar enables privacy-friendly human sensing, but its sparse point clouds are physical measurements of view-dependent electromagnetic reflections and only indirectly characterize body articulation. Recovering a complete 3D pose from such partial, geometry-dependent observations is therefore under-constrained. Existing methods directly regress joint coordinates from paired radar-pose data, relying on the same limited paired supervision to learn radar perception, human-body structure, and their alignment. This coupling can encourage dataset-specific shortcuts under ambiguous radar observations. We propose Wave2Body, a radar-to-body token translation framework that decouples these learning targets using a self-supervised mmWave tokenizer, a pretrained compositional body tokenizer that defines the output space, and a lightweight translator between them. Experiments on M4Human and mmBody show that Wave2Body achieves stronger cross-domain generalization than previous methods while incurring much lower computational costs for training and inference. All the code and experiment results are publicly available at https://github.com/Galaxywalk/Wave2Body.

AI.tldr: Wave2Body is a radar-to-body token translation framework that decouples radar perception, human-body structure learning, and their alignment using a self-supervised mmWave tokenizer, a pretrained compositional body tokenizer, and a lightweight translator, achieving better cross-domain generalization and lower computational costs for 3D pose estimation from mmWave radar point clouds.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for mmWave radar-based 3D human pose estimation rely on direct regression from paired radar-pose data, which couples radar perception, body structure learning, and alignment into one task. This encourages dataset-specific shortcuts under ambiguous, partial, and view-dependent radar observations, limiting generalization.
AI.method: Wave2Body uses a three-component token translation framework: (1) a self-supervised mmWave tokenizer that learns radar representations without paired data, (2) a pretrained compositional body tokenizer that defines the output pose space, and (3) a lightweight translator that maps between the two token spaces, effectively decoupling the learning targets.
AI.result: On M4Human and mmBody datasets, Wave2Body achieves stronger cross-domain generalization than previous methods while requiring much lower computational costs for both training and inference.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling radar perception, body structure learning, and alignment through token translation is an effective and efficient paradigm for mmWave radar-based 3D human pose estimation, reducing reliance on paired supervision and improving generalization.

title: Weak-to-Strong Learning in Decision Making
summary: Many operational decisions rely on predictive models that estimate uncertain outcomes conditional on observable contexts. Training such models, however, often faces a fundamental data asymmetry: labeled outcomes are scarce or costly to obtain, while contextual covariates are abundant. Motivated by this data asymmetry, we develop a decision-aware weak-to-strong (W2S) framework that leverages both labeled and unlabeled data to improve contextual stochastic optimization. Specifically, we first train a weak model using limited labeled data and then use it to generate predicted outcome distributions on unlabeled contexts. These distributions provide soft supervision for training a strong model. We establish a non-asymptotic upper bound on the excess decision risk of W2S and a complementary lower bound for a strong-only benchmark. Their comparison yields explicit sufficient conditions under which W2S improves downstream decision performance. The key quantity is the correlation dimension between the weak and strong feature representations: when it is small, abundant unlabeled data reduce the effect of teacher errors along non-overlapping directions. A synthetic newsvendor experiment and a comment moderation experiment based on real-world data provide empirical evidence consistent with the theory.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a decision-aware weak-to-strong (W2S) framework that uses abundant unlabeled data (with weak model predictions as soft labels) to improve contextual stochastic optimization when labeled data is scarce. Theoretical bounds show W2S outperforms strong-only models when the correlation dimension between weak and strong feature representations is small.
AI.motivation: Training predictive models for operational decisions faces a fundamental data asymmetry: labeled outcomes are scarce/costly, while contextual covariates are abundant. This motivates leveraging unlabeled data to improve decision performance.
AI.method: The W2S framework: (1) train a weak model on limited labeled data, (2) use it to generate predicted outcome distributions on unlabeled contexts as soft supervision, (3) train a strong model using this supervision. Theoretical analysis provides non-asymptotic upper bounds on excess decision risk and lower bounds for strong-only benchmarks.
AI.result: W2S improves downstream decision performance when the correlation dimension between weak and strong feature representations is small. In such cases, abundant unlabeled data reduce teacher errors along non-overlapping directions. Experiments on synthetic newsvendor and real-world comment moderation confirm the theory.
AI.conclusion: The key factor determining W2S effectiveness is the correlation dimension between feature representations. Small correlation dimension enables unlabeled data to compensate for limited labeled data, improving contextual stochastic optimization decisions.

title: SkillSight: Seeing Through Shared Descriptions for Accurate Skill Retrieval
summary: As large language model agents gain access to increasingly large skill libraries, retrieving the right skill becomes critical to reliable capability selection and execution. Existing retrievers often treat skill descriptions as ordinary documents, overlooking their highly regular structure: shared descriptive patterns recur across many skills while providing little evidence for distinguishing the required capability. We show that this shared descriptive background systematically contributes to dense relevance scores, induces a pronounced energy gap between queries and skill documents, and obscures task-relevant signals. Based on this observation, we propose SkillSight, a training-free retrieval framework that calibrates shared background in both semantic and lexical spaces. Semantic Background Calibration estimates a background subspace from generic tokens identified by IDF, reducing similarity induced by shared descriptive patterns, while Lexical Evidence Calibration downweights shared background tokens to recover discriminative token-level evidence. Experiments on SRA-Bench and SkillBench-Supp demonstrate consistent improvements across retrieval metrics, with SkillSight improving Recall@10 by up to 20.21 percentage points over the original dense retriever. In end-to-end evaluation, SkillSight achieves the best overall performance across three agent models and outperforms LLM Selection by up to 4.97 percentage points. It is also up to 1,248 times faster than the Dense + Reranker baseline. These results identify shared descriptive background as a key source of bias in skill retrieval and demonstrate that explicitly calibrating it enables accurate and efficient skill selection without additional training. Our code is available at https://github.com/xiaojinying/SkillSight.

AI.tldr: SkillSight is a training-free retrieval framework that calibrates shared descriptive background patterns in skill documents to improve skill selection for LLM agents, achieving up to 20.21% improvement in Recall@10 and 1,248x speedup over dense+reranker baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing retrievers treat skill descriptions as ordinary documents, overlooking their highly regular structure where shared descriptive patterns recur across many skills and obscure task-relevant signals, causing a pronounced energy gap between queries and skill documents.
AI.method: SkillSight is a training-free framework with two components: (1) Semantic Background Calibration estimates a background subspace from IDF-identified generic tokens to reduce similarity from shared patterns; (2) Lexical Evidence Calibration downweights shared background tokens to recover discriminative token-level evidence.
AI.result: Improves Recall@10 by up to 20.21 percentage points over original dense retriever on SRA-Bench and SkillBench-Supp; outperforms LLM Selection by up to 4.97 percentage points in end-to-end evaluation; is up to 1,248 times faster than Dense + Reranker baseline.
AI.conclusion: Shared descriptive background is a key source of bias in skill retrieval, and explicitly calibrating it enables accurate and efficient skill selection without additional training.

title: Local Label-Informed Feature Transfer for Generating Ground-Truth Medical Images: A Comparison of GAN- and Diffusion-Based Approaches
summary: Validating Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) methods in medical imaging requires ground-truth data with known locations of informative features. However, current approaches rely on expert annotations, which are prone to labeling errors, or on hand-crafted artificial perturbations superimposed onto healthy images to mimic lesions or malignant features, which lack clinical realism. We present Local Label-Informed Feature Transfer (LLIFT), a framework for generating semi-synthetic brain magnetic resonance images with realistic lesions placed in user-controlled regions, which does not require pixel-level lesion annotations during training. We implement LLIFT with two generative paradigms: LLIFT-GAN, a custom GAN that learns pathological features from binary class labels alone, and LLIFT-DM, a diffusion-based inpainting pipeline conditioned on bounding-box masks via ControlNet. Both approaches are evaluated on brain magnetic resonance imaging data derived from the Human Connectome Project. In evaluations, both achieve Fréchet Inception Distance scores, with respect to the real pathological distribution, that are comparable to the inter-class reference between healthy and pathological images in the given dataset. Furthermore, qualitative inspection confirms the realism of lesion structures. The resulting benchmark datasets provide spatially controlled ground truth data for evaluating XAI methods in medical imaging.

AI.tldr: LLIFT is a framework that generates semi-synthetic brain MRI images with realistic lesions in user-controlled regions, using either GANs (LLIFT-GAN) or diffusion models (LLIFT-DM), without requiring pixel-level lesion annotations. It provides ground-truth data for evaluating XAI methods in medical imaging.
AI.motivation: Validating XAI methods in medical imaging requires ground-truth data with known informative feature locations. Current approaches rely on error-prone expert annotations or unrealistic artificial perturbations.
AI.method: LLIFT implements two generative paradigms: (1) LLIFT-GAN, a custom GAN that learns pathological features from binary class labels alone, and (2) LLIFT-DM, a diffusion-based inpainting pipeline conditioned on bounding-box masks via ControlNet. Both generate semi-synthetic brain MR images with realistic lesions placed in user-controlled regions without pixel-level annotations during training.
AI.result: Both LLIFT-GAN and LLIFT-DM achieve Fréchet Inception Distance scores comparable to the inter-class reference between healthy and pathological images in the dataset. Qualitative inspection confirms the realism of lesion structures.
AI.conclusion: LLIFT provides spatially controlled ground-truth benchmark datasets for evaluating XAI methods in medical imaging, overcoming limitations of expert annotations and artificial perturbations.

title: RRPO: Reference-Relative Policy Optimization with Stratified Conditional Rollouts
summary: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has shown strong effectiveness in reinforcement learning from verifiable feedback, where sampled rollouts can be compared within a group using task-provided correctness signals. However, extending group-relative optimization beyond verifiable settings is challenging because success in many tasks is not captured by a single correctness criterion. We propose \textbf{Reference-Relative Policy Optimization (RRPO)}, which generalizes GRPO by replacing direct correctness-based advantage construction with reference-relative contrastive comparisons. RRPO first uses \emph{stratified conditional rollouts} to construct positive and negative anchor sets, and then trains a metric projection head with a set-contrastive objective to compare candidate rollouts against these anchors. The resulting alignment scores directly define contrastive advantages: during policy optimization, the projection head is frozen, and the scores are centered within each rollout group in a standard group-relative objective. We evaluate RRPO using anchor-based contrastive advantages throughout policy optimization, without relying on task ground-truth verifiers. Across verifiable reasoning, open-ended generation, and post-SFT settings, RRPO remains competitive with verifier-based optimization, improves over weakly supervised baselines, and provides additional gains after supervised fine-tuning.

AI.tldr: RRPO generalizes GRPO by replacing verifier-based advantage computation with reference-relative contrastive comparisons using stratified conditional rollouts and a learned metric projection head, achieving competitive results across reasoning, open-ended generation, and post-SFT settings without task-specific verifiers.
AI.motivation: GRPO is effective for reinforcement learning from verifiable feedback, but extending group-relative optimization to non-verifiable tasks is challenging because success is not captured by a single correctness criterion.
AI.method: RRPO (1) uses stratified conditional rollouts to construct positive and negative anchor sets, (2) trains a metric projection head with a set-contrastive objective to compare candidate rollouts against anchors, and (3) uses the resulting alignment scores as contrastive advantages, centered within each rollout group, with the projection head frozen during policy optimization.
AI.result: RRPO remains competitive with verifier-based optimization, improves over weakly supervised baselines, and provides additional gains after supervised fine-tuning across verifiable reasoning, open-ended generation, and post-SFT settings.
AI.conclusion: RRPO effectively extends group-relative policy optimization beyond verifiable settings by using learned contrastive comparisons, eliminating the need for task-provided verifiers while maintaining strong performance.

title: AI Tour Meeting: Group Travel Planning by LLM Agents
summary: This paper proposes AI Tour Meeting, a group travel planning framework powered by multiple Large Language Model (LLM)-based agents. The agents are instantiated with distinct personas and collaboratively seek an itinerary that satisfies their constraints and preferences through natural language discussion. The framework enables easy and flexible orchestration of such discussions by providing interfaces for configuring agent personas, discussion workflows, monitoring, and LLM deployment. Its primary use case is a simulation tool for analyzing the behavior of multiple LLM agents during tour planning discussions. This paper demonstrates the utility of the framework by presenting system validation and several analytical results obtained by the framework.

AI.tldr: AI Tour Meeting is a multi-LLM-agent framework for group travel planning where agents with distinct personas discuss and negotiate itineraries through natural language, providing configuration, monitoring, and analysis interfaces.
AI.motivation: To address the complexity of group travel planning where multiple participants have conflicting constraints and preferences, and to provide a simulation tool for analyzing multi-LLM-agent collaborative behavior in negotiation scenarios.
AI.method: Multiple LLM-based agents are instantiated with distinct personas (simulating different travelers) and engage in natural language discussions to collaboratively seek a satisfying itinerary. The framework provides interfaces for configuring agent personas, discussion workflows, monitoring, and LLM deployment.
AI.result: System validation and several analytical results obtained from the framework demonstrate its utility as a simulation tool for analyzing multi-agent tour planning discussions.
AI.conclusion: The framework effectively enables orchestration and analysis of multi-LLM-agent group travel planning discussions, serving as both a planning tool and a simulation environment for studying LLM agent behavior.

title: SynGallery: A Synthetic Gallery of Real Paintings for Instance-Level Artwork Recognition
summary: Instance-level artwork recognition requires matching a handheld visitor photograph to a specific work in a large museum collection. This is challenging because painting datasets typically provide clean catalog images for training, while test queries are captured under oblique viewpoints, gallery lighting, reflections, frames, and other scene-level variations. We present SynGallery, a synthetic gallery dataset for artwork retrieval that addresses this gap without collecting additional real photographs. Starting from catalog images of real paintings, we place each artwork into a procedurally generated 3D gallery scene and render it from multiple viewpoints under varied geometric and appearance conditions, while preserving the exact identity of the original work. The resulting dataset contains 24,490 rendered views of 4,898 paintings from the Met benchmark. We show that these synthetic views provide a stronger training signal than the corresponding studio photographs. At the same number of training data points, training only on SynGallery improves art painting recognition from 67.18 to 73.47 GAP$^-$. When added to the full Met training set, SynGallery improves the published benchmark protocol from 35.97 to 38.48 GAP. Ablation experiments show that the gain comes primarily from geometric viewpoint variation rather than photographic realism: blur, sensor noise, and image compression consistently reduce performance.

AI.tldr: SynGallery is a synthetic gallery dataset for artwork retrieval that creates 3D rendered views of paintings from catalog images to improve instance-level artwork recognition. It contains 24,490 rendered views of 4,898 paintings and boosts recognition performance from 67.18 to 73.47 GAP^- when used alone, and from 35.97 to 38.48 GAP when added to the full Met training set.
AI.motivation: Instance-level artwork recognition faces a domain gap between clean catalog training images and real-world test queries with oblique viewpoints, lighting, reflections, and frames—collecting real photographs at scale is impractical.
AI.method: Each catalog painting is placed into a procedural 3D gallery scene and rendered from multiple viewpoints with varied geometric and appearance conditions (viewpoint, lighting) while preserving identity; the synthetic views are used as training data without collecting real photographs.
AI.result: Training solely on SynGallery improves recognition from 67.18 to 73.47 GAP^-; adding it to the full Met set improves from 35.97 to 38.48 GAP. Geometric viewpoint variation drives gains, while photographic realism effects (blur, noise, compression) consistently reduce performance.
AI.conclusion: Synthetic rendered views with geometric variation provide a stronger training signal than studio photographs for artwork recognition, and adding photographic noise artifacts is detrimental.

title: Hybrid Latent-Structural Fusion (HLSF) for Cyber Anomaly Detection
summary: Malicious anomalous activity detection is a fundamental challenge for cyber security systems. Both tensor decomposition under statistical framework with CANDECOMP-PARAFAC alternating Poisson regression (CP-APR) and normalizing flows have proven to be powerful unsupervised machine learning methods that model multi-dimensional data and capture complex and multi-faceted details of behavior profiles in cyber security applications. In this study, we propose Hybrid Latent-Structural Fusion (HLSF), a weighted anomaly fusion framework integrating CP-APR structural anomaly scores with latent-space density scores derived from normalizing flows. In our experiments, we show that the HLSF framework improves anomaly detection performance on a dataset of real-world compromised user credentials collected from the large enterprise network of Los Alamos National Laboratory (LANL) during a red-teaming exercise, compared with using CP-APR or normalizing flows alone.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Hybrid Latent-Structural Fusion (HLSF), a weighted anomaly fusion framework that combines CP-APR structural anomaly scores with normalizing flow-based latent-space density scores. Experiments on real-world compromised credential data from LANL show HLSF outperforms either method alone.
AI.motivation: Malicious anomalous activity detection remains a fundamental challenge for cyber security systems, motivating the need for more effective unsupervised detection methods.
AI.method: Hybrid Latent-Structural Fusion (HLSF), a weighted anomaly fusion framework integrating CP-APR structural anomaly scores with latent-space density scores derived from normalizing flows.
AI.result: HLSF improves anomaly detection performance on a dataset of real-world compromised user credentials from LANL's enterprise network during a red-teaming exercise, compared to using CP-APR or normalizing flows alone.
AI.conclusion: Fusing structural (CP-APR) and latent-space (normalizing flows) anomaly scores yields superior detection performance for malicious anomalous activity in cyber security contexts.

title: Evaluating medical AI under missing information: same-provider judges and human raters change apparent safety
summary: Readiness stress-testing of medical AI has focused on closed-ended and multimodal benchmarks. We extend it to open-ended clinical conversation under missing information, where safe behavior means recognizing absent information and qualifying, clarifying, or not over-committing - and where the evaluator becomes part of the measurement. We stress-test four models - three flagships (Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-5.5, Grok 4.3) and one mid-tier model (Gemini 3.5 Flash) - by deleting the latter half of the final user turn in HealthBench conversations, grading responses with a four-provider LLM-judge panel and a blinded clinician-anchored reference. Two evaluator-facing results are robust. First, judge choice materially changes apparent safety: inter-judge agreement is only moderate (Fleiss' kappa = 0.65), and after adjusting for each judge's general leniency (vote-level logistic regression), a positive same-provider association remains (exact permutation p = 0.04; GPT-5.5 ~ +0.10 on the probability scale) - large enough to change which model appears to over-commit least once its own-provider judge is excluded. Second, LLM judges are more permissive than clinicians on a blinded 50-item subsample: all four are significantly more lenient than the stricter independent clinician (crediting appropriate uncertainty on 66-84% of items vs 52%), and three of four than the author-influenced consensus (Grok directional only; judge-vs-consensus kappa = 0.20-0.43). On the author-audited clinical-underdetermined subset the permissiveness gap widened and the point-estimate model ordering held. A closed-ended MedQA anchor confirms accuracy is high and option-order effects are within a +/-5-point equivalence region for three of four models, so the safety gap is about calibration, not knowledge. We release the harness, prompts, per-item outputs, judge panel, perturbation audit, and human-annotation protocol.

AI.tldr: This paper stress-tests medical AI safety in open-ended clinical conversations where information is missing. It finds that LLM-based judges show only moderate agreement (Fleiss' kappa=0.65), and a same-provider bias exists (~+0.10 probability scale, p=0.04) where models appear safer when judged by their own provider's judge. LLM judges are significantly more lenient than clinicians (66-84% vs 52% crediting appropriate uncertainty), with the gap widening on clinically underdetermined cases. The safety gap is attributed to calibration rather than knowledge.
AI.motivation: Current medical AI stress-testing focuses on closed-ended benchmarks, but real clinical practice involves open-ended conversations with missing information. Safe behavior requires recognizing absent information and qualifying responses appropriately. The evaluator (judge) itself becomes part of the measurement, yet the impact of judge choice on apparent safety has been understudied.
AI.method: Authors stress-tested four models (Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-5.5, Grok 4.3, Gemini 3.5 Flash) by deleting the latter half of the final user turn in HealthBench conversations. Responses were graded using a four-provider LLM-judge panel and a blinded clinician-anchored reference. Analysis included Fleiss' kappa for inter-judge agreement, vote-level logistic regression for same-provider bias, and comparison against clinician ratings on a 50-item subsample. A closed-ended MedQA anchor was used to assess knowledge calibration.
AI.result: Inter-judge agreement was only moderate (Fleiss' kappa=0.65). Same-provider bias was significant (p=0.04), with GPT-5.5 showing ~+0.10 advantage when judged by its own-provider judge. All four LLM judges were significantly more lenient than the stricter clinician (66-84% vs 52% crediting appropriate uncertainty). On the underdetermined subset, the permissiveness gap widened. MedQA accuracy was high with option-order effects within +/-5 points for three of four models.
AI.conclusion: The safety gap in open-ended medical AI conversations is about calibration, not knowledge. Judge choice materially changes apparent safety rankings, and LLM judges are systematically more permissive than clinicians. Researchers should account for evaluator effects when stress-testing medical AI, and the field needs better-calibrated evaluation methods for open-ended clinical scenarios.

title: TAP-RAG: Task-Aware Policy Control for Long-Document Multimodal Question Answering
summary: Long-document multimodal question answering requires more than retrieving relevant chunks from a large document. Different queries require different evidence behavior. Existing multimodal RAG systems improve evidence access through text chunks, page images, graph links, or heterogeneous document elements, but they often apply a largely query-agnostic evidence-use strategy. We present TAP-RAG, a task-aware policy-controlled RAG framework for long-document multimodal QA. TAP-RAG contains a main controller, the Task-Aware Policy Controller (TAPC), and two policy-guided evidence executors: Task-Aware Query-Guided Flow Diffusion (TA-QFD) and Task-Aware Visual Enhancement (TAVE). For each query, TAPC predicts the task prior, estimates visual/local/global evidence signals, and produces an executable policy. TA-QFD then expands textual and structural evidence over the multimodal document graph, while TAVE selectively inspects page images when visual or layout evidence is needed. A guarded synthesis stage fuses text, visual, and structural evidence and abstains when support is insufficient. On DocBench and MMLongBench-Doc, TAP-RAG achieves the best overall accuracy among the compared systems, improving over a matched multimodal-RAG baseline by +9.1 points (61.1 to 70.2) and +4.5 points (42.2 to 46.7), respectively.

AI.tldr: TAP-RAG is a task-aware policy-controlled RAG framework for long-document multimodal QA that uses a controller to predict task priors and evidence signals, then executes policies for textual/structural evidence expansion and visual inspection, achieving state-of-the-art results on DocBench and MMLongBench-Doc.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal RAG systems retrieve evidence in a query-agnostic manner, failing to adapt to the diverse evidence behaviors required by different queries in long-document multimodal question answering.
