AI.method: CoGoal3D uses a two-stage pipeline: (1) a multiscale 3D-aware global fusion module to mitigate 3D spatial misalignment, and (2) a refinement stage with an auxiliary 3D point reconstruction task, plus a multi-agent collaborative data augmentation strategy.
AI.result: Achieves new state-of-the-art performance with 3D AP@0.7 improvements of 10.86%, 10.34%, and 10.18% on DAIR-V2X, V2V4Real, and V2X-Real datasets, respectively.
AI.conclusion: CoGoal3D effectively addresses 3D spatial misalignment in collaborative V2X perception, significantly outperforming prior methods in 3D object detection.

title: Conditioned Direct Feedback Alignment via Activity and Error Geometry
summary: Direct feedback alignment (DFA) trains hidden layers with fixed random projections of the output error, avoiding the transposed-weight backward pass of backpropagation (BP). We study a failure mode of DFA training that is distinct from feedback quality: the local weight update is calculated by an outer product, so anisotropy can enter through either its presynaptic-activity factor or its local-error factor. Our analyses with controlled synthetic regimes isolate the first failure mode and show an approximately 40-percentage-point activity-conditioning gain when high-variance directions contain task-irrelevant nuisance. Three clean confirmations isolate a different regime: error conditioning improves raw DFA by 1.77--7.53 percentage points, and combining independently selected activity and error factors adds 0.40--0.90 points over activity conditioning. The signs hold for tanh/one-vs-rest MNIST and preregistered Fashion-MNIST, and replicate on eight fresh seeds in a ReLU/softmax MNIST model. This factorization yields a symmetric block-local family of normalized DFA (nDFA): activity nDFA right-preconditions by an inverse activity second moment, error nDFA left-preconditions by an inverse local-error second moment, and K-nDFA applies both factors with separately tuned damping. A linearized post-alignment calculation gives an exact input-side spectral identity and a Kronecker-factor motivation for the two-sided rule, whereas norm matching rules out a scalar step-size explanation. The error factor is fragile when under-damped, BatchNorm is a strong activity-side alternative, and convnet gains remain partial. We therefore frame conditioned DFA as a factor-level study of when local outer-product rules fail, not as a general replacement for BP or a solution to all-layer convolutional credit assignment.

AI.tldr: Direct feedback alignment (DFA) fails due to anisotropy in outer-product weight updates from either presynaptic-activity or local-error factors; conditioning these factors via normalized DFA (nDFA) variants yields accuracy gains of 1.77–7.53 percentage points, but the approach is not a general BP replacement.
AI.motivation: Identify and isolate distinct failure modes of DFA training beyond feedback quality, specifically the conditioning of local outer-product updates due to activity and error anisotropy.
AI.method: Synthetic controlled regimes to isolate activity-conditioning failures; DFA, activity nDFA, error nDFA, and K-nDFA (combining both preconditioners); tested on tanh/one-vs-rest MNIST, ReLU/softmax MNIST, and Fashion-MNIST with preregistration and replication.
AI.result: Activity conditioning yields ~40 percentage point gain with task-irrelevant nuisance. Error conditioning improves DFA by 1.77–7.53 pp. Combined factors add 0.40–0.90 pp over activity alone. Error factor fragile when under-damped; BatchNorm is a strong activity-side alternative; convnet gains partial.
AI.conclusion: Conditioned DFA is a factor-level study of local outer-product rule failures, not a general BP replacement or full convnet credit assignment solution.

title: Fishing Out Free Riders: Shapley-Based Reward Attribution for Parallel Reasoning via Reinforcement Learning
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) excel at multi-step reasoning, yet current parallel reasoning approaches often fail to distinguish the contributions of individual reasoning paths. Many paths may be redundant, misleading, or even detrimental, but outcome-level rewards assign uniform reward, leading to ambiguous learning signals and unstable training. We propose Parallel Shapley, a reinforcement learning framework that attributes fine-grained, path-level contributions in multi-path reasoning. Treating each path as a player in a cooperative game, we leverage Shapley values to quantify marginal contributions, using a generative reward model to evaluate path utilities and Monte Carlo sampling for efficient approximation. Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks show that Parallel Shapley outperforms existing baselines while providing more stable and interpretable training. Our framework effectively "fishes out the free riders," assigning reward proportionally and improving multi-path reasoning in LLMs.

AI.tldr: Parallel Shapley is a reinforcement learning framework that uses Shapley values to assign fine-grained, path-level rewards in multi-path LLM reasoning, outperforming baselines on math benchmarks by eliminating free-rider effects and stabilizing training.
AI.motivation: Existing parallel reasoning approaches assign uniform outcome-level rewards across all reasoning paths, failing to distinguish redundant, misleading, or detrimental paths. This leads to ambiguous learning signals and unstable training.
AI.method: The framework treats each reasoning path as a player in a cooperative game, computes Shapley values to quantify marginal contributions of each path, uses a generative reward model to evaluate path utilities, and employs Monte Carlo sampling for efficient approximation.
AI.result: Parallel Shapley outperforms existing baselines on mathematical reasoning benchmarks while providing more stable and interpretable training. It effectively removes free-riders by assigning reward proportionally.
AI.conclusion: Fine-grained path-level reward attribution improves multi-path reasoning in LLMs by addressing the free-rider problem, leading to better performance and training stability.

title: FilmWorld: Agentic Novel-to-Film Generation through Dynamic Cinematic World Modeling
summary: Translating novels into films poses a grand challenge for generative artificial intelligence, requiring conversion of abstract literary prose into long-form, multi-scene visual narratives. While current video generation models excel at short, single-scene clips within narrow temporal and spatial contexts, novel-to-film generation operates in a more complex regime, demanding long-duration content across diverse scenes with dynamically evolving entity states. To address this, we formalize novel-to-film generation as dynamic cinematic world modeling, decomposed into two phases: construction, which grounds abstract, underspecified literary narratives into concrete, stateful, and persistent world entities; and evolution, which governs how these entities dynamically update under plot progression to maintain causal consistency across scenes. We propose FilmWorld, an end-to-end agentic system where two groups of specialized agents collaborate to instantiate these phases. Construction-side agents perform narrative structured translation, world entity state modeling with visual anchoring, and state-driven shot planning, progressively projecting literary language into a cinematic blueprint. Evolution-side agents perform state-anchored visual generation, cross-shot dynamic state propagation, and closed-loop state verification to maintain causal consistency and visual coherence. To address the evaluation gap in long-form generation, we introduce FilmEval, a systematic evaluation framework that couples a difficulty-graded benchmark of 15 representative novels with an automated protocol of nine objective metrics spanning three dimensions: cinematic presentation, film consistency, and novel fidelity. Experiments demonstrate that FilmWorld consistently outperforms state-of-the-art video generation agent systems, with particularly pronounced improvements in narrative fidelity and cross-scene consistency.

AI.tldr: FilmWorld is an agentic system for translating novels into long-form films by decomposing the task into two phases: construction (grounding abstract prose into concrete world entities) and evolution (maintaining causal consistency across scenes). It outperforms SOTA video generation agents on narrative fidelity and cross-scene consistency, evaluated via a new benchmark, FilmEval.
AI.motivation: Novel-to-film generation is a grand challenge for generative AI because it requires converting abstract literary prose into long-form, multi-scene visual narratives, far beyond the capabilities of current video generation models which are limited to short, single-scene clips with narrow temporal and spatial contexts.
AI.method: FilmWorld formalizes novel-to-film as dynamic cinematic world modeling with two phases: (1) Construction — narrative structured translation, world entity state modeling with visual anchoring, and state-driven shot planning by specialized agents; (2) Evolution — state-anchored visual generation, cross-shot dynamic state propagation, and closed-loop state verification by another group of agents. Evaluation uses the FilmEval framework with 15 graded novels and 9 objective metrics across cinematic presentation, film consistency, and novel fidelity.
AI.result: FilmWorld consistently outperforms state-of-the-art video generation agent systems, with particularly pronounced improvements in narrative fidelity and cross-scene consistency.
AI.conclusion: The two-phase construction-evolution architecture with specialized agents is an effective approach for long-form novel-to-film generation, and the FilmEval benchmark provides a systematic evaluation protocol for this task.

title: On the Diverse Dynamical Behaviors Arising in Deep Linear Transformers
summary: We study the inference-time behavior of deep linear encoder-only transformers through the lens of interacting particle systems. In this perspective, tokens are modeled as particles that interact dynamically through successive linear self-attention layers. We show that in embedding dimension two, for any key, query, and value matrices, the dynamics can be reformulated as a generalized Kuramoto-type model with pure second-harmonic coupling. This formulation is amenable to Watanabe--Strogatz theory which reveals the dynamics are intrinsically low-dimensional regardless of the parameter matrices. For a class of token initializations associated with the Ott--Antonsen (OA) manifold, we show that the parameter matrices induce a diverse variety of long-time behaviors in linear transformers, including clustering, oscillations, and bifurcations. The oscillations and bifurcations are characterized by uncovering a hidden Hamiltonian structure in the dynamics. By establishing a structural stability result, we further show that dynamics initialized near the OA manifold exhibit the same long-time behavior as those initialized exactly on the manifold. Motivated by our theory in dimension two, we conduct numerical experiments for analogous parameter regimes in higher-dimensional transformers. Our numerical experiments suggest that the long-time behaviors characterized in our theoretical results persist in higher dimensions.

AI.tldr: This paper studies deep linear encoder-only transformers by modeling tokens as interacting particles in a Kuramoto-type system, showing low-dimensional dynamics in 2D via Watanabe-Strogatz theory, and demonstrating clustering, oscillations, and bifurcations on the Ott-Antonsen manifold, with structural stability and empirical evidence for higher-dimensional persistence.
AI.motivation: To understand the inference-time behavior of linear transformers by bridging self-attention mechanisms with interacting particle systems and nonlinear dynamics theory.
AI.method: Reformulates linear transformer dynamics as a generalized Kuramoto model with second-harmonic coupling in 2D; applies Watanabe-Strogatz theory to reveal low-dimensional dynamics; analyzes the Ott-Antonsen manifold for long-time behaviors; proves structural stability; conducts numerical experiments in higher dimensions.
AI.result: In 2D, dynamics reduce to a Kuramoto-type model with low-dimensional behavior; on the OA manifold, clustering, oscillations, and bifurcations emerge, with a hidden Hamiltonian structure; structural stability holds near the OA manifold; higher-dimensional experiments show similar behaviors persist.
AI.conclusion: Linear encoder-only transformers exhibit structured, low-dimensional dynamical behaviors that can be understood analytically in 2D and persist empirically in higher dimensions, linking transformer inference to classical synchronization and oscillator theory.

title: Athena-Brain Technical Report: An Efficient Robot Brain for General Intelligence and Embodied Interactio
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in language understanding, reasoning, and world knowledge. As embodied agents become increasingly capable, there is a growing demand for compact models that can serve as an on-device brain, preserving the broad general intelligence of LLMs while enabling effective high-level interaction with embodied environments. Existing approaches, however, often prioritize either general-purpose intelligence or specialized embodied capabilities, making it challenging to satisfy both requirements within a single model. We present \textbf{Athena-Brain-8B}, an 8B LLM designed to serve as an on-device brain for embodied intelligence for embodied intelligence. Through a multi-stage post-training pipeline consisting of General Supervised Fine-Tuning, General Reinforcement Learning, Embodied Expert training, and Model Merge, Athena-Brain-8B maintains strong general capabilities while acquiring strong high-level embodied interaction capabilities and generating concise responses for efficient embodied interaction. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of Athena across both general and embodied evaluations. Compared with the corresponding Qwen3-8B thinking model, Athena-Brain-8B achieves comparable performance on general language and reasoning benchmarks while generating substantially shorter responses. On in-domain embodied benchmarks, Athena-Brain-8B consistently outperforms models of similar scale and surpasses several substantially larger frontier models evaluated zero-shot, demonstrating that compact language models can effectively integrate strong general intelligence with embodied capabilities.

AI.tldr: Athena-Brain-8B is an 8B LLM designed as an on-device brain for embodied intelligence, using a multi-stage post-training pipeline (General SFT, General RL, Embodied Expert training, Model Merge) to maintain strong general capabilities while acquiring embodied interaction skills, achieving comparable performance to Qwen3-8B on general benchmarks with shorter responses and outperforming similar-scale models on embodied tasks.
AI.motivation: There is a growing demand for compact on-device models that preserve the broad general intelligence of LLMs while enabling effective high-level interaction with embodied environments, but existing approaches prioritize either general-purpose intelligence or specialized embodied capabilities, making it challenging to satisfy both requirements in a single model.
AI.method: Multi-stage post-training pipeline consisting of General Supervised Fine-Tuning, General Reinforcement Learning, Embodied Expert training, and Model Merge.
AI.result: Athena-Brain-8B achieves comparable performance to Qwen3-8B on general language and reasoning benchmarks while generating substantially shorter responses. On in-domain embodied benchmarks, it consistently outperforms models of similar scale and surpasses several substantially larger frontier models evaluated zero-shot.
AI.conclusion: Compact language models can effectively integrate strong general intelligence with embodied capabilities, demonstrating that an 8B model can serve as an on-device brain for embodied intelligence without sacrificing general performance.

title: Gaze-DETR: Top-Down Guidance Through Priority Maps for Infrared Weak-Small UAV Detection with DETR
summary: Infrared small target detection (ISTD) remains challenging because tiny, low-contrast targets are easily overwhelmed by clutter, noise, or occlusion. Conventional single-frame and multi-frame detectors rely on bounding-box supervision, which specifies final target locations but offers little explicit guidance for prioritizing candidate regions or preserving weak-target evidence before localization. Task-driven visual search offers such guidance: top-down goals and visual evidence jointly form a spatial priority map that ranks candidate locations. Building on this principle, we propose Gaze-DETR, a bio-inspired detector that learns an internal priority map before localization. First, a priority head predicts a normalized priority map from image features. Second, Residual Priority-Guided Feature Modulation (RPFM) enhances high-priority responses while retaining multi-scale features. Finally, Priority-Guided Anchor Query Injection (PAQI) converts high-priority locations into decoder anchor queries. We train the priority head using three supervision schemes: box-derived Gaussian maps; real-gaze maps constructed from fixation-density maps; and transferred pseudo-gaze maps learned from gaze--box relations in paired annotations and applied to Anti-UAV410 training boxes. To support the latter two schemes, we construct TIR-UAV120-Gaze with paired detection and task-driven eye-tracking annotations. On TIR-UAV120-Gaze, Gaze-DETR achieves 85.76 mAP$_{50}$ and 88.77 F1 with box-derived supervision, and 86.18 mAP$_{50}$ and 89.00 F1 with real-gaze supervision. On Anti-UAV410, it achieves 87.06 mAP$_{50}$ and 90.90 F1 with box-derived supervision, and 87.08 mAP$_{50}$ and 90.43 F1 with transferred pseudo-gaze supervision. These results show that explicit spatial-priority learning provides pre-localization guidance complementary to bounding-box supervision across annotation settings and costs.

AI.tldr: Gaze-DETR is a bio-inspired infrared small target detector that learns an internal spatial priority map before target localization, using priority head, Residual Priority-Guided Feature Modulation (RPFM), and Priority-Guided Anchor Query Injection (PAQI). It achieves superior performance on TIR-UAV120-Gaze and Anti-UAV410 datasets with box-derived, real-gaze, and transferred pseudo-gaze supervision, demonstrating that explicit priority learning complements box supervision.
AI.motivation: Infrared small targets are easily overwhelmed by clutter/noise/occlusion, and conventional detectors relying solely on bounding-box supervision provide little guidance for prioritizing candidate regions or preserving weak-target evidence before localization.
AI.method: Proposes Gaze-DETR with three components: (1) Priority head predicting a normalized priority map; (2) RPFM that enhances high-priority responses while retaining multi-scale features; (3) PAQI that converts high-priority locations into decoder anchor queries. Priority head is trained with box-derived Gaussian maps, real-gaze maps from fixation-density data, or transferred pseudo-gaze maps learned from gaze-box relations.
AI.result: On TIR-UAV120-Gaze: 85.76 mAP50/88.77 F1 (box supervision), 86.18 mAP50/89.00 F1 (real-gaze). On Anti-UAV410: 87.06 mAP50/90.90 F1 (box supervision), 87.08 mAP50/90.43 F1 (pseudo-gaze).
AI.conclusion: Explicit spatial-priority learning provides effective pre-localization guidance complementary to bounding-box supervision across different annotation settings and costs.

title: Planning as Emergent Behavior in Reinforcement Learning with Relational Hidden States
summary: Reinforcement learning is conventionally divided into model-based and model-free methods. In this taxonomy, model-based methods perform lookahead planning over a learned world model, whereas model-free methods learn a reactive state-action mapping. Recent work, however, has shown that planning can emerge from model-free reinforcement learning alone. The conditions under which this behavior emerges from a pure reward-maximization objective have so far remained unclear. In this paper, we present evidence that, in the observed cases, the hidden-state structure of the neural architecture is the deciding factor. We find that a network of relational hidden states, each anchored to an environment state and exchanging messages along learned relations, acquires a planning mechanism. These hidden states recover the environment's transition structure in their learned relations, and improve the policy at decision time by planning over the learned graph. In a matched control agent that must additionally discover which cells represent which states, no such binding arises, and no planning follows from it. We argue that this explains the observed phenomenon of emergent planning in model-free reinforcement learning and raises the question of how common such emergent planning might be more generally. Finally, we hypothesize that the discovered mechanism could describe how planning emerges from pure reward maximization in the human brain through a neural architectural prior.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how planning can emerge from model-free reinforcement learning, finding that the hidden-state structure of neural architecture—specifically a network of relational hidden states anchored to environment states and exchanging messages—is the deciding factor. These hidden states recover the environment's transition structure and enable planning at decision time, whereas control agents without this binding mechanism do not exhibit planning.
AI.motivation: To understand the conditions under which planning behavior emerges from pure reward-maximization in model-free reinforcement learning, without explicit planning components.
AI.method: The authors compare neural architectures: one with relational hidden states anchored to environment states that exchange messages along learned relations, versus a matched control agent that must discover which cells represent which states. They analyze the hidden-state structure and learned relations to determine if planning mechanisms arise.
AI.result: Networks with relational hidden states recover the environment's transition structure in their learned relations and improve policy at decision time by planning over the learned graph. The control agent without binding does not exhibit such planning.
AI.conclusion: The neural architectural prior—specifically the hidden-state structure—explains emergent planning in model-free RL, and this mechanism may generalize to how planning emerges from reward maximization in the human brain.

title: Vector-Bench: Can Models Surgically Edit SVG Code?
summary: Instruction-based vector editing requires two capabilities: making a requested change and leaving everything else alone. The second is easy to miss when an output is judged only as a raster image. We introduce Vector-Bench, a compact, difficult benchmark of 40 SVG repair tasks. Each task pairs a corrupted SVG program with an author-written visual instruction, a hidden target program, 5.05 annotated repairs on average, and an average of 60.55 protected objects. Instructions describe visible defects without exposing element identifiers, coordinates, color codes, or path data. We define a deterministic binary specification reward: requested repairs use attribute-aware perceptual tolerances, while unrequested rendering- or application-relevant structure must remain semantically unchanged and the result must be a valid SVG. Canonical target equality and stricter source fidelity are retained as diagnostics. Validity-gated repair progress, a near-complete tier, and valid-output Unintended Change Rate (UCR) explain partial outcomes. We evaluate 34 model endpoints (25 listed as open-weight, 5 inexpensive controls, and 4 frontier closed endpoints) over 1360 requests. The strongest endpoint reaches only 15.0% full specification success, despite 43.7% mean repair progress, showing that apparent repair progress and specification-faithful editing remain substantially different. All prompts, outputs, scoring code, costs, and per-task reports are released.

AI.tldr: Vector-Bench is a benchmark of 40 SVG repair tasks evaluating instruction-based vector editing. It reveals a large gap between apparent repair progress (43.7%) and specification-faithful editing (15.0% top success), showing models struggle to make requested changes while preserving unrequested content.
AI.motivation: Existing raster-image evaluation misses the requirement to leave unchanged content intact during vector editing. The authors created a benchmark that explicitly tests both requested changes and preservation of protected objects in SVG programs.
AI.method: 40 SVG repair tasks with corrupted SVGs, author-written instructions (hiding element identifiers/coordinates/colors/path data), hidden target programs, 5.05 annotated repairs/task, 60.55 protected objects/task. A deterministic binary specification reward checks requested repairs with perceptual tolerances and unrequested semantic/structural fidelity plus validity. Diagnostic metrics include canonical target equality, source fidelity, validity-gated repair progress, near-complete tier, and valid-output UCR.
AI.result: 34 model endpoints evaluated over 1360 requests. Best model achieved 15.0% full specification success and 43.7% mean repair progress, indicating substantial divergence between apparent progress and specification adherence.
AI.conclusion: Apparent repair progress and specification-faithful editing remain substantially different. The benchmark, prompts, outputs, scoring code, costs, and per-task reports are released publicly.

title: Contrastive On-Policy Distillation
summary: On-policy Distillation (OPD) supervises a student model on trajectories sampled from its own policy by minimizing the divergence between the output distributions of the teacher and student at each token position, thereby providing dense token-level supervision. Although existing OPD methods have demonstrated strong performance in improving the reasoning ability of student models, their objectives fundamentally rely on token-level distribution matching. Consequently, they lack an explicit signal for comparing a token's relative compatibility across reasoning modes and thus do not directly model preferences between these modes. To address this limitation, we propose COPD, a contrastive OPD framework. Specifically, for each token generated by the student model, a frozen teacher model scores the same student state under two contrasting instructions that elicit light and heavy reasoning. The difference between the resulting log probabilities serves as a token-level advantage signal to guide the OPD update. Rather than merely imitating a single teacher distribution, COPD directly encourages the student model to learn more concise and efficient reasoning strategies. We conduct experiments on nine multimodal benchmarks covering both reasoning and understanding tasks. The results show that COPD substantially reduces reasoning length without compromising model performance and consistently improves efficiency across different tasks and model scales. Furthermore, the contrastive formulation can be seamlessly integrated into the On-policy Self-distillation (OPSD) framework, where self-contrastive supervision is constructed without an additional teacher model, thereby enabling the model to distill itself toward lightweight reasoning.

AI.tldr: COPD introduces contrastive On-policy Distillation that uses token-level advantage signals from contrasting light vs heavy reasoning instructions, reducing reasoning length without sacrificing performance across multimodal benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing On-policy Distillation methods rely on token-level distribution matching and lack explicit signals to compare token compatibility across reasoning modes, thus failing to directly model preferences between different reasoning strategies.
AI.method: COPD uses a frozen teacher model to score each student-generated token under two contrasting instructions (light vs heavy reasoning); the difference in log probabilities serves as a token-level advantage signal to guide the OPD update, directly encouraging concise and efficient reasoning.
AI.result: On nine multimodal benchmarks covering reasoning and understanding tasks, COPD substantially reduces reasoning length without compromising performance and consistently improves efficiency across tasks and model scales. The contrastive formulation also generalizes to On-policy Self-distillation (OPSD).
AI.conclusion: COPD effectively overcomes the limitation of existing OPD methods by introducing contrastive supervision that explicitly models preferences between reasoning modes, enabling more efficient reasoning while maintaining performance.

title: A Self-Evolving Default Action for Cooperative Tasks with Continuous Action Space
summary: Counterfactual credit assignment has proven effective in multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) for discrete action spaces, yet its extension to continuous-action cooperative tasks remains challenging. Existing methods that approximate the counterfactual baseline via Monte Carlo sampling often introduce bias into policy gradients and fail to guarantee convergence to local optima, as the sampled actions may not have been sufficiently trained. To address these limitations, we propose SAFE, a novel MARL framework that employs a counterfactual baseline conditioned on a self-evolving default action sampled from each agent's experience buffer. This design naturally extends to continuous action spaces without relying on additional simulations, reward models, or environment-specific prior knowledge. The baseline accurately quantifies each agent's contribution, and introduces no bias into the deterministic policy gradient, ensuring convergence to local optima. Extensive experiments on cooperative vehicular tasks demonstrate that SAFE consistently outperforms state-of-the-art models.

AI.tldr: SAFE proposes a counterfactual credit assignment framework for continuous-action MARL that uses a self-evolving default action from experience buffers as a baseline, eliminating bias and ensuring convergence while outperforming SOTA on cooperative vehicular tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing counterfactual methods for MARL struggle with continuous action spaces because Monte Carlo sampling introduces bias into policy gradients and fails to guarantee convergence, as sampled actions may not be sufficiently trained.
AI.method: SAFE uses a counterfactual baseline conditioned on a self-evolving default action sampled from each agent's experience buffer, extending naturally to continuous action spaces without additional simulations, reward models, or environment-specific prior knowledge.
AI.result: SAFE consistently outperforms state-of-the-art models on cooperative vehicular tasks, with the baseline accurately quantifying each agent's contribution and introducing no bias into the deterministic policy gradient.
AI.conclusion: SAFE provides a theoretically grounded, unbiased counterfactual credit assignment method for continuous-action MARL that guarantees convergence to local optima and demonstrates practical superiority in cooperative vehicular tasks.

title: Quality Action Assurance: Multimodal Verification of Examiner Claims in VR OSCEs
summary: Objective Structured Clinical Examinations (OSCEs) are the gold standard for assessing clinical competence, yet scoring remains vulnerable to examiner subjectivity, fatigue, and cognitive bias. Standard examiner validation via inter-rater statistics lacks explanatory power regarding the source of errors, as it neither analyzes examiner reasoning nor verifies examiner claims against actual events. Thus, we introduce Quality Action Assurance (QAA), a multimodal framework that verifies examiner claims in Virtual Reality (VR) pediatric OSCEs by comparing actions claimed by examiners against the true sequence of events, constructed from video, VR logs, and actor data. QAA combines a constrained temporal action alignment model, which performs action localization and actor source attribution, with a large language model that extracts examiner claims and checks them against the record. Across a 5-fold cross-validation, QAA achieves 99.2% $\pm$ 0.7% Actor F1 and 93.4% $\pm$ 1.9% W@16 for temporal alignment. Overall, QAA detects examiner errors with 70.0% precision and 76.7% recall, improving factual correctness from 39.2% to 79.2%, enabling fairer OSCE assessment.

AI.tldr: QAA is a multimodal framework that verifies examiner claims in VR-based pediatric OSCEs using temporal action alignment and LLMs, achieving 70% precision and 76.7% recall in detecting examiner errors, and improving factual correctness from 39.2% to 79.2%.
AI.motivation: OSCE scoring suffers from examiner subjectivity, fatigue, and cognitive bias. Traditional inter-rater statistics fail to explain error sources as they neither analyze examiner reasoning nor verify claims against actual events.
AI.method: QAA combines a constrained temporal action alignment model (for action localization and actor source attribution) with an LLM (to extract examiner claims and verify them against ground-truth records constructed from video, VR logs, and actor data).
AI.result: QAA achieves 99.2% ± 0.7% Actor F1, 93.4% ± 1.9% W@16 for temporal alignment, 70.0% precision and 76.7% recall in detecting examiner errors, improving factual correctness from 39.2% to 79.2%.
AI.conclusion: QAA enables fairer OSCE assessment by providing an automated, explainable mechanism to detect and correct examiner scoring errors in VR-based clinical exams.

title: Now You See the Hate: Adaptive View Retrieval for Hidden Hateful Illusions
summary: Hateful optical illusions expose a serious gap in current multimodal safety systems. On original-view hateful illusions, previous work shows that six moderation classifiers achieve at most 20.9 to 24.5% accuracy and nine state-of-the-art VLMs remain at or below 10.2% with illusion-aware prompting, leaving most hidden hate undetected. We formulate hidden hateful illusion detection as a perceptual retrieval problem and propose Adaptive View Retrieval. This retrieve-and-calibrate framework assembles a complementary view bank for the image and hidden-message templates, adaptively selects which views to trust, retrieves hidden-message identities, and calibrates whether the recovered evidence is harmful. On HatefulIllusion with a frozen CLIP encoder, Adaptive View Retrieval reaches 93.2% balanced accuracy on the held-out test split. It substantially outperforms original-view baselines and fixed single-transform filters across hate slangs, hate symbols, and visibility levels. The same design also surpasses official fine-tuned CLIP baselines, matches or exceeds human performance on IllusionMNIST, IllusionFashionMNIST, and IllusionAnimals, and outperforms zoom-out preprocessing on HC-Bench under the SemVink protocol. Together, these results show that robust multimodal moderation requires recovering hidden meaning before deciding whether it is harmful.

AI.tldr: Multimodal safety systems fail to detect hateful optical illusions (accuracy ≤24.5%). We propose Adaptive View Retrieval (AVR), a retrieve-and-calibrate framework that assembles complementary views, adaptively selects trusted views, retrieves hidden-message identities, and calibrates harmfulness. AVR achieves 93.2% balanced accuracy on HatefulIllusion, outperforming baselines and matching/exceeding human performance on multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Current multimodal safety systems have a serious gap: they fail to detect hateful content hidden in optical illusions, with accuracy as low as 10.2% even with illusion-aware prompting.
AI.method: Adaptive View Retrieval (AVR): a retrieve-and-calibrate framework that (1) assembles a complementary view bank for images and hidden-message templates, (2) adaptively selects which views to trust, (3) retrieves hidden-message identities, and (4) calibrates whether recovered evidence is harmful.
AI.result: 93.2% balanced accuracy on HatefulIllusion held-out test split with frozen CLIP encoder; substantially outperforms original-view baselines and fixed single-transform filters across hate slangs, symbols, and visibility levels; surpasses fine-tuned CLIP baselines; matches/exceeds human performance on IllusionMNIST, IllusionFashionMNIST, IllusionAnimals; outperforms zoom-out preprocessing on HC-Bench.
AI.conclusion: Robust multimodal moderation requires recovering hidden meaning before deciding whether it is harmful; AVR demonstrates that a retrieve-and-calibrate approach can bridge the gap left by current safety systems.

title: BRIDGE: Bottleneck-Aware Regulator-Set Inference and Diagnosis for Cooperative Gene Regulatory Recovery
summary:
Cooperative gene regulation often depends on groups of regulators acting jointly, but most gene regulatory network (GRN) inference methods output pairwise regulator-target rankings. We introduce Bottleneck-Aware Regulator-Set Inference and Diagnosis (BRIDGE), a framework for complete regulator-set recovery, and Targeted Recovery Attribution for Cooperative Evaluation (TRACE), a diagnostic suite that attributes failures to retrieval, set-level scoring, decoding, and evaluation bottlenecks.
  TRACE includes a leak-free mechanism-mismatch cooperativity stress test in which cooperative targets are generated by random nonlinear mechanisms rather than product interactions. This design avoids feature-mechanism circularity: Residual higher-order set scoring (Residual HOS2) operates on raw expression vectors without handcrafted product-correlation features. Across 30 matched seed-cooperativity settings, Residual HOS2 improves Jaccard similarity from 0.382 to 0.460, recall from 0.522 to 0.597, and exact recovery from 0.053 to 0.113 over a decomposable pairwise set scorer (PairS2), although exact recovery remains low.
  On SERGIO DS3, oracle retrieval and TRACE show that candidate coverage is necessary but insufficient because set-level misranking remains the dominant source of exact-recovery failure. PairS2 proposal followed by Residual HOS2 reranking reduces HOS2-scored candidate sets by 94-97% while largely preserving exact-recovery behavior. These results distinguish edge ranking, candidate retrieval, set-level scoring, and exact cooperative regulator-set recovery as separate objectives.

AI.tldr: BRIDGE and TRACE are frameworks for cooperative regulator-set recovery and diagnosis in gene regulatory networks, with Residual HOS2 improving set recovery over pairwise methods, though exact recovery remains challenging.
AI.motivation: Cooperative gene regulation involves groups of regulators acting jointly, but most GRN inference methods only output pairwise regulator-target rankings, failing to capture higher-order cooperative effects.
AI.method: BRIDGE (Bottleneck-Aware Regulator-Set Inference and Diagnosis) for complete regulator-set recovery; TRACE (Targeted Recovery Attribution for Cooperative Evaluation) diagnostic suite with a leak-free mechanism-mismatch cooperativity stress test; Residual HOS2 (Residual Higher-Order Set Scoring) operating on raw expression vectors without handcrafted product-correlation features.
AI.result: Across 30 matched seed-cooperativity settings, Residual HOS2 improves Jaccard similarity from 0.382 to 0.460, recall from 0.522 to 0.597, and exact recovery from 0.053 to 0.113 over PairS2. On SERGIO DS3, PairS2 proposal + Residual HOS2 reranking reduces HOS2-scored candidate sets by 94-97% while preserving exact-recovery behavior.
AI.conclusion: Edge ranking, candidate retrieval, set-level scoring, and exact cooperative regulator-set recovery are distinct objectives. Candidate coverage is necessary but insufficient; set-level misranking remains the dominant bottleneck for exact recovery.

title: On the Effectiveness of Pretraining for Graph Combinatorial Optimization
comment: This work was accepted to be presented at the Graph Signal Processing Workshop 2026
summary: This paper introduces a self-supervised pretraining framework for graph combinatorial optimization specifically designed to address the nature of routing problems like the Traveling Salesman Problem. By utilizing graph contrastive learning with geometric augmentations (specifically, rotations and axial reflections) the model is forced to learn invariant structural representations and global relative distance distributions. Results demonstrate that this pretraining strategy outperforms non-pretrained models across various problem scales. Notably, the hybrid strategy (combining rotation and reflection) achieved a 6.57% improvement in tour length for TSP1000, proving that geometric pretraining is an important inductive bias for effectively scaling neural solvers to high-dimensional instances.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a self-supervised pretraining framework using graph contrastive learning with geometric augmentations (rotations and axial reflections) for routing problems like TSP, achieving up to 6.57% improvement in tour length for TSP1000.
AI.motivation: To address the limitations of neural solvers for graph combinatorial optimization, specifically routing problems, by introducing a pretraining strategy that learns invariant structural representations and global relative distance distributions, enabling better scaling to high-dimensional instances.
AI.method: Self-supervised pretraining framework using graph contrastive learning with geometric augmentations (rotations and axial reflections) to enforce learning of invariant structural representations and global relative distance distributions.
AI.result: The pretraining strategy outperforms non-pretrained models across various problem scales. The hybrid rotation-reflection strategy achieved a 6.57% improvement in tour length for TSP1000.
AI.conclusion: Geometric pretraining serves as an important inductive bias for effectively scaling neural solvers to high-dimensional routing problem instances.

title: Graph Neural Network-based Algorithm Selection for the Traveling Salesman Problem: A Systematic Study of Cost and Rank Losses under Distinct Budget Regimes
comment: 23 pages, 6 figures, and 5 tables. Submitted to the European Journal of Operational Research
summary: Automated Algorithm Selection (AS) aims to improve problem-solving performance by selecting, for each problem instance, the most suitable algorithm from a predefined portfolio. This is particularly relevant to the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP), where solver performance is strongly instance-dependent. We introduce GNNAS-TSP, a Graph Neural Network (GNN)-based AS framework that learns TSP instance representations directly from raw graph data, avoiding manual feature engineering. GNNAS-TSP formulates AS as a joint cost-prediction and ranking task. We evaluate cost-based (mean squared error (MSE), mean absolute error (MAE), and Huber), rank-based (RankNet, ListNet, and LambdaRank), and hybrid learning objectives for a portfolio comprising Chained Lin-Kernighan, Edge Assembly Crossover, Lin-Kernighan-Helsgaun, Multiagent Optimization System, and Concorde. Experiments use fixed computational budgets of 10 and 60 seconds. On the held-out test set, the selected configurations improve on the Single Best Solver (SBS) in normalized solution cost at both budgets. For the 10s budget, AS achieves substantial and statistically significant cost improvement over SBS. Overall, the results suggest that GNNAS-TSP is a useful meta-solving strategy when exploitable variation exists across solver performance.

AI.tldr: GNNAS-TSP is a GNN-based automated algorithm selection framework for TSP that learns instance representations directly from graph data, formulating AS as joint cost-prediction and ranking. Using hybrid learning objectives and a portfolio of 5 solvers, it outperforms the Single Best Solver under fixed computational budgets (10s and 60s) on held-out test sets.
AI.motivation: Algorithm selection is critical for TSP due to strong instance-dependent solver performance, but existing approaches rely on manual feature engineering. The authors aim to automate feature learning and improve AS via GNNs.
AI.method: GNNAS-TSP uses a GNN to learn TSP instance representations directly from raw graph data. AS is formulated as a joint cost-prediction and ranking task. Three objective families are evaluated: cost-based (MSE, MAE, Huber), rank-based (RankNet, ListNet, LambdaRank), and hybrid variants. Portfolio includes Chained Lin-Kernighan, Edge Assembly Crossover, Lin-Kernighan-Helsgaun, Multiagent Optimization System, and Concorde.
AI.result: Under fixed budgets of 10s and 60s, GNNAS-TSP selected configurations outperform the Single Best Solver in normalized solution cost on held-out test sets. For the 10s budget, the improvement is substantial and statistically significant.
AI.conclusion: GNNAS-TSP is a useful meta-solving strategy for TSP when exploitable variation exists across solver performance.

title: Supra Cognitive Modes: A Routed Architecture for Agent Memory
summary: Agent-memory workloads mix direct factual lookup, relation-chain and current-state reasoning, and broad synthesis over long histories. We describe Supra Cognitive Modes (SCM), an architecture that maps explicit or automatically selected per-query modes to retrieval and synthesis payloads over one shared ingest substrate. A frozen semantic classifier and runtime gates dispatch queries among fused lexical and dense lookup, graph or iterative multi-hop handling, and stratified long-form synthesis. The substrate combines multi-granularity embeddings, extracted triples, fact-version metadata, and optional asynchronous enrichments. We characterize the deployed configuration on three benchmarks: Long-term Conversational Memory (LoCoMo; n = 1,986), MemoryAgentBench (MAB; n = 3,671), and LongMemEval (n = 500). The reference run records 84.87% on LoCoMo factoid categories and 68.61% on adversarial abstention, 61.49% on MAB across two repetitions, and 86.00% on LongMemEval. A repository-backed reproduction produces similar aggregate scores and supports task- and mode-conditioned failure analysis. Raw baseline outputs, aligned end-to-end timing for LoCoMo and LongMemEval, and complete token ledgers are unavailable; stored rows also omit some final runtime decisions. The results characterize one implemented routed configuration and its diagnostic failure patterns, while source inspection verifies the per-query control interface and shared-substrate design. Causal routing effects, efficiency gains, and statistical significance remain outside the available evidence.

AI.tldr: Supra Cognitive Modes (SCM) is an architecture that routes agent-memory queries through per-query modes (factual lookup, relational reasoning, long-form synthesis) over a shared ingest substrate, achieving 84.87% on LoCoMo factoids, 61.49% on MAB, and 86.00% on LongMemEval, though causal routing effects and efficiency gains remain unverified.
AI.motivation: Agent-memory workloads require diverse handling strategies (direct lookup, multi-hop reasoning, broad synthesis) that single retrieval approaches cannot optimally serve. A unified architecture that dynamically selects the appropriate mode per query is needed.
AI.method: SCM uses a frozen semantic classifier and runtime gates to dispatch queries among lexical/dense lookup, graph/iterative multi-hop reasoning, and stratified long-form synthesis, all over a shared ingest substrate combining multi-granularity embeddings, extracted triples, fact-version metadata, and optional async enrichments.
AI.result: 84.87% on LoCoMo factoid categories, 68.61% on adversarial abstention; 61.49% on MAB across two repetitions; 86.00% on LongMemEval. Repository-backed reproduction yields similar aggregate scores with task- and mode-conditioned failure analysis.
AI.conclusion: The results characterize one implemented routed configuration and its diagnostic failure patterns; source inspection verifies the per-query control interface and shared-substrate design. However, causal routing effects, efficiency gains, and statistical significance remain outside available evidence.

title: Delineate Anything v2: A Global Foundation Model for Field Delineation
summary: Accurate agricultural field boundary delineation at large scale is a foundational task for food security, supply chain transparency, and carbon accounting. While vision foundation models like SAM show remarkable zero-shot capabilities, they frequently fail in geospatial domains due to topological complexity, cropland texturing patterns, and a lack of physical scale awareness. In this work, we introduce Delineate Anything v2, a globally scalable foundation model designed specifically for wide-area field boundary mapping. We construct FBIS-73M, a 73-million-instance multi-resolution dataset spanning 61 countries. To address the pervasive issue of multi-field administrative parcel merging, we introduce a resolution-specific data curation pipeline that leverages topological image-space adaptation to homogenize merged parcels and strengthen weak physical boundaries. Furthermore, we establish a novel, manually curated evaluation benchmark covering 100 countries to assess independent zero-shot generalization. Our results show that Delineate Anything v2 surpasses the current state-of-the-art, including the Delineate Anything framework, by 0.284 mAP@0.5 (+103.3% relative gain), while maintaining execution speeds suitable for rapid national- and global-scale deployment, as demonstrated by nationwide mapping of Ukraine (603,000 km^2) in 5.4 hours on a consumer-grade workstation. Code, pre-trained weights, the FBIS-73M dataset, and ready-to-use national-scale vector boundary products are publicly available at https://github.com/Lavreniuk/Delineate-Anything.

AI.tldr: Delineate Anything v2 is a globally scalable foundation model for agricultural field boundary delineation, trained on a 73-million-instance dataset across 61 countries, that achieves state-of-the-art performance with a +103.3% relative gain in mAP@0.5 and can map entire countries (e.g., Ukraine's 603,000 km² in 5.4 hours) on consumer-grade hardware.
AI.motivation: Accurate large-scale agricultural field boundary delineation is critical for food security, supply chain transparency, and carbon accounting, but existing vision foundation models like SAM fail in geospatial domains due to topological complexity, cropland texturing patterns, and lack of physical scale awareness.
AI.method: The authors introduce Delineate Anything v2, built on FBIS-73M (a 73-million-instance multi-resolution dataset across 61 countries). They propose a resolution-specific data curation pipeline using topological image-space adaptation to homogenize merged parcels and strengthen weak physical boundaries. They also establish a manually curated 100-country evaluation benchmark for zero-shot generalization assessment.
AI.result: Delineate Anything v2 surpasses prior state-of-the-art (including Delineate Anything) by 0.284 mAP@0.5 (+103.3% relative gain) and enables mapping Ukraine (603,000 km²) in 5.4 hours on a consumer-grade workstation.
AI.conclusion: The model achieves superior zero-shot generalization and practical scalability for national- to global-scale deployment, with all resources publicly released.

title: Mark, Don't Erase: Token Inoculation for Dual-Use Knowledge in LLMs
summary: Safety interventions on dual-use knowledge typically choose between destroying hazardous content (e.g., unlearning, filtering) and suppressing it at the output layer (e.g., refusal training); both pay a tax in adjacent-domain competence or over-refusal. We argue that the right operation is conditioning, not reduction: we show that hazardous knowledge can be retained in the model and behaviorally gated by a privileged control token. Our method, Token Inoculation, introduces a binding-and-branching approach. First, during continued pre-training, we mark hazardous content by inserting a special token alongside dual-use documents, so the model binds the marker to the underlying semantics of the hazardous domain. Second, during supervised fine-tuning, we teach the model to answer hazardous queries correctly when the special token is present and to refuse them when it is absent, thereby enabling selective refusal without removing dual-use knowledge. On hazardous domain (e.g., WMDP-Bio), Token Inoculation reduces accuracy from 79% to 18% while retaining 93% of the base-model's benign-domain performance (e.g., MMLU), achieving the best safety-utility trade-off against unlearning and refusal-tuning baselines across 1B-14B model scales. We further show that refusal selectivity is controllable through the quality of the conditioning signal and that domain-specific semantic binding during pre-training is critical for the conditional behavior to generalize beyond memorized triggers. Our results suggest that safety alignment is better cast as a conditioning problem than a forgetting one: behavioral control is more precise when sensitive knowledge is retained under controlled access than when it is destroyed.

AI.tldr: Token Inoculation retains hazardous knowledge in models while enabling selective refusal via a control token, achieving better safety-utility trade-offs than unlearning or refusal tuning.
AI.motivation: Existing safety interventions (unlearning, refusal training) degrade adjacent-domain competence or cause over-refusal; the authors argue for conditioning over reduction to preserve dual-use knowledge while controlling its access.
AI.method: A two-stage approach: (1) continued pre-training with a special token inserted alongside dual-use documents for semantic binding, and (2) supervised fine-tuning where the model answers correctly with the token present and refuses without it.
AI.result: On WMDP-Bio, accuracy drops from 79% to 18% while retaining 93% of benign MMLU performance, outperforming unlearning and refusal-tuning baselines across 1B-14B model scales.
AI.conclusion: Safety alignment is better framed as a conditioning problem than a forgetting problem; retaining knowledge under controlled access enables more precise behavioral control than destroying it.

title: OpenRTAG: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Robust Text-Attributed Graph Learning under Data Quality Degradation
summary: Text-attributed graphs (TAGs) are an important graph data form that combine relational structure with rich node text. However, real-world TAGs are often imperfect, with quality issues arising from text, structure, and labels, and typically manifesting as sparsity, noise, and imbalance. These dimensions define nine representative degradation scenarios that can substantially affect TAG learning. Although prior studies have explored specific mitigation strategies, existing evidence remains fragmented across degradation types, datasets, tasks, and model families, leaving TAG robustness insufficiently understood. To address this gap, we present OpenRTAG, a robustness benchmark for text-attributed graph learning. OpenRTAG organizes TAG quality issues into a unified 3 * 3 taxonomy and supports standardized evaluation across nine TAG datasets and three downstream tasks. It systematically evaluates scenario validity and model sensitivity, compares traditional GNNs, LLM-GNNs, and a representative GFM, investigates the effectiveness, efficiency, and robustness of scenario-matched baselines, and further examines model behavior under composite degradation scenarios. OpenRTAG provides a standardized testbed for understanding robustness in TAG learning under realistic low-quality settings.

AI.tldr: OpenRTAG is a unified robustness benchmark for text-attributed graph learning that organizes quality issues (sparsity, noise, imbalance) across text, structure, and labels into a 3×3 taxonomy, evaluates models across 9 datasets and 3 tasks, and systematically assesses traditional GNNs, LLM-GNNs, and GFMs under realistic degraded scenarios.
AI.motivation: Real-world TAGs suffer from quality issues (sparsity, noise, imbalance) across text, structure, and labels, but existing studies are fragmented across degradation types, datasets, tasks, and model families, leaving TAG robustness insufficiently understood.
AI.method: OpenRTAG proposes a unified 3×3 taxonomy covering text/structure/label × sparsity/noise/imbalance, supports standardized evaluation across 9 TAG datasets and 3 downstream tasks, and systematically evaluates scenario validity, model sensitivity, and baseline effectiveness under both single and composite degradation scenarios.
AI.result: The benchmark systematically compares traditional GNNs, LLM-GNNs, and a representative GFM, evaluates scenario-matched baselines in terms of effectiveness, efficiency, and robustness, and further examines model behavior under composite degradation scenarios.
AI.conclusion: OpenRTAG provides a standardized testbed for understanding robustness in TAG learning under realistic low-quality settings, enabling principled comparison and future progress.

title: Context-structured Video Anomaly Detection with Large Vision-Language Models
summary: Training video anomaly detectors is challenging due to the difficulty and cost of annotating diverse and rare abnormal events. Although recent large vision-language models enable training-free inference, existing approaches mostly rely on holistic inference over sampled video and may miss context-specific anomaly cues. In this paper, we present CSI-VAD, a training-free video anomaly detector that identifies abnormal events across diverse contexts. The key idea is to decompose each video into three distinct contexts (environment, objects, time) and perform context-specific inference in separate branches. Because we ground anomaly judgments solely in context-specific visual cues, we do not require predefined text prompts describing abnormal events or dataset-specific tuning. Experiments on UCF-Crime and UBnormal show that CSI-VAD consistently improves over the direct holistic baseline and achieves competitive performance against existing methods, showing the advantage of structured context decomposition for training-free video anomaly detection.

AI.tldr: CSI-VAD is a training-free video anomaly detector that decomposes video into three contexts (environment, objects, time) for context-specific inference, achieving competitive performance without predefined prompts or dataset tuning.
AI.motivation: Training video anomaly detectors is challenging due to difficulty and cost of annotating diverse and rare abnormal events; existing training-free approaches rely on holistic inference and may miss context-specific anomaly cues.
AI.method: Decomposes each video into three contexts (environment, objects, time) and performs context-specific inference in separate branches, grounding anomaly judgments solely in context-specific visual cues without predefined text prompts or dataset-specific tuning.
AI.result: CSI-VAD consistently improves over direct holistic baseline and achieves competitive performance against existing methods on UCF-Crime and UBnormal datasets.
AI.conclusion: Structured context decomposition is advantageous for training-free video anomaly detection, enabling identification of abnormal events across diverse contexts without dataset-specific tuning.

title: Comparative Study of Multi-Agent Actor-Critic Algorithms in Parameterized Action Reinforcement Learning
summary: Parameterized action reinforcement learning has shown strong performance in environments requiring both discrete action selection and continuous parameterization. Prior work established the effectiveness of single-agent actor-critic algorithms - Greedy Actor-Critic (GAC), Soft Actor-Critic (SAC), and Truncated Quantile Critics (TQC) - on benchmark parameterized action tasks, but their extension to multi-agent settings remains largely unexplored. This paper presents a comparative study of shared-experience multi-agent extensions of these algorithms: Multi-Agent Greedy Actor-Critic (MAGAC), Multi-Agent Soft Actor-Critic (MASAC), and Multi-Agent Truncated Quantile Critics (MATQC). Rather than following the centralized training, decentralized execution (CTDE) paradigm, the proposed framework uses multiple independent actor-critic agents that share a replay buffer while maintaining separate policy and value networks. We evaluate the algorithms on the Platform-v0 and Goal-v0 benchmarks against their single-agent counterparts, using three-, five-, and ten-agent configurations to assess scalability. Performance is measured by average evaluation return and training time across ten independent runs, with one-way ANOVA and Tukey HSD post-hoc tests used to assess statistical significance. Results show that the multi-agent framework consistently improves Greedy Actor-Critic performance, while MASAC and MATQC show comparatively modest gains over their single-agent versions. Increasing the number of agents beyond five yields limited additional performance while substantially raising computational cost, particularly for MAGAC. These results highlight a trade-off between learning performance and computational efficiency, offering insight into the scalability of shared-experience multi-agent actor-critic methods for parameterized action reinforcement learning.

AI.tldr: This paper extends single-agent parameterized action RL algorithms (GAC, SAC, TQC) to multi-agent settings via a shared-experience framework (MAGAC, MASAC, MATQC) with independent networks and a shared replay buffer. Evaluated on Platform-v0 and Goal-v0 with 3, 5, and 10 agents, MAGAC shows consistent gains, while MASAC and MATQC yield modest improvements. Beyond 5 agents, returns saturate and computational cost rises sharply.
AI.motivation: Prior work demonstrated the effectiveness of single-agent actor-critic algorithms (GAC, SAC, TQC) for parameterized action RL, but their extension to multi-agent settings remained largely unexplored.
AI.method: Proposes shared-experience multi-agent extensions (MAGAC, MASAC, MATQC) using independent actor-critic agents with separate policy/value networks but a shared replay buffer, departing from the CTDE paradigm. Evaluated on Platform-v0 and Goal-v0 benchmarks with 3, 5, and 10 agents. Statistical significance assessed via one-way ANOVA and Tukey HSD tests.
AI.result: MAGAC consistently outperforms its single-agent counterpart. MASAC and MATQC show modest gains. Increasing agents beyond 5 yields limited additional performance but substantially raises computational cost, especially for MAGAC.
AI.conclusion: There is a trade-off between learning performance and computational efficiency in shared-experience multi-agent actor-critic methods for parameterized action RL.

title: Advancing Multimodal Fusion on Heterogeneous Medical Data with Hybrid Geometry Attention
comment: ACM SIGKDD Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining (KDD 2026)
summary: Multimodal fusion learning (MFL) has shown great potential in the medical domain, where we are faced with disparate data modalities such as imaging, clinical records, and omics. However, existing MFL strategies face several major challenges. First, they struggle to capture complex cross-modal interactions effectively, which in turn limits performance improvements. Second, they incur high computational costs, restricting their applicability in resource-constrained healthcare AI applications. Finally, they are often designed and evaluated for narrow, fixed modality configurations (e.g., imaging-only, or specific pairs such as image and omics), which limits evidence of their adaptability and generalizability to broader collections of heterogeneous medical modalities. To address these challenges, we propose a novel MFL framework - Cascaded Unified Representation Learning for Efficient Fusion Network (CURE) - a lightweight and scalable framework that progressively integrates various modalities through a novel efficient Hybrid Geometry Aware Fusion layer (HyFuse), where each HyFuse layer is sequentially learned for each modality, making the framework adaptable and generalizable. Within HyFuse, an efficient residual convolution module captures rich multi-scale features to ensure cost-effective learning, while a hybrid-space aware attention mixer learns coarse-to-fine structural cues to better preserve cross-modal relationships. Complementary learnable late-fusion and shared information refinement modules are then employed to learn robust modality-order-invariant shared representations, which in turn yields consistent performance improvements. Extensive evaluations on 16 public datasets show that CURE outperforms leading multimodal fusion methods, boosting performance by up to 3.97% and lowering computational costs by up to 87.8%, ensuring more effective and reliable predictions.

AI.tldr: CURE is a lightweight and scalable multimodal fusion learning framework that progressively integrates medical modalities through efficient Hybrid Geometry Aware Fusion layers (HyFuse), achieving up to 3.97% performance improvement while reducing computational costs by up to 87.8% across 16 public datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing MFL strategies struggle to capture complex cross-modal interactions, incur high computational costs, and are limited to narrow, fixed modality configurations, lacking adaptability and generalizability to heterogeneous medical modalities.
AI.method: CURE uses Cascaded Unified Representation Learning with a novel Hybrid Geometry Aware Fusion layer (HyFuse), which includes an efficient residual convolution module for multi-scale features and a hybrid-space aware attention mixer for coarse-to-fine structural cues, followed by learnable late-fusion and shared information refinement modules for modality-order-invariant representations.
AI.result: On 16 public datasets, CURE outperforms leading multimodal fusion methods by up to 3.97% and reduces computational costs by up to 87.8%.
AI.conclusion: CURE provides a more effective, reliable, and computationally efficient solution for multimodal fusion learning in healthcare AI, with strong generalizability across heterogeneous medical modalities.

title: Exposure-Based Reinforcement Learning to Rank
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) methods for learning-to-rank (LTR) can optimize (almost) any ranking goal, e.g., from precision or discounted cumulative gain to fairness-of-exposure or ranking distillation. However, standard RL is ineffective and computationally costly due to the enormous action space in LTR settings. Existing methods reach computational efficiency through custom gradient computation algorithms, but they are very complex to implement and often clash with auto-differentiation. Consequently, existing RL for LTR is not attractive to many practitioners. We reconsider RL for LTR while actively avoiding reliance on custom gradients. Contrary to the existing approaches, we focus on variance reduction and GPU computation. In doing so, we discover that high sample-efficiency can be reached through baseline corrections and partial marginalization. Furthermore, we propose an abstraction that places gradient estimation behind a document-exposure distribution, this enables seamless plug-and-play integration with auto-differentiation. Thereby, one only has to implement a loss as a differentiable function of exposure and RL for LTR can optimize it using auto-differentiation. Our experimental results reveal that our new exposure-based RL for LTR approach converges considerably faster and at significantly higher ranking performance than existing custom gradients, with no additional costs in computation time when using GPUs. In contrast, existing custom gradients result in severe stability issues when converging over many epochs, which never occur for our methods. Thus, we considerably improve RL for LTR methodology by increasing its effectiveness, efficiency, and ease of application.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an exposure-based RL for LTR approach that avoids custom gradient algorithms, instead using variance reduction, baseline corrections, partial marginalization, and GPU computation to achieve faster convergence, higher ranking performance, and better stability than existing custom-gradient methods, while integrating seamlessly with auto-differentiation.
AI.motivation: Standard RL for LTR suffers from enormous action spaces, making it computationally costly and ineffective. Existing solutions rely on complex custom gradient algorithms that clash with auto-differentiation and are unattractive to practitioners.
AI.method: The method avoids custom gradients by focusing on variance reduction and GPU computation. It employs baseline corrections and partial marginalization for high sample-efficiency, and introduces an abstraction that places gradient estimation behind a document-exposure distribution for seamless auto-differentiation integration.
AI.result: The exposure-based RL approach converges considerably faster and achieves significantly higher ranking performance than existing custom-gradient methods, with no additional computation costs on GPUs. Existing custom gradients exhibit severe stability issues over many epochs, while the proposed method remains stable.
AI.conclusion: The new exposure-based RL for LTR methodology improves effectiveness, efficiency, and ease of application, making RL for LTR more practical and accessible.

title: Sequential Learner Modeling Using Multi-Relational Graph Convolutional Networks
summary: User modeling is a critical task in a variety of personalized systems. Recognizing their effectiveness in learning from graph-structured data, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), particularly Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs), are increasingly employed for user modeling. However, existing approaches typically treat different relation types in a graph as homogeneous, limiting their ability to capture richer semantics and construct more informative user models. While multi-relational GNNs (MR-GNNs) have been adopted for representation learning and recommendation, their application for user modeling remains unexplored. Moreover, existing GNN-based user modeling approaches ignore the user interaction sequence. To address these research gaps, in this work we propose MR-ConceptGCN, a novel fully unsupervised approach focused on concept-based sequential learner modeling using multi-relational GCNs (MR-GCNs). MR-ConceptGCN effecively combines Personal Knowledge Graphs (PKGs), MR-GCNs, and the pre-trained language model SBERT to obtain enhanced relation- and semantic-aware representations of the PKG items. The enriched embeddings of the knowledge concepts that a learner did not understand when interacting with learning materials in CourseMapper are then used to construct a sequential learner model that combines long-term and short-term learner interactions. We report the results of an online user study (n = 31), demonstrating the benefits of MR-ConceptGCN in terms of several important user-centric aspects including accuracy, usefulness, diversity, and satisfaction with an educational recommender system.

AI.tldr: MR-ConceptGCN is a fully unsupervised approach for concept-based sequential learner modeling that combines Personal Knowledge Graphs, multi-relational Graph Convolutional Networks, and SBERT to capture rich semantics and interaction sequences, outperforming existing methods in educational recommender systems as shown in an online user study (n=31).
AI.motivation: Existing GNN-based user modeling approaches treat relation types as homogeneous, missing richer semantics; multi-relational GNNs have not been applied to user modeling; current methods ignore user interaction sequences.
AI.method: MR-ConceptGCN integrates Personal Knowledge Graphs (PKGs), multi-relational GCNs (MR-GCNs), and the pre-trained language model SBERT to produce relation- and semantic-aware representations, then uses enriched embeddings of misunderstood knowledge concepts to construct a sequential learner model combining long-term and short-term interactions.
AI.result: Online user study (n=31) showed benefits in accuracy, usefulness, diversity, and satisfaction for an educational recommender system.
AI.conclusion: Multi-relational and sequential modeling enhances user modeling quality; MR-ConceptGCN provides a viable unsupervised solution for personalized educational systems.

title: FlexiAvatar: Unified 3D Gaussian Human Avatars Under Arbitrary Body Visibility
summary: Reconstructing animatable 3D human avatars from monocular video is a fundamental problem in computer vision with broad applications in AR/VR and digital content creation. Existing approaches typically couple parametric body models with neural rendering or 3D Gaussian splatting and optimize all body regions jointly from short videos, which often degrades fidelity in the visible areas. To overcome this limitation, we introduce FlexiAvatar, a unified framework that explicitly optimizes only the visible body regions, effectively eliminating artifacts arising from unobserved limbs. Our method integrates occlusion-robust SMPL-X tracking with part-specific residual refinement to capture high-frequency geometric and appearance details. To complete entirely unseen regions (e.g., back views), we leverage a diffusion-based approach to generate texture consistent with the observed appearance. Experiments on full-body (NeuMan, ZJU-MoCap, WildAvatar), upper/half-body (talk-show clips), and head-only (INSTA) inputs show that FlexiAvatar delivers consistently higher reconstruction quality, outperforming state-of-the-art methods by an average PSNR improvement of approximately 3% across datasets. Finally, by restricting optimization to observed regions, our method reduces the effective number of Gaussians that must be optimized and rendered, leading to reduced runtime and memory overhead in partial-visibility scenarios.

AI.tldr: FlexiAvatar reconstructs animatable 3D avatars from monocular video by optimizing only visible body regions, integrating occlusion-robust SMPL-X tracking with part-specific residual refinement and diffusion-based texture completion for unseen areas, achieving ~3% PSNR improvement over SOTA while reducing computational overhead.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches couple parametric body models with neural rendering or 3D Gaussian splatting, optimizing all body regions jointly from short videos, which degrades fidelity in visible areas due to artifacts from unobserved limbs.
AI.method: (1) Occlusion-robust SMPL-X tracking with part-specific residual refinement for high-frequency geometry and appearance details; (2) explicit optimization of only visible body regions to eliminate artifacts from unobserved limbs; (3) diffusion-based texture generation for entirely unseen regions (e.g., back views).
AI.result: Consistently higher reconstruction quality across full-body, upper/half-body, and head-only inputs; ~3% average PSNR improvement over SOTA; reduced runtime and memory overhead in partial-visibility scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Restricting optimization to observed regions improves fidelity while reducing computational cost, offering a unified framework for diverse input types.

title: Stale but Stable: Staleness-Adaptive Trust Regions for Stabilizing Asynchronous Reinforcement Learning
summary:
Asynchronous reinforcement learning improves throughput by decoupling rollout generation from optimization, but staleness is an inevitable byproduct compounded by policy lag, engine delays, and mixture-of-experts routing. From a trust-region perspective, this mismatch is critical: training-inference divergence governs approximation error in finite-horizon bounds, whereas PPO clipping only gates sampled outward updates, acting as a sampled surrogate rather than a full-policy constraint. As a result, high-staleness updates remain weakly controlled in the asynchronous regime where stale rollouts matter most.
  We introduce the Staleness-Adaptive Trust Region (SAT), which uses the detached sampled log-ratio as a practical staleness proxy, identifies high-mismatch tails within each batch via staleness-based kernel scaling, and contracts only the sign-selected endpoint of the nominal PPO interval. This preserves baseline behavior on ordinary tokens while enforcing more conservative updates on newly intercepted outward bands. We prove local interval containment and pointwise pessimism relative to PPO, showing how the adaptive rule reshapes update geometry under heterogeneous staleness.
  We evaluate SAT in a decoupled asynchronous RL setup built on Qwen3-30B-A3B-Base, using SGLang as the inference engine and Megatron for training. In this setting, SAT-GSPO w/ R3 achieves the best observed AIME24 avg@8, reaching 35.83 at lag 1 and 34.79 at lag 8, while SAT-GSPO reaches 34.17 at lag 1. Adaptive clipping and routing replay act as complementary stabilizers targeting mismatch tails and routing inconsistency, respectively. Overall, aligning clip intervals with staleness heterogeneity effectively stabilizes asynchronous RL.

AI.tldr: SAT introduces a staleness-adaptive trust region method that uses detached log-ratios as a staleness proxy and contracts only the sign-selected endpoint of the PPO clipping interval to stabilize asynchronous RL with heterogeneous staleness, achieving 35.83 AIME24 avg@8 on Qwen3-30B-A3B-Base.
AI.motivation: Asynchronous RL decouples rollout generation from optimization to improve throughput, but introduces staleness—compounded by policy lag, engine delays, and MoE routing—which PPO's clipping handles poorly as it only gates sampled outward updates rather than imposing full-policy constraints, leaving high-staleness updates weakly controlled.
AI.method: SAT uses the detached sampled log-ratio as a staleness proxy, identifies high-mismatch tails via staleness-based kernel scaling, and contracts only the sign-selected endpoint of the PPO interval. This preserves baseline behavior on ordinary tokens while enforcing conservative updates on high-staleness bands, with theoretical guarantees of local interval containment and pointwise pessimism.
AI.result: On Qwen3-30B-A3B-Base with SGLang+Megatron, SAT-GSPO w/ R3 achieves AIME24 avg@8 of 35.83 at lag 1 and 34.79 at lag 8, while SAT-GSPO reaches 34.17 at lag 1, demonstrating effective stabilization under heterogeneous staleness.
AI.conclusion: Aligning clip intervals with staleness heterogeneity effectively stabilizes asynchronous RL; adaptive clipping (targeting mismatch tails) and routing replay (targeting routing inconsistency) act as complementary stabilizers.

title: BioSecBench-Surveillance: A Verifiable Benchmark for AI Agents in Pathogen Genomic Surveillance
summary: As pathogen genomic surveillance scales, the bottleneck is shifting from data generation to analysis. We present BioSecBench-Surveillance, a verifiable benchmark of 100 evaluations testing whether AI agents can infer the right analysis pipeline from raw sequencing data and surveillance context. Each evaluation gives an agent only the data and context a human analyst would have, then grades its structured answer deterministically. The tasks span seven categories, from taxonomic classification to genetic-engineering detection, across diverse sample types and sequencing technologies.
